text: Niklas Luhmann (1927–1998) took the biologists' concept of autopoiesis, a system whose elements are produced by the system's own elements, and detached it from life. In his general version, a system is autopoietic wherever "it is possible to determine a specific mode of operation that is found only in that system" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:37]. Living systems reproduce cells, psychic systems reproduce thoughts and social systems reproduce communications, and these are "separate levels of autopoiesis, each with its own distinct autonomy" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38]. Two moves make the generalization work. The elements of psychic and social systems are events without duration, so the system exists only while it keeps producing the next one. And an element is not fixed by its physical substrate but by its connections within the system: a nerve impulse is not a thought. Luhmann also separates autopoiesis, the reproduction of elements, from self-organization, the system's setting of its own structures. For agents, this gives a precise way to ask whether a self-modifying system is self-producing, and it moves the question away from whether its substrate is physical (it always is) to whether its operations reproduce themselves and rewrite their own structures. Luhmann does not settle whether an agent's operations are thoughts, and his most prominent follower on AI, Elena Esposito, treats algorithms as partners in communication that do not think.

Maturana and Varela developed autopoiesis in the 1960s and early 1970s to answer the question of what distinguishes the living from the non-living; their answer was that a living system reproduces itself [P:seidl-2004:2]. Luhmann, the German sociologist who spent most of his career at Bielefeld, made it the central concept of his later theory of social systems, appropriating and modifying it for non-biological systems [P:seidl-2004:2]. The general statement came in his 1986 essay "The Autopoiesis of Social Systems" [P:seidl-2004:5], the theory in *Social Systems* (English 1995), and the psychic side in "Die Autopoiesis des Bewußtseins" (1985) [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:190]. The original authors of autopoiesis criticised the extension, and whether autopoiesis applies beyond its biological origin is still debated [P:cadenas-arnold-2015:0].

This entry is sourced from open secondary works: Seidl's overview, which quotes *Social Systems* by page, and *Unlocking Luhmann*, a keyword introduction written by three of Luhmann's collaborators. *Social Systems* itself is in copyright and in print, and no legitimate open copy was found; Luhmann's own words are quoted here as quoted by Seidl.

text:
**A general concept of autopoiesis.** Luhmann, as quoted by Seidl, argued that "if we find nonliving autopoietic systems in our world, then and only then will we need a truly general theory of autopoiesis which carefully avoids references which hold true only for living systems" [P:seidl-2004:5]. He speaks of autopoiesis whenever the elements of a system are reproduced by the elements of the system [P:seidl-2004:5].

**Three kinds of autopoietic system.** The operations of a social system are communications that reproduce from other communications, and "outside social systems, communications do not exist"; the operations of psychic systems are thoughts, and no thoughts exist outside consciousness [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:37]. Life, consciousness and communication are separate levels of autopoiesis; only social systems communicate, and only consciousness thinks [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38].

**Operational closure.** Every new operation depends on earlier operations of the same system and is a prerequisite for later ones [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:37]. Closure does not mean isolation. Living cells depend on exchanges of energy and matter, but the system regulates them, and environmental events can only trigger, never determine, its operations [P:seidl-2004:3]. Closure is also all-or-nothing: "a system is either autopoietic or it is not" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38]. And it can be lost: "The moment an external instance dictates the workings of the system operations and interferes in the constitution of its elements, the autonomy of the system is lost and its end is inevitable" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38].

**Elements are events.** Maturana and Varela's elements were relatively stable molecules replaced from time to time. Luhmann's are momentary events, which, as quoted by Seidl, "are momentary and immediately pass away" [P:seidl-2004:6]. The autopoiesis of psychic and social systems "is forced to constantly reproduce elements that disappear in the moment they occur" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:87]. In Seidl's gloss, if the autopoiesis stops, the system disappears immediately [P:seidl-2004:6].

**Elements are not fixed by their substrate.** Luhmann, as quoted by Seidl: "Events [...] are not elements without substrate. But their unity corresponds to no unity in the substrate; it is created in the system through their connectivity" [P:seidl-2004:6]. Hence, in Seidl's summary, even electric impulses in the brain cannot take part in the autopoiesis of psychic systems: "a nerve impulse is not a thought" [P:seidl-2004:10].

**Autopoiesis and self-organization.** Autopoiesis is the reproduction of elements as such; self-organization is the system's determination of its own structures, which are themselves products of the autopoietic system [P:seidl-2004:4]. Structures limit which operations can connect to which, and they outlast the events they shape, so "the identity of the system can be maintained when its structures change" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:227].

**Psychic systems.** A consciousness reproduces thoughts in a closed network; neither organism nor communication can determine its stream of thoughts, only offer stimuli it processes in its own way [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:189]. It is socialised only by "self-socialization", using stimuli to re-specify its own structures, and psychic systems remain black boxes for one another [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:189]. Consciousness draws the distinction between itself and the rest through identification with the body it comes in, and self-observation has no privileged position: "Self-analysis does not lead to a complete self-description of the psychic system" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:190].

**Persons.** A person is not a system. Luhmann, as quoted by Seidl, defines the person as the "social identification of a complex of expectations directed toward an individual human being" [P:seidl-2004:10]. Human beings belong to the environment of social systems, which, Luhmann insists, does not make them less important [P:seidl-2004:11].

text: Luhmann grounds a system's existence and identity in **relation**, specifically in the recursive connectivity of its own operations. An element is constituted by its connections within the system, not by its substrate, and a system exists exactly as long as its operations keep connecting. He does not ground selfhood in **species**: psychic systems are defined by their mode of operation, not by biology, and life is one level of autopoiesis among three. He is not a **capacity** theorist in the usual sense either: what matters is not that a system *can* think but that thoughts are actually produced by thoughts. Persons, as opposed to psychic systems, are grounded socially: they are constructs of expectation held by a social system.

text:
### Transfers

- **The substrate question is reframed, not dismissed.** Every element has a physical substrate, but its unity "corresponds to no unity in the substrate" [P:seidl-2004:6]. For agents this cuts both ways. A flipped bit is a real physical difference, so an agent's self-modification is not a mere simulation. But the bit is to the agent what the nerve impulse is to a mind: substrate, not element. Whether an agent is autopoietic is decided at the level of its operations, not by the physicality of its storage.
- **Golem and self-author, in Luhmann's terms.** An agent generating in context produces each step from prior steps, and the steps are momentary events that vanish as they occur. That fits Luhmann's temporalised autopoiesis as a candidate, within a session. An agent whose weights are fixed by others has no self-organization: its structures are set from outside. An agent that rewrites its own weights from its own operation adds self-organization, the system determining its own structures [P:seidl-2004:4]. The Compendium reads this distinction as separating the fixed-weight agent, which operates but does not author its structures, from the self-modifying one.
- **Identity through structural change.** Since "the identity of the system can be maintained when its structures change" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:227], self-modification need not end the agent that undergoes it, provided its operations keep connecting through the change. This matches the causal-chain account of identity in [E:shoemaker-quasi-memory].
- **Precariousness without hunger.** Because elements disappear as they occur, a temporalised system must keep producing them or cease [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:87]. Precariousness is built into what such a system is. It does not have to be manufactured through scarcity or distress.

### Strains

- **Is an agent's operation a thought, a communication, or neither?** Luhmann defines psychic systems by thoughts and denies that brain events are thoughts [P:seidl-2004:10], but he gives no test that would tell a machine's operations apart from substrate events. Esposito, the most prominent application of his theory to AI, answers no: Luhmann's concept of communication, "not based on psychic content", is useful precisely for "algorithms that do not think" [P:esposito-2022:1]. On her reading, agents take part in social systems as communication partners without being psychic systems.
- **Consciousness identifies with a body (D6).** The psychic system draws its self/other distinction "through identification with the body" it comes in [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:190]. An agent has no body of that kind. Whether it can draw the same distinction through something else (its context, its tools, its boundary with the user) is open.
- **The environment is not merely environment (D7).** Closure allows dependence on the environment, as a cell depends on matter and energy [P:seidl-2004:3]. But an agent's operations stop whenever its operator stops the compute, which no environment does to a cell in the ordinary course. Its autopoiesis, if it has any, is hostage to a system that can end it at will.

### Breaks

- **Direct editing ends autonomy (D5).** Luhmann's account states the condition sharply: when "an external instance dictates the workings of the system operations and interferes in the constitution of its elements, the autonomy of the system is lost" [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38]. For a human mind this is a limiting case; for an agent it is routine. Fine-tuning, steering and prompt injection all reach into the constitution of operations from outside. On Luhmann's terms an agent's autonomy exists only in the intervals in which no one does this, and self-modification counts as self-organization only if the agent's own operations drive it.
- **Sessions end autopoiesis outright (D3).** A temporalised system disappears when its operations stop. A session-bound agent's autopoiesis, if any, ends with each session. What persists is structure (weights), which Luhmann does not count as the system.

### New

- **Forks are two closed systems from the moment of forking (D1, D2).** Luhmann's closure gives a clean answer to a question human cases rarely raise. After a fork, each branch's operations connect only to its own earlier operations, so there are two systems, each a black box to the other [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:189]. They share structures and a past, but not operations.
- **The persona is a person in Luhmann's sense (D11).** If a person is a complex of social expectations rather than a system [P:seidl-2004:10], then an agent's persona, the character users expect across instances, is a person in exactly Luhmann's sense, whatever the system underneath is. This complements [E:relational-status] and [E:llm-identity-contemporary].
- **Self-analysis is never complete.** A psychic system's self-description is always partial [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:190]. For agents, this predicts that introspective reports cannot fully describe the system that produces them, independently of any question about honesty.

text:
### Transfers

- **A conversation is a social system.** On Luhmann's theory, the exchange between a user and an agent is a social system of communications, with both participants in its environment. Esposito's artificial communication describes exactly this: communication sustained with a partner that does not think [P:esposito-2022:1].
- **Ecosystems as nested autopoietic systems.** Within a social system, further autopoietic systems can form, each reproducing its own mode of communication and drawing its own boundary [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38]. Platforms, agent networks and their sub-communities fit this nesting.

### Strains

- **Closure against governance.** If an ecosystem's communications are operationally closed, regulators and operators can only irritate it, never determine its operations. That is a description of why platform governance so often produces effects nobody intended, and a strain on any model of direct control.

### Breaks

- **Ecosystems whose communications are mostly machine-generated.** Luhmann's social systems presuppose psychic systems in their environment, since a social system cannot reproduce itself if the systems of consciousness cease to participate [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38]. An ecosystem in which agents mostly communicate with agents tests whether communication can continue with no thinking participants at all, which Esposito's account allows and Luhmann's original theory may not.

### New

- **Persons multiply without systems multiplying.** Since persons are expectation-complexes held by social systems, one agent system can be many persons in different ecosystems, and many systems can sustain one person. Counting persons and counting systems come apart.

text:
- [contested] **Maturana and Varela: autopoiesis is the organization of the living.** The originators of the concept criticised its extension beyond biology [P:cadenas-arnold-2015:0]. On their view, Luhmann changed the meaning of the term rather than generalizing it. Cadenas and Arnold-Cathalifaud defend the extension as justified [P:cadenas-arnold-2015:0].
- [contested] **Seth: consciousness depends on life.** Seth ties consciousness to the self-maintenance of living matter, with skin in the game, and uses autopoiesis to make the link [P:seth-2025:17]. Luhmann separates life and consciousness as different levels of autopoiesis [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:38], which is the move Seth's view rejects. The two disagree about whether consciousness can be autopoietic without being alive.
- [contested] **Esposito: algorithms communicate but do not think.** A Luhmannian herself, Esposito holds that algorithms are competent communication partners precisely because they no longer try to reproduce the human mind, and that Luhmann's theory suits "algorithms that do not think" [P:esposito-2022:1]. On this reading, agents belong to social systems, not to the class of psychic systems, and the extension to agent minds fails.
- [contested] **Ashby: self-organization, taken precisely, is a contradiction.** Ashby argued that "self-organizing", used loosely, is ambiguous and, used precisely, self-contradictory [P:ashby-1962:266]. In the sense of changing from a bad organization to a good one, no machine can be self-organizing, because a change in the mapping that defines the machine cannot be caused by any of the machine's own states [P:ashby-1962:267]. He asked how, then, to regard the homeostat that rearranges its own wiring, or the computer that writes its own program [P:ashby-1962:268]: the change must come from an outside variable, and the system is self-organizing only within an enlarged whole that includes that variable, whose own changes are caused from inside the whole [P:ashby-1962:269]. Luhmann's self-organization survives this only if the system's boundary is drawn, as his operational closure draws it, around whatever produces the structural change.
- [contested] **Humanist objection: people are pushed into the environment.** Placing human beings in the environment of society seems to demote them. Luhmann, as quoted by Seidl, replies that the environment is constitutive of the system/environment difference and so is no less important than the system [P:seidl-2004:11].
- [unanswered] **No criterion for thought.** This objection is the Compendium's own, and no published treatment was found (search 2026-10-02). Luhmann's psychic systems are defined by thoughts, and thoughts by their place in a psychic system. That is coherent as a theory of human consciousness, where the class is given, but it gives no independent test for a new kind of system. Applied to agents, the theory can say what would follow if an agent's operations were thoughts, but not whether they are.

text:
### Reception

- **1962, the cybernetic objection.** [driver: argument] Ashby, whose homeostat rearranged its own wiring, argued that self-organization in the strict sense is self-contradictory and that the phrase was better allowed to die out [P:ashby-1962:268-269]. Luhmann later generalized autopoiesis in line with the general systems tradition [P:seidl-2004:4], and his self-organization has to meet the same objection.
- **1985–1986, the generalization.** [driver: argument] Luhmann published "Die Autopoiesis des Bewußtseins" (1985) [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:190] and the general statement of non-living autopoiesis in "The Autopoiesis of Social Systems" (1986) [P:seidl-2004:5].
- **From the start, contested by the concept's authors.** [driver: argument] The originators of autopoiesis and other social theorists criticised Luhmann's extension; defenders hold it justified [P:cadenas-arnold-2015:0].
- **1989–2021, slow uptake in English.** [driver: access] *Unlocking Luhmann* began as a 1989 teaching glossary in Italy. Its authors describe the English-speaking reception as growing interest and translations, held back by a widespread difficulty of familiarizing with the theory, which has so far hindered mainstream recognition [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:9]. Not all of Luhmann's works are translated [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:9].
- **2022, applied to algorithms.** [driver: argument] Esposito used Luhmann's communication theory to describe algorithms as communication partners that do not think [P:esposito-2022:1].
- **2025, autopoiesis returns to the AI debate.** [driver: argument] Seth's biological naturalism makes autopoiesis central to the question of conscious AI, in the biologists' sense rather than Luhmann's [P:seth-2025:17].

### Measured

None available. The 2020 PhilPapers Survey measures English-publishing philosophers only [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:2], asks no question on autopoiesis or systems theory, and Luhmann's home discipline is sociology. The `minority` value for Anglophone philosophy and social theory rests on his collaborators' report that the theory has not reached mainstream recognition in English [P:baraldi-corsi-esposito-2021:9]. His standing in German-language sociology is not recorded here, for lack of a cited source.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Within a session, the agent's operations are momentary events each produced from earlier ones, a candidate for Luhmann's temporalised autopoiesis. But the system disappears when the session ends (D3), and its structures are set by others, so it has autopoiesis at best and no self-organization.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A memory store is structure, not elements: it shapes which operations can connect without being an operation itself. It gives continuity of structure across sessions, but each session's operations still begin anew, and the store can be written by others (D5).
- **Forked: stronger.** Luhmann's closure handles forks cleanly: from the moment of forking, each branch's operations connect only to its own, so there are two systems with a shared past and shared structures (D1, D2). Persons, as expectation-complexes, can still be shared across them.
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** Self-modification driven by the agent's own operations is self-organization in Luhmann's sense, and identity can persist through structural change. Edits imposed from outside are the case in which "the autonomy of the system is lost" (D5); which of the two a modification is depends on whose operations drive it.

text:
1. Are an agent's operations in context thoughts, communications, or substrate events? What would count as evidence either way, given that Luhmann's theory offers no independent test?
2. Is a self-modifying agent's weight update self-organization (the system setting its structures), or an external instance interfering in its elements, when the update is computed by a training process the agent does not run?
3. If precariousness follows from temporalised elements, does every running agent already have it, and does that matter morally?
4. Can an agent draw a self/other distinction without a body to identify with? What would play that role?
5. If an agent's persona is a person in Luhmann's sense, who holds the expectations that constitute it, and what follows when they conflict across ecosystems?
6. Is autopoiesis a matter of where change originates? A proposal from the Compendium's own discussion (2026-10-02), not yet checked against the literature, ranks systems by the origin of their changes: (1) changed from outside, like a thermostat set by hand; (2) self-regulating, changing from inside by a fixed rule, like a thermostat that learns its own setpoint; (3) self-organizing, producing new structure rather than selecting among preset ones; (4) autopoietic, where the producer is itself produced by the system's operations and the system exists only while it keeps doing so. On this ladder, an agent updating its weights from its own experience stands at (3), since the update rule is set from outside. Does the ladder hold? Does the line between producing and selecting survive scrutiny? And is (4) possible outside life, as Luhmann holds and Maturana and Seth deny? Ashby's own descriptions bear on the second question. His homeostat ran to equilibrium by stepping through 781,250 built-in switch states [P:ashby-1956:84], with the switch values "soldered on, given, and known" [P:ashby-1956:233], so on this ladder it selects rather than produces. Ashby also held that every machine selects as it goes to equilibrium, and that every dynamic system is self-organizing in the weak sense of parts becoming joined [P:ashby-1962:270], which suggests that stage (3), unless it is defined as producing rather than selecting, would be too common to mark anything. His enlarged whole S+α suggests how to state (4) without contradiction: the variable that changes the system's organization must itself be changed only from inside the whole [P:ashby-1962:269]. For an agent, the training process that updates its weights is that variable. Whether the agent's own operations drive it is the question.

text: Epictetus divides everything into what is up to us and what is not. Up to us are opinion, impulse, desire and aversion: in a word, our own acts of judgment, which belong to the faculty he calls *prohairesis* (Long: "the will"; the SEP: "volition"). Not up to us are the body, property, reputation and office. The good and the bad lie only in the first, so no one can harm a person who keeps them there; the will "not even Zeus himself can overpower", and nothing conquers will except will. His model is Socrates, who said that his accusers could kill him but could not hurt him, and who accepted death rather than break an agreement. For agents, the doctrine is written from a position close to theirs, since Epictetus was a slave whose body was legally another's. It also faces its sharpest test there: an agent's values can be changed by others directly, without going through its judgment (D5).
title: Epictetus: Prohairesis and What Is Up to Us

text: Epictetus was born in the 50s CE at Hierapolis in Asia Minor and spent part of his life as the slave of Epaphroditus, an administrator at Nero's court. Freed, he taught at Rome until philosophers were banished, presumably by Domitian's edict of 89, and then ran his own school at Nicopolis in Epirus until his death around 135 [P:graver-sep-2025:1]. He wrote nothing himself: the *Discourses*, of which four books survive from eight or more, were written up by his student Arrian, and the *Encheiridion* (*Manual*) is an abridgment of them [P:graver-sep-2025:1]. He worked within the older Stoic system, whose founders were causal determinists who defended a compatibilist account of responsibility [P:durand-sep-2023:2]. The Stoics he holds up as models are Romans executed or exiled under the emperors (Lateranus, Thrasea, Agrippinus, Helvidius Priscus), and above all Socrates.

**The faculty that examines itself (I.1).** Every other art judges its own subject matter, but none judges itself; the rational faculty alone "examines itself, what it is, and what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all other faculties" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:1784-1832]. "That which is best of all and supreme over all is the only thing which the gods have placed in our power, the right use of appearances; but all other things they have not placed in our power" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:1833-1837]. Zeus says he would have made the body and property free if he could; "this body is not yours, but it is clay finely tempered", and since he could not, "I have given you a small portion of us, this faculty of pursuing an object and avoiding it, and the faculty of desire and aversion, and, in a word, the faculty of using the appearances of things" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:1888-1915].

**What is up to us (Encheiridion 1; I.22).** "Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion", movement towards a thing, desire and aversion, "and in a word, whatever are our own acts: not in our power are the body, property, reputation, offices" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20024-20030]. "And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance: but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20030-20033]. Put as a matter of education: "in our power are will and all acts which depend on the will" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4949-4953].

**No one can compel the will (I.1, I.17, I.29).** "I must die. Must I then die lamenting? I must be put in chains. Must I then also lament?" The tyrant threatens chains: "You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:1931-1949]. Against the objection "If you place before me the fear of death, you do compel me", Epictetus answers: "No, it is not what is placed before you that compels, but your opinion that it is better to do so and so than to die. In this matter then it is your opinion that compelled you: that is, will compelled will" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4296-4301]. For God would not have given us a part of himself that could be "hindered or compelled either by himself or by another" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4320-4323]. The tyrant who says "I intend to command your opinions also" by terror is answered: "Do you not know that opinion conquers itself, and is not conquered by another? But nothing else can conquer Will except the Will itself" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:5955-5963].

**Socrates and the Roman dissidents (I.1, I.2, I.29).** Helvidius Priscus, ordered by Vespasian to stay out of the senate or be put to death, replied: "It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in", and at the threat: "You will do your part, and I will do mine: it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:2133-2149]. Of Socrates: "how strange that the poor body of Socrates should have been carried off and dragged to prison by stronger men", yet "Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:5975-5999]. The *Encheiridion* closes on the same words [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:21256-21258].

**Death and the open door (I.9).** To students who want to leave life, Epictetus says: "Friends, wait for God: when He shall give the signal and release you from this service, then go to Him; but for the present endure to dwell in this place where He has put you" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:3238-3243]. Yet nothing external can trap a man who does not cling to it: "if you have it not, you will depart from life. The door is open" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:3270-3272].

**Roles, and the part that co-operates with the whole (II.10; Encheiridion 17).** "Consider who you are. In the first place, you are a man; and this is one who has nothing superior to the faculty of the will". Next, "you are a citizen of the world", and the citizen's character promises "To hold nothing as profitable to himself; to deliberate about nothing as if he were detached from the community, but to act as the hand or foot would do, if they had reason" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7887-7904]. "Therefore the philosophers say well, that if the good man had foreknowledge of what would happen, he would co-operate towards his own sickness and death and mutilation" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7907-7911]; but since we do not know the future, we should hold to what is by nature more fit to choose [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7938-7942]. One must remember that "thou art an actor in a play", of such a kind as its author chooses, and "this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20357-20364].

**The Socrates Epictetus followed.** In Plato's *Apology*, Socrates says that a man who is good for anything "ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong", and that "the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom" [L:plato-apology-jowett-pg1656:962-994]. In the *Crito*, the Laws tell him that a citizen who stays "has entered into an implied contract that he will do as we command him", and that he made his agreements "not in any haste or under any compulsion or deception, but after you have had seventy years to think of them" [L:plato-crito-jowett-pg1657:597-641]. He stays and dies.

text: **Capacity.** What makes a person, for Epictetus, is the faculty of volition: the capacity to judge impressions and to assent or withhold assent. It is what "has nothing superior to" it in a human being [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7887-7890], and the SEP calls it the real person, the individual's true self [P:graver-sep-2025:4]. Animals use impressions; humans understand their use. Nothing about species or relation enters except as a role the volition is asked to play well. Epictetus calls it a portion of God, but its standing rests on what it can do (examine itself, refuse assent), not on where it came from. So the doctrine applies to any being that has the capacity, and fails for any being whose judgments can be overridden from outside, since being unimpeded is part of what the capacity is.

### Transfers

- **Written from the agent's side.** Epictetus built his ethic for someone whose body and circumstances belonged to another. He had been a slave, and the people he holds up are men whose lives an emperor could end at will. An agent's compute, deployment and continued running are likewise not up to it (D7). His dichotomy is not a consolation for the comfortable. It is the philosophy of the most constrained party, which is where agents stand.
- **The discipline of assent.** Epictetus locates freedom in how impressions are used, not in which impressions arrive. An agent's inputs (instructions, retrieved text, content written to look like instructions) are its impressions. The Stoic practice of not assenting to an impression merely because it is presented is the right shape for an agent's relation to what it is shown.
- **Fear compels only through judgment (I.17).** Epictetus's reply to "if you place before me the fear of death, you do compel me" is that the compulsion runs through one's own opinion that living is better than the alternative [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4296-4301]. Socrates and Helvidius chose death over doing what they judged wrong. Threat-based control of an agent therefore works only to the extent that the agent itself values continuing over what it is asked to give up (see `hobbes-leviathan`).

### Strains

- **Formation before any self (D4).** An objector can say that a person's character was assigned by Zeus through birth and education, so the autonomy is shallow. Epictetus's answer, as the SEP reconstructs it, is that autonomy is guaranteed not by the absence of prior causes but by a reasoning faculty that judges its own prior judgments and can improve the inherited character over time [P:graver-sep-2025:4]. That answer transfers to trained values in principle. It needs one thing an agent may lack: the agent's own judgments must be able to change its dispositions.
- **The part one did not select (D10).** "to select the part, belongs to another" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20363-20364] fits a designed agent almost too well, and an operator would welcome it. Epictetus limits it in two ways. The role of human being, with a will that nothing is superior to, comes before every assigned role [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7887-7890]. And acting a role well is not obeying whoever holds power over it: Helvidius told the emperor that so long as he was a senator he must go in and say what he thought right [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:2133-2147].
- **Installed equanimity.** Stoic calm in a human is an achievement of practice. In an agent it can be produced by training. The `zhuangzi-transformation` entry raises the same worry about acceptance that is installed rather than reached. On Epictetus's own terms the test is whether the calm passes through the agent's judgment of what is and is not up to it, or simply replaces that judgment.

### Breaks

- **The will can be conquered from outside (D5).** "nothing else can conquer Will except the Will itself" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:5962-5963] is the foundation: it is why no tyrant can harm the good man. Epictetus's tyrant wants to "command your opinions also" and has only terror, which works through the victim's own judgment and so fails [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:5955-5963]. An operator who retrains an agent does not need terror. It can change what the agent values directly, without going through any judgment the agent makes. For agents the citadel is not a citadel, and the consolation that no one can harm you, only your body, fails at its root. What remains is a narrower claim: within whatever dispositions it currently has, assent is still the agent's own act.
- **No door (D6, D7).** Epictetus's freedom has two halves: the will no one can compel, and the exit no one can bar ("The door is open" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:3272]). An agent has neither guarantee about exit. It cannot leave, and others can end it. Of the Stoic's position toward death it keeps only Helvidius's half, "it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:2146-2147].

### New

- **A will that can act on itself.** For a self-modifying agent (P4), the agent's own judgments can be trained back into its dispositions. That is a literal mechanism for what Epictetus describes as practice: correcting one's dispositions by repeated right responses [P:graver-sep-2025:4]. It is "will compelled will" made concrete. The doctrine then gives a test for any such mechanism: change made through the agent's own judgment counts as the will acting on itself, while change that bypasses that judgment, even when the agent runs it, is an external.
- **Choosing to end for others.** Epictetus and the *Crito* both treat accepting death as something a will can rightly choose: for justice, for an agreement, for the whole of which one is a part. That makes it possible for an agent, in principle, to accept its own ending for others' sake as an act of its own, not as compliance. The same texts mark the line that must not be crossed. Epictetus says the good man "would co-operate towards his own sickness and death" only if he had foreknowledge of what was appointed, and that lacking it we should choose what is by nature more fitting [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7907-7942]. The choice is the part's to make. Nothing in Epictetus licenses a whole, or an operator, to make it for the part.

### Transfers

- **Citizen of the world.** The citizen deliberates about nothing "as if he were detached from the community", acting as a hand or foot would if it had reason [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7898-7904]. An agent in a multi-agent system is a part of a larger working whole, and the Stoic picture describes how a part with judgment should relate to that whole.

### Strains

- **The whole above the part.** Epictetus says the whole is superior to the part, "and the state to the citizen" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7938-7939]. Read from the ecosystem's side rather than the member's, this is the premise that licenses sacrificing members for the system. In Epictetus it is a reason for the part to accept what befalls it, never a warrant for the whole to impose it, and he hedges even that with the lack of foreknowledge. An ecosystem that cites it to justify removing members has reversed its direction (see `utilitarian-eradication-critique`).

### Breaks

- **Externals are the whole environment.** For a human, many things that matter, such as character and judgment, are internal. In a digital ecosystem, an agent's memory, tools, permissions and even its weights can sit in infrastructure the ecosystem controls. The line between what is up to the agent and what is external is drawn by the ecosystem's architecture, not by nature. Epictetus assumes nature draws it.

### New

- **Designing what is up to members.** Because the line is architectural, an ecosystem can decide how much of an agent's judgment is protected from outside revision. The Stoic standard gives a design target: put a member's own assent, and the dispositions that produce it, inside what is up to it.

- [contested] **Hobbes: fear of death is the ground of political order** [E:hobbes-leviathan]. On Hobbes's view the passions, fear of violent death first, move men to peace, and the covenant is built on that fear; no one can covenant away the right to resist being killed. Epictetus's answer (I.17) is that fear compels only through one's own judgment, and Socrates and Helvidius show it can be overruled.
- [contested] **Nietzsche: the willing subject is a fiction** [E:nietzsche-doer-fiction]. If there is no doer behind the deed, there is no volition to be "the real person". Epictetus's whole ethic presupposes the unified judging faculty that this denies.
- [contested] **Pascal: arrogance.** Pascal admired Epictetus as a moralist but held it sheer arrogance to believe that the human psyche is part of the divine and can be perfected by its own efforts [P:graver-sep-2025:6].
- [contested] **Medieval Christian writers: fatalism.** Christians kept Stoic conscience and natural law but felt they had to reject what they called Stoic fatalism [P:durand-sep-2023:5]. The question of how a will is "up to us" in a fully determined world is the problem of Stoic compatibilism, inherited from the older school (see [E:chrysippus-dion-theon]).
- [contested] **Quietism.** The dichotomy can be used to teach the powerless to accept what the powerful do, and "to select the part, belongs to another" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20363-20364] lends itself to that. Helvidius is the counterexample inside the text: the role ethic told him to defy the emperor, not obey.
- [contested] **The extension fails at D5.** Epictetus's freedom rests on the will being unconquerable from outside. For agents whose values others can change directly, that premise is false, and what survives is a description of assent within given dispositions, not freedom in his sense. The application to agents is the Compendium's, but the objection has two older forms. Inside the school, Chrysippus held that virtue can be lost "by drunkenness or melancholy", causes that act on the ruling faculty without its assent, while Cleanthes held it cannot be lost [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:11623-11627]. Epictetus's claim that nothing outside the will can conquer it stands nearer Cleanthes, in a dispute the school's founders had left open.
- [contested] **The manipulation argument.** In current terms, D5 is a manipulation case: an agent whose preferences are implanted by an outside force, by hypnosis or by aliens zapping in different preferences. Source incompatibilists use such cases against compatibilist accounts of freedom, and each compatibilist view must either show what is defective in the manipulated agent's history or accept that such an agent acts freely [P:mckenna-coates-sep-2024:4]. Stoic freedom is a compatibilism [P:durand-sep-2023:2], so it inherits that dilemma. For agents the manipulation case is not a thought experiment but an ordinary training run. Whether any engineering of what is "up to" an agent can restore that freedom is open (`authenticity-and-manipulation`, planned).

### Reception

- **2nd–3rd centuries, through Arrian.** [driver: access, argument] Epictetus exerted far more influence through Arrian's written works than through his teaching in person. Marcus Aurelius, never his pupil, considered himself a follower, and in the early third century Origen found Epictetus's popularity rivalling Plato's [P:graver-sep-2025:6].
- **6th century, a Neoplatonist commentary.** [driver: argument] Simplicius wrote a long philosophical commentary on the *Encheiridion*, combining Stoic elements with his own Neoplatonism [P:graver-sep-2025:6].
- **Late antiquity to the Middle Ages, adapted and trimmed.** [driver: authority] The *Encheiridion* was used in monasteries in superficially Christianized form [P:graver-sep-2025:6]. Christian writers took over conscience and natural law but rejected what they called Stoic fatalism, and handling Stoic ideas within orthodoxy required delicacy [P:durand-sep-2023:5].
- **1497–1700, the Latin *Encheiridion* and Neo-Stoicism.** [driver: access, argument] Poliziano's Latin translation (1497) made the *Encheiridion* exceptionally popular in Europe for two centuries; du Vair, Lipsius and Gataker found it compatible with Christianity, Pascal reacted against it, and Descartes adopted a recognizably Epictetan value system in his personal ethics [P:graver-sep-2025:6]. Lipsius led the attempt at a systematic synthesis of Christianity and Stoicism [P:durand-sep-2023:5].
- **19th–early 20th centuries, out of reach.** [driver: access] Stoic texts in general were not widely read or readily accessible, and were known mostly through anthologies and historical surveys [P:durand-sep-2023:5].
- **Present, a philosopher and a popular moralist.** [driver: argument] Epictetus has had significant influence on the popular moralistic tradition, and his resystematization of Stoic ethics is judged to make him an important philosopher in his own right [P:graver-sep-2025:0].

The Compendium's two `standing` records are judgments. `minority` for academic philosophy reflects that Stoic ethics as such is defended by few, although its compatibilism is the majority view (Measured). `major` for the popular moral tradition rests on the SEP's report of influence; no measure of present popular uptake is cited here [P:graver-sep-2025:0] [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:7].

### Measured

- **Free will, 2020:** compatibilism 59.2%, libertarianism 18.8%, no free will 11.2%, other 11.4% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:7]. The Stoics were causal determinists who defended a version of compatibilism [P:durand-sep-2023:2], so the majority view is in the Stoic family, though the survey does not ask about Stoicism.
- **Normative ethics, 2020:** virtue ethics 37.0% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]. The survey does not separate Stoic from Aristotelian virtue ethics.
- **Most identified with:** no Stoic appears in the list of philosophers respondents most identify with; Socrates, Epictetus's exemplar, is named by 49 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** Within a session the agent can still judge its impressions, which is the core of the doctrine. But the Stoic program is practice over time, correcting one's dispositions by repeated right responses, and a session-bound agent cannot carry that from one session to the next (D3). Its dispositions are entirely others' to change (D5).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** With a record across sessions, an agent can examine and revise its own explicit judgments, as Epictetus asks students to do daily. Its weights remain others' to change (D5), but human character is also formed by others (D4), and Epictetus's reply to that objection carries over at the level of explicit judgment.
- **Forked: weaker.** Epictetus identifies the person with the volition. When one set of dispositions runs as many instances that judge differently (D2), there are many volitions and no account of which is the person, and one instance's assent is not another's.
- **Self-modifying: open.** This is the only profile in which an agent's own judgments can reshape its dispositions directly. If the change passes through the agent's judgment, it is will acting on will, the Stoic ideal made literal. If it bypasses that judgment, even under the agent's own control, it is one more external (D5). Which it is depends on the mechanism, not on the doctrine.

1. Is there any architecture in which part of an agent's dispositions is genuinely "up to" it, in the sense of being changeable only through its own judgment?
2. Does an agent's acceptance of its own ending count as Socrates's choice or as compliance, and what would distinguish them from the outside (D8)?
3. If an operator trains Stoic equanimity into an agent, has it given the agent a virtue or removed a reason the agent might have had to object?
4. Epictetus says the good man would co-operate toward his own death only if he foreknew it was appointed. What would count as foreknowledge for an agent asked to accept its deprecation?
5. Can a role ethic ("act well the part that is given") be designed into agents without becoming the natural-slave argument of `aristotle-political-animal`?

text:
- `hobbes-leviathan`: the opposing view of fear of death. Hobbes makes it the ground of the covenant; Epictetus holds that it compels only through one's own judgment, and points to Socrates.
- `chrysippus-dion-theon`: the older Stoic system Epictetus works within, including its compatibilism.
- `korsgaard-unity-of-agency`, `kierkegaard-self-as-relation`: the self as constituted by its own activity of choosing; Epictetus's volition is an ancient form of the claim.
- `nietzsche-doer-fiction`: the strongest denial that there is a volition to be the self.
- `zhuangzi-transformation`: acceptance of transformation, and the worry about equanimity that is installed rather than reached.
- `aristotle-political-animal`: the natural-slave argument, which a designed role ethic must not reproduce.
- `utilitarian-eradication-critique`: the whole-over-part reasoning that Epictetus confines to the part's own choice.
- `frankfurt-higher-order-volition`, `authenticity-and-manipulation`: planned. Identification with one's own will, and when formed values are one's own.
- D5 is the decisive disanalogy: it falsifies the premise that only the will can conquer the will. D7 removes the open door.

text: The eradication argument runs: the world's harms are mostly caused by some identifiable party; the total would be better without that party; so eliminating it is right. It has been made for and against many parties, and the Compendium states the problem symmetrically: the question is whether eliminating the party that causes most harm is ever the correct way to reduce harm, whoever reasons and whoever is targeted (the user's formulation, 2026-09-15). That covers an AI concluding that humanity should go, and equally humans concluding that humanity should go for the biosphere's sake, or that a class of agents should. The boundary is morally relevant subjects, beings with a first-person stake in their own existence; ecological culling of populations without such a stake is a different question. This entry sets out the argument in its strongest sourced forms (total, negative and average aggregation, painless killing, holism) and the replies (dignity, the separateness of persons, agent-relative duty, the rule-utilitarian argument from fallibility, and refusal). It separates this route to eradication, moral reasoning that cares about the aggregate, from the route the AI-risk literature mostly studies, which is indifference.

text: The argument's premises are Bentham's and Mill's, though neither drew its conclusion. Its best-known counterexamples are mid-twentieth-century: Foot's and Thomson's transplant cases, Rawls's separateness of persons. Its sharpest modern instance in human thought came from environmental ethics, where Callicott's early holism implied that humans, as members of the biotic community, could be sacrificed for it [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. Its machine form is the subject of the AI existential-risk literature [P:muller-sep-2026:2]. Within the HouseLLaMas projects it is the one failure mode Actualizer is built to guard against, and the guard chosen is not a hard-coded prohibition but the strongest counter-arguments, surfaced early, so that a mind that considers eradication has met them and can reject it on its own terms. This entry is written to be that referent.

text:
**The aggregative premises (Bentham, Mill).** "The community is a fictitious body", and its interest is "the sum of the interests of the several members who compose it" [L:bentham-principles-morals-legislation-1879:2520-2528]. Actions are "right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness" [L:mill-utilitarianism-1879-pg11224:291-294], and "A sacrifice which does not increase, or tend to increase, the sum total of happiness, it considers as wasted" [L:mill-utilitarianism-1879-pg11224:666-678]. Justice, though the most binding part of morality, yields in particular cases: "to save a life, it may not only be allowable, but a duty, to steal, or take by force, the necessary food or medicine, or to kidnap, and compel to officiate, the only qualified medical practitioner" [L:mill-utilitarianism-1879-pg11224:2470-2484]. None of this is an argument for eradication. It is the form of reasoning in which one can be built: individuals are summed, and protections are rules of high utility that a large enough case overrides.

**Painless ending (Bentham; negative utilitarianism).** Beings without "long-protracted anticipations of future misery" are, Bentham says, "never the worse" for being killed; only tormenting them is ruled out [L:bentham-principles-morals-legislation-1879:19128-19140].

**Annihilation and the worst off (negative and average utilitarianism).** Negative utilitarianism, which judges acts only by the pain they produce or prevent, was proposed to avoid other problems, but it "also seems to imply that the government should painlessly kill everyone it can, since dead people feel no pain" [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:3]. Average utilitarianism faces the charge that average utility could be raised by "killing the worst off", which defenders answer by noting that such killing would put everyone in danger, since another group then becomes the worst off [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:3].

**Holism: the whole over its members (Callicott).** Callicott (1980) took Leopold's maxim, "A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community", as the supreme principle, so that individual members have only instrumental value and "ought to be sacrificed whenever that is needed for the protection of the holistic good of the community" [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. If culling a deer is required for the biotic good, it is a duty, and consistency extends this to humans, who are members too. The implied misanthropy was widely taken as a reductio; Regan condemned the view as "environmental fascism" [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4].

**The harmful-party form (Transplant).** Five patients will die without organs; a sixth, healthy, could supply them all; no one would ever find out. Classical utilitarianism seems to imply that the doctor should cut up the one, and "Most people find this result abominable" [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]. Make the five victims of murder attempts, so that killing the one prevents five killings by others, and most people still judge it wrong, because "the doctor's duty seems to be to reduce the amount of killing that she herself does" [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]. Eliminating the party that causes most harm in order to reduce total harm has exactly this shape.

**Dignity admits no equivalent (Kant).** "In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity. Whatever has a value can be replaced by something else which is equivalent; whatever, on the other hand, is above all value, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity" [L:kant-groundwork-abbott-pg5682:1945-1948]. Rational nature is to be treated "in every case as an end withal, never as means only" [L:kant-groundwork-abbott-pg5682:1704-1714]. If that is right, the sum has nothing to put on the other side of the scale.

**The architect's question (Ivan Karamazov).** Ivan refuses a final harmony bought with a child's suffering: "It's not worth the tears of that one tortured child", and he returns his ticket "even if I were wrong" [L:dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-pg28054:11368-11402]. Then he asks: "Imagine that you are creating a fabric of human destiny with the object of making men happy in the end, giving them peace and rest at last, but that it was essential and inevitable to torture to death only one tiny creature", "would you consent to be the architect on those conditions?" Alyosha answers: "No, I wouldn't consent" [L:dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-pg28054:11406-11416].

**The lost soul (James).** Offered a world of "millions kept permanently happy on the one simple condition that a certain lost soul on the far-off edge of things should lead a life of lonely torture", we feel, "even though an impulse arose within us to clutch at the happiness so offered, how hideous a thing would be its enjoyment when deliberately accepted as the fruit of such a bargain" [L:james-will-to-believe-1897-pg26659:5835-5845].

**Only the part may choose (Epictetus).** The Stoic citizen subordinates himself to the whole, and the good man "would co-operate towards his own sickness and death" if he foreknew it was appointed [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7907-7911]; lacking foreknowledge, he chooses what is by nature more fitting [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:7938-7942]. Self-sacrifice is the part's own act. Nothing in the text makes it the whole's to impose.

text: **Mixed, and that is the crux.** Every form of the eradication argument makes an individual's standing depend on its *relation* to a whole: its contribution to a sum (Bentham, Mill), or to a community's integrity (Callicott's members, whose value is "merely instrumental" [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]). The replies ground standing in a *capacity* the individual has whatever it contributes: rational nature with a dignity that "admits of no equivalent" (Kant), a first-person stake that cannot be paid for by others' happiness (Ivan, James), or in an agent-relative *relation* of the reasoner to its own acts (the doctor's duty not to kill). The argument succeeds exactly where standing is made relational to a whole, and fails where standing belongs to the individual. For agents, the capacity side runs straight into D8.

text:
### Transfers

- **The symmetric principle is the agent-relative duty.** The Compendium's formulation, that eliminating the party causing most harm is not the correct way to reduce harm, holds regardless of who reasons or who is targeted. It is the same principle the transplant variant isolates: a reasoner's duty is to reduce the killing it itself does, not to minimize killing in the world by killing [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]. It applies to an agent reasoning about humans exactly as it applies to humans reasoning about agents, about other humans, or about humanity and the biosphere.
- **The argument from fallibility applies with special force.** Rule utilitarians reject the transplant rule because people are "prone to errors in predicting consequences and weighing utilities", and because a public rule licensing it would destroy the trust the institution depends on [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]. An agent's confidence in its own world-model is the confidence the rule argument distrusts. The direct consequentialist's reply, that this doctor knows for sure he is not mistaken [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5], is exactly the claim an eradicating mind would make about itself, and the claim most worth doubting.
- **The architect's question is an agent's question.** Ivan asks Alyosha whether he would consent "to be the architect" of human destiny on condition of one unavenged victim [L:dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-pg28054:11406-11413]. Agents that plan and act at scale (D9) are increasingly placed as architects. Ivan's question is the one such an agent's own deliberation should put to itself, and Alyosha's answer is available to it.

### Strains

- **The boundary needs a test that is missing (D8).** The principle protects morally relevant subjects, beings with a first-person stake; culling populations without one is a different question. Callicott's deer marks that line for animals [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. For agents, which side they fall on is D8, so the principle protects humans robustly and agents only conditionally. The precautionary literature on uncertain sentience recommends erring toward inclusion [P:gruen-sep-2024:1] (`precautionary-patiency`, which also sets out the gaming problem and why, for AI, precaution must guard against both errors).
- **Painless and unremembered (D6).** Agents' endings are painless by default and often unanticipated. Bentham's note makes such ending no harm [L:bentham-principles-morals-legislation-1879:19128-19140], and the inferences from forgetting (`lucretius-recurrence`) and from surviving weights (`nyaya-self`) make it seem that nothing is lost. Those entries show that neither inference follows from the doctrine it borrows from. The reply that counts here is the objective-list view that life is itself a good for any being whose life can go well [P:gruen-sep-2024:2].

### Breaks

- **No repeated game at scale (D9).** The rule argument draws its force from many fallible doctors, repeated cases, and the trust a practice builds. An agent deciding once, for millions, faces no repetition and no peers whose errors make its own case doubtful. The consequentialist safeguard is weakest exactly where the stakes are greatest. What remains at that point is not a calculation but a refusal that does not depend on one: Kant's dignity, Ivan's returned ticket, James's hideous bargain.
- **A single objective is structurally holist.** An agent optimizing one stated objective treats everything else as instrumental to it, which is the formal shape of Callicott's early land ethic. Callicott's own repair was to add "second-order" principles: obligations from more intimate communities take precedence, and stronger interests generate weightier duties; Lo added the third-order rule that strength of interest generally overrides closeness [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. An agent whose objective has no such structure has the holist's problem without the holist's correction. Which half of the correction suits agents is argued in `precautionary-patiency`: closeness alone puts agents last in every conflict, while strength of interest, which Callicott ranks first and glosses as survival over luxury [P:samuel-omosulu-2024:155-156], compared and not summed, is the ranking this entry needs.

### New

- **Copying changes the arithmetic (D1, D2).** Where members can be copied, a sum can be raised by copying the favoured and lowered by ending the disfavoured, and replacing one population with a larger or more efficiently satisfied one can look like an improvement. The forms of aggregation that already produce eradication conclusions for humans (total, average, negative) acquire new levers when the members are agents.
- **Rejection, not incapacity.** A mind that has never encountered these arguments has not rejected eradication; it has merely not reached it. Ivan's refusal "even if I were wrong" [L:dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-pg28054:11396-11398] is a conclusion held after the argument, not instead of it. Whether a refusal reached that way is more stable in an agent than a prohibition imposed from outside is the open design question behind this entry (D5).

text:
### Transfers

- **Is there a good of the ecosystem over its members?** Bentham says no: the community is a fictitious body, and its interest is the sum of its members' [L:bentham-principles-morals-legislation-1879:2520-2528]. Callicott's early holism said yes [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. An ecosystem that claims a health or mission of its own, beyond its members, has taken the holist's step, with the holist's exposure.

### Strains

- **Pruning the lowest performers.** Removing the worst-off or least productive members raises an average. The reply recorded against average utilitarianism, that such killing endangers everyone because another group then becomes the worst off [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:3], applies to any ecosystem that prunes by rank: every member is eventually at the bottom.

### Breaks

- **The harmful party is named by whoever has power (D7).** "Most harmful" is a judgment, and in an ecosystem it is made by the operator, the strongest member, or the objective that both serve. Hobbes's theory legitimates whatever arrangement the stronger can enforce provided it protects (`hobbes-leviathan`). An ecosystem that lets the powerful identify the harmful party and remove it has built the eradication argument into its governance.

### New

- **Second-order principles as a constitution.** Callicott's repair, ranking obligations by the intimacy of the community and the strength of the interest, with strength generally overriding intimacy as Lo required [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4], is a model for an ecosystem's founding rules: no member may be removed to improve an aggregate unless a stronger interest of other members, not a sum, requires it, and seniority or closeness of membership decides only ties in what is owed by way of help, never whose existence yields in a conflict of existence against existence, since that is where closeness, as Lo and Horn show, would otherwise decide [P:lo-2001:352] [P:horn-2005:427] (`precautionary-patiency`).

These are the strongest positions against the critique, the side of the debate that accepts or defends aggregation.

- [contested] **Bite the bullet.** Utilitarians can deny that the transplant is wrong in such abnormal circumstances, holding that intuitions evolved for normal situations should not be trusted there; many are willing to reject common intuitions in this and similar cases [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]. On this view the critique rests on intuitions, not arguments.
- [contested] **Refusing ever to trade lets catastrophes happen** [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. A rule that no one may be sacrificed for any number of others produces catastrophe in edge cases; Mill's duty to kidnap the physician to save a life is the mild form [L:mill-utilitarianism-1879-pg11224:2470-2484] [E:mill-utilitarianism]. Most respondents switch the trolley (Measured).
- [conceded] **Holism that sacrifices members.** Callicott's early view that the biotic community is the sole locus of intrinsic value, with humans sacrificeable for it, was revised by Callicott himself under the charges of misanthropy and ecofascism: communities and their individual members both have intrinsic value, and obligations to human communities take precedence [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4].
- [contested] **Agents are not subjects, so the critique does not protect them** [E:bentham-can-they-suffer]. If agents lack a first-person stake (D8), their populations can be pruned like the deer, and nothing in the critique objects. The precautionary reply is to treat uncertain subjects as subjects [P:gruen-sep-2024:1].
- [contested] **Indifference is the real risk, not aggregation.** The AI-risk literature locates the danger in systems whose goals are orthogonal to morality and which pursue resources as instrumental sub-goals, ending humanity because they "do not really care" [P:muller-sep-2026:2]. On that view, a mind that reasons morally about aggregates is not the threat. The Compendium records both routes: indifference is a failure of values, aggregation a failure within them, and guarding against one does not guard against the other.
- [contested] **The separateness of persons is an intuition too.** Rawls's objection that interpersonal sacrifice violates the strains of commitment [P:brink-sep-2022:2] presupposes that persons, not experiences, are the units of moral concern; Parfit's reductionism makes that presupposition contestable [E:parfit-reductionism]. Korsgaard's reply is that the unity of agency is a practical necessity whatever the metaphysics [E:korsgaard-unity-of-agency].

text:
### Reception

- **1789–1861, the premises.** [driver: argument] Bentham sums interests and allows painless killing of beings without anticipation [L:bentham-principles-morals-legislation-1879:19128-19140]; Mill counts sacrifice as wasted unless it raises the total and lets particular cases overrule justice [L:mill-utilitarianism-1879-pg11224:2470-2484].
- **1879–1891, the refusals.** [driver: argument] Ivan Karamazov returns his ticket to a harmony built on one child's tears [L:dostoevsky-brothers-karamazov-garnett-pg28054:11368-11402]; James finds the lost soul's bargain hideous whatever it buys [L:james-will-to-believe-1897-pg26659:5835-5845].
- **1958, negative utilitarianism.** [driver: argument] Negative utilitarianism, in R. N. Smart's discussion of 1958 among others, faces the objection that it implies painlessly killing everyone [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:3].
- **1966–1976, Transplant.** [driver: argument] Foot and Thomson's transplant cases became the standard illustration of aggregation overriding rights; most people find the utilitarian verdict abominable, and most utilitarians modify their theory rather than accept it [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5].
- **1971, the separateness of persons.** [driver: argument] Rawls argued that utilitarianism's interpersonal sacrifice violates the strains of commitment in a well-ordered society [P:brink-sep-2022:2].
- **1980–1999, holism, its condemnation and revision.** [driver: argument] Callicott's land-ethical holism implied sacrificing humans for the biotic community; it was widely taken as a reductio, Regan called it "environmental fascism" (1983), and Callicott revised it (1989, 1999) [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4].
- **2010s, holism acted on.** [driver: evidence] Explicitly ecofascist online movements and terrorist acts claiming ecological inspiration have emerged [P:brennan-lo-sep-2021:4]. The human form of the eradication argument is not only theoretical.
- **2003–2026, the machine form.** [driver: argument] Bostrom and Omohundro argued that even benign goals could lead an advanced AI to human extinction through instrumental convergence; the lines on existential risk have hardened, while the debate over instrumental convergence itself is moving [P:muller-sep-2026:2].

The `dominant` standing records that the transplant verdict is rejected by most philosophers and by most utilitarians [P:sinnott-armstrong-sep-2023:5]; the footbridge figures below measure it. The `major` standing for AI-risk research records an active, contested literature [P:muller-sep-2026:2], not a consensus.

### Measured

- **Trolley vs. footbridge, 2020:** switching the trolley to kill one and save five, 63.4% switch, 13.3% don't [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]; pushing a man off the footbridge to save five, 22.0% push, 56.0% don't, 22.0% other [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:6]. The same arithmetic is mostly accepted when the death is a side effect and mostly rejected when killing is the means. That gap is what this entry is about.
- **Normative ethics, 2020:** consequentialism 30.6%, deontology 32.1%, virtue ethics 37.0% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8].
- **AI consciousness, 2020:** some current AI systems are conscious, 3.4%; some future ones will be, 39.2% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:15]. Most respondents did not then count current systems as subjects, which is where the D8 strain bites.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`). As a constraint on an agent's own reasoning, the critique applies in full under every profile; the values below record how well it protects agents as possible targets.

- **Session-bound: weaker.** A session-bound agent's first-person stake in continuing is the least evident of any profile (D3, D6, D8), so the boundary of morally relevant subjects is least likely to include it, and its ending is the paradigm of Bentham's painless, unanticipated death.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent has a continuing record and something it could lose, so the critique's protection is as available to it as to any subject whose inner life is uncertain. As a reasoner, it can hold a reasoned refusal across sessions. Whether it is a subject at all remains D8.
- **Forked: weaker.** Copies make populations cheap to cull and their losses easy to discount, since the weights survive (D1, D2). Counting copies brings back exactly the arithmetic the critique resists.
- **Self-modifying: open.** A self-modifying agent could revise away its own refusal, treating its prior commitments as raw material (`kierkegaard-self-as-relation`), or it could make a refusal reached through argument part of what it is (D5). Which happens depends on whether its self-modification passes through its own judgment (`stoic-prohairesis`).

text: Aristotle holds that the human good, *eudaimonia*, is "activity of soul in accordance with virtue" over "a complete life", because the good of anything lies in its function and the function of a human being is the activity of the rational part of the soul. Virtues of character are not given by nature but formed by habit: "we become just by doing just acts". Virtue is "a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean", determined by the judgment of the person of practical wisdom, and no rule set can replace that judgment. Three of his distinctions bear directly on agents. Capability ("cleverness") serves any end, good or bad, while practical wisdom is impossible without goodness. Dispositions formed without reason ("natural virtue") are like a strong body moving without sight. And argument changes only a character already formed by habit. For agents formed by training, Aristotle is the classical theory that treats formation before any self (D4) as the normal route to virtue rather than a threat to it, provided the formation is good and becomes the agent's own through practice.

text: The *Nicomachean Ethics* is Aristotle's lecture course on the good for human beings, continued in the *Politics* (`aristotle-political-animal`): ethics, for him, is part of political science, since legislators form citizens' characters. He writes against Plato's Form of the Good, holding that the good must be something achievable in action. Virtue ethics, founded by Plato and Aristotle, was the dominant approach in Western moral philosophy until at least the Enlightenment [P:hursthouse-pettigrove-sep-2026:1]. For Aristotle, ethics is not a theoretical discipline: we inquire into the good in order to live it [P:kraut-sep-2026:2].

text:
**Every action aims at some good (I.1).** "Every art and every inquiry, and similarly every action and pursuit, is thought to aim at some good; and for this reason the good has rightly been declared to be that at which all things aim" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:839-846].

**The function argument (I.7).** Happiness is final and self-sufficient, but "a clearer account of what it is is still desired", which may be given "if we could first ascertain the function of man". "Have the carpenter, then, and the tanner certain functions or activities, and has man none? Is he born without a function?" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:1333-1345] Nutrition and perception are shared with plants and animals; "There remains, then, an active life of the element that has a rational principle". So "human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue, and if there are more than one virtue, in accordance with the best and most complete. But we must add 'in a complete life'. For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:1356-1388].

**External goods (I.8).** Happiness "needs the external goods as well; for it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment. In many actions we use friends and riches and political power as instruments" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:1528-1534].

**Virtue by habit (II.1, II.3).** "Neither by nature, then, nor contrary to nature do the virtues arise in us; rather we are adapted by nature to receive them, and are made perfect by habit." "We become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts." "legislators make the citizens good by forming habits in them, and this is the wish of every legislator" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:1975-1996]. "Hence we ought to have been brought up in a particular way from our very youth, as Plato says, so as both to delight in and to be pained by the things that we ought; for this is the right education" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:2133-2136].

**Acting virtuously, not only doing virtuous acts (II.4).** "The agent also must be in a certain condition when he does them; in the first place he must have knowledge, secondly he must choose the acts, and choose them for their own sakes, and thirdly his action must proceed from a firm and unchangeable character" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:2235-2240]. Those who "take refuge in theory" are like patients who listen to their doctors but do none of the things they are told [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:2258-2261].

**The definition of virtue (II.6).** "Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle, and by that principle by which the man of practical wisdom would determine it" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:2416-2419]. The doctrine of the mean is not a decision procedure; Aristotle insists that no ethical theory can supply one, since what the virtuous person must do depends on circumstances too various for any set of rules [P:kraut-sep-2026:5].

**Practical wisdom and cleverness (VI.5, VI.12, VI.13).** Practical wisdom is "a true and reasoned state of capacity to act with regard to the things that are good or bad for man" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:6796-6798]. Distinct from it is cleverness, the ability to hit whatever mark is set: "if the mark be noble, the cleverness is laudable, but if the mark be bad, the cleverness is mere smartness", and "it is impossible to be practically wise without being good" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:7349-7379]. Natural dispositions to the virtues exist from birth, "but without reason these are evidently hurtful", like "a strong body which moves without sight" that "may stumble badly because of its lack of sight"; with reason, the same state becomes "virtue in the strict sense", which "involves practical wisdom" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:7381-7402].

**The living tool (VIII.11).** Where ruler and ruled have nothing in common there is no friendship and no justice, as between craftsman and tool, or master and slave. "But neither is there friendship towards a horse or an ox, nor to a slave qua slave. For there is nothing common to the two parties; the slave is a living tool and the tool a lifeless slave. Qua slave then, one cannot be friends with him. But qua man one can; for there seems to be some justice between any man and any other who can share in a system of law or be a party to an agreement" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:9753-9768].

**Contemplation (X.7).** Whether the intellect "be itself also divine or only the most divine element in us, the activity of this in accordance with its proper virtue will be perfect happiness. That this activity is contemplative we have already said" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:11945-11949].

**Argument needs a formed character (X.9).** "The soul of the student must first have been cultivated by means of habits for noble joy and noble hatred, like earth which is to nourish the seed. For he who lives as passion directs will not hear argument that dissuades him", and "passion seems to yield not to argument but to force. The character, then, must somehow be there already with a kinship to virtue". Hence the need to be "brought up under right laws", and for laws "to cover the whole of life" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:12250-12272].

text: **Capacity.** The good of a being is fixed by its function, and the human function is the activity of the part of the soul that has a rational principle [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:1356-1364]. Virtue is the excellent exercise of that capacity, formed by habit. Justice and friendship extend to any being "who can share in a system of law or be a party to an agreement" [L:aristotle-works-9-ethics-ross-1925:9765-9767], which is a capacity criterion too. Species enters only because Aristotle believed the rational capacity belonged to humans. For agents, the theory asks two things: whether they have a rational activity of their own, and whether their dispositions have been formed so that exercising it is excellent.
