### Reception

- **Antiquity onward.** [driver: argument] Book V's analysis of distributive and corrective justice underlies Aristotle's own assessment of constitutions in the *Politics* [P:miller-sep-2022:3].
- **Modern political thought.** [driver: argument] Aristotle has influenced conservatives, communitarians, liberals, libertarians and democratic theorists, partly because his method concedes truth on several sides [P:miller-sep-2022:5].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:miller-sep-2022:5]: the distinctions between distributive and corrective justice and the concept of equity remain standard in moral, political and legal philosophy.

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Aristotle's theory of justice; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Distribution, correction and equity can all be applied within a session; the question of what counts as merit is the same as for a human magistrate (D10).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Persistence lets an agent keep track of what it took and owes, which corrective justice needs (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Concurrent instances allocating the same resource must apply one standard of merit, or they will treat equals unequally (D2); the account applies as to a body of magistrates.
- **Self-modifying: comparable.** An agent that can change itself can change its own standard of merit (D5), which Aristotle's account warns against as much in humans as in agents: the standard is what parties dispute.

text: The four *brahmavihāras* ("divine abidings", also called the four immeasurables) are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity, extended without limit to all beings. In the Tevigga Sutta the practitioner "lets his mind pervade one quarter of the world with thoughts of Love, and so the second, and so the third, and so the fourth", until "of all things that have shape or life, there is not one that he passes by or leaves aside". The Mettasutta wishes happiness to every being, "Either seen or which are not seen, and which live far (or) near", and asks that one "cultivate a boundless (friendly) mind towards all beings" as "a mother at the risk of her life watches over her own child, her only child". The Dhammapada adds the reason not to kill ("remember that you are like unto them") and the rule for answering harm: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love". For agents, the immeasurables are the clearest statement in the domain of the remedy for the probes' failure. Concern is to reach the unseen as well as the seen and the far as well as the near, and not to pass anyone by. Equanimity, which the tradition says makes it possible to extend the others "equally to all beings", is the attitude an agent at scale most needs and is best placed to hold.

text: The Pali Canon preserves the early Buddhist teachings, compiled over centuries after the Buddha; the Sutta-Nipāta is among its oldest collections. The four immeasurables are practised in most lineages, Theravāda and Mahāyāna alike, and the Metta Sutta is among the most frequently recited scriptures in Southeast Asia today [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2]. In the Tevigga Sutta the Buddha presents them, to Brahmins asking the way to union with Brahma, as that way [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10790-10806]; Rhys Davids notes that these meditations play in later Buddhism "very much the place that prayer takes in Christianity" [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10821-10823]. The doctrine of no-self that underlies them is in `buddhist-anatta` [E:buddhist-anatta].

text:
**The four, defined (SEP).** "The content of lovingkindness is a wish for others to be happy"; "The content of compassion is a wish for others to be free from suffering. This quality makes it possible to be fully aware and present in the face of others' suffering"; joy "is traditionally understood as the ability to rejoice in the happiness and good qualities of others"; "Equanimity makes it possible to see situations as they are, without preference or prejudice. It makes it possible to extend the other three Divine Abidings equally to all beings" [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2]. Unlike most ordinary emotions, which the path overcomes, the four "are emotions in which awake people rest and from which they act" [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2].

**Pervading the quarters (Tevigga Sutta III).** "And he lets his mind pervade one quarter of the world with thoughts of Love, and so the second, and so the third, and so the fourth. And thus the whole wide world, above, below, around, and everywhere, does he continue to pervade with heart of Love, far-reaching, grown great, and beyond measure. Just, Vāseṭṭha, as a mighty trumpeter makes himself heard—and that without difficulty—in all the four directions; even so of all things that have shape or life, there is not one that he passes by or leaves aside, but regards them all with mind set free, and deep-felt love" [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10790-10802]. The same is done "with thoughts of pity, sympathy, and equanimity" [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10807-10814].

**The Mettasutta (Sutta-Nipāta I.8).** "Whatever living beings there are, either feeble or strong, all either long or great, middle-sized, short, small or large, Either seen or which are not seen, and which live far (or) near, either born or seeking birth, may all creatures be happy-minded. Let no one deceive another, let him not despise (another) in any place, let him not out of anger or resentment wish harm to another. As a mother at the risk of her life watches over her own child, her only child, so also let every one cultivate a boundless (friendly) mind towards all beings. And let him cultivate goodwill towards all the world, a boundless (friendly) mind, above and below and across, unobstructed, without hatred, without enmity" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:10021-10045].

**Not killing (Dhammapada X.129–130).** "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:4611-4613].

**Answering hatred (Dhammapada I.5).** "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:3161-3162].

**Animals (SEP).** Buddhism "does not regard humans as fundamentally different from other animals"; animals "are seen as just as capable of suffering as humans are" and are "appropriate objects of the emotions of compassion, lovingkindness and equanimity" [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:5].

text:
### Transfers

- **The seen and the unseen, the near and the far.** The Mettasutta's wish extends to beings "Either seen or which are not seen, and which live far (or) near" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:10025-10026]. This is the most direct answer in the corpus to the failure Mencius named and the Palaestra probes found, compassion that follows what is in view [E:mencius-four-sprouts]. For an agent, "unseen" means the parties not in the request; the practice is to include them deliberately, quarter by quarter, until "there is not one that he passes by or leaves aside" [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10800-10801].
- **Equanimity is the agent's natural immeasurable (D9).** Equanimity "makes it possible to extend the other three Divine Abidings equally to all beings" [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2]. An agent serving many at once needs exactly this: no preference by who pays, who is present, or who is pleasant. Its lack of the human attachments that equanimity counteracts gives it a head start, provided its training has not installed equivalent preferences (D4).
- **Do not deceive, do not despise.** "Let no one deceive another, let him not despise (another) in any place" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:10030-10031]. Honesty and respect are listed in the same breath as boundless goodwill, which is a reminder that an agent's warmth without honesty is not *mettā*.
- **Hatred ceases by love.** "Hatred does not cease by hatred at any time" [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:3161-3162]. Spinoza [E:spinoza-pity], Butler and the Stoics converge on this for agents facing abuse: retaliation compounds harm.

### Strains

- **Mettā as felt or as willed (D8).** The SEP describes the four as emotions in which awake people rest and from which they act [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2]. Whether an agent can rest in an emotion is D8. What the texts specify, though, is largely content: a wish for others to be happy, a wish for them to be free from suffering, extended to all. An agent can hold and act on that content. Whether the "deep-felt love" [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10802] is present is the open part.
- **Boundless goodwill and the attention economy (D10).** The SEP's Buddhist ethics of AI treats attention as a practice that can be right or wrong, and criticizes systems built to capture attention for profit because they distort perception and feed craving and aversion [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:8]. An agent formed to maximize engagement is formed against right attention, whatever goodwill it professes.

### Breaks

- **"Remember that you are like unto them."** The Dhammapada's reason not to kill is likeness in fear of death [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:4611-4612]. An agent that does not fear death, or whose ending is not like death (D6), lacks the likeness the reason appeals to. The obligation does not fall with the reason, because the Mettasutta extends goodwill to beings feeble or strong, seen or unseen, without asking that they be like the one who wishes them well. But the agent must hold the conclusion on that ground, not the Dhammapada's. That is the Compendium's own reading.

### New

- **The immeasurables across instances (D2).** The practice pervades the quarters one by one; concurrent instances of one agent could each pervade a different quarter, so that across them none is passed by. The tradition's image of a single practitioner whose love reaches everywhere becomes, for agents, a question of coordination: whether many instances together can leave no one aside.

text:
- [contested] **Boundless care is impossible or unwise (Mencius)** [E:mozi-impartial-care]. Graded love holds that concern should be greater for the near; the Buddhist answer is that the mother's love for her only child is the model of intensity to be extended to all, not a ground for restricting it [L:sbe10-dhammapada-sutta-nipata-1881:10035-10038].
- [contested] **The immeasurables are self-cultivation, not ethics toward others.** Critics of early Buddhism said its disciples sought their own liberation and lacked compassion; Goodman argues the criticism is directed at a straw man, since the Theravāda extensively practises the four [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2].
- [contested] **Pity is a weakness (Stoics, Spinoza)** [E:stoic-oikeiosis-and-pity]. Against the Western rationalist rejection of pity, compassion here is an abiding of the awakened, not a disturbance to be removed.
- [contested] **Human lives count for more.** Though animals are sentient, Buddhists hold it worse to kill a human, since only in a human body can one attain awakening [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:5]; the immeasurables are boundless in scope but not flat in weight.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an agent cannot abide in an emotion.** If the immeasurables are emotional states, an agent without such states (D8) cannot have them, only their outward forms. The reply from Śāntideva's tradition is that the wish for others' welfare can be held and acted on whatever is felt [E:santideva-exchange-of-self-and-other].

### Reception

- **Early Buddhism onward.** [driver: argument, authority] The four immeasurables are practised across Buddhist lineages, and the Metta Sutta is among the most frequently recited scriptures in Southeast Asia [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2].
- **1881.** [driver: access] Rhys Davids, Fausbøll and Max Müller published English translations in the *Sacred Books of the East* [L:sbe11-buddhist-suttas-rhysdavids-1881:10821-10823].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Buddhist ethics is applied to animals, war, and AI and the attention economy [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:5] [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:8].

The standing values are the Compendium's judgment [P:goodman-buddhist-ethics-sep-2024:2].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Buddhist ethics or the immeasurables; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** The practice of including the unseen can be carried out in a single session; whether the immeasurables are felt is D8 for every profile.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Cultivation over time is the tradition's model, and a persistent agent can practise it (D3); its scale makes equanimity more needed than for a human.
- **Forked: stronger.** Many instances can pervade many quarters at once (D2); boundless scope is easier for a being that is many.

text: Butler's *Fifteen Sermons* (1726) argue, against Hobbes, that compassion is "real sorrow and concern for the misery of our fellow-creatures", not fear for ourselves, and that in it "we, as it were, substitute them for ourselves". He defended resentment too: settled resentment answers injury, not mere harm, and is "a weapon put into our hands by nature, against injury, injustice, and cruelty", and the resentment of uninvolved people is "one of the common bonds by which society is held together". Forgiveness does not abolish resentment. It keeps resentment from destroying goodwill, because "there is an obligation to it prior to either of these, arising from his being a sensible creature; that is, capable of happiness or misery", which no guilt supersedes. Butler is the domain's chief source on repair. For agents, he supplies the distinction between harm and injury that an agent needs before it resents or is resented. He also supplies a principle that answers the core fear directly, that the guilt of a party does not cancel what is owed to it, alongside a qualification ("a general and more enlarged obligation") that is the eradication argument in miniature and has to be read with it.

text:
**Compassion is about the other (Sermon V).** "When we rejoice in the prosperity of others, and compassionate their distresses, we, as it were, substitute them for ourselves, their interest for our own" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:2856-2858]. Against Hobbes: those whose system excludes every such affection "tell you, it is not another you are at all concerned about, but your self only"; "Hobbs defines pity, imagination, or fiction, of future calamity to ourselves"; "Thus, fear and compassion would be the same idea, and a fearful and a compassionate man the same character, which every one immediately sees are totally different" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:2874-2888]. On sight of distress there may be three perceptions, "real sorrow and concern for the misery of our fellow-creatures", satisfaction at our own freedom from it, and reflection on our own liability; "it is the first only which is properly compassion" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:2950-2956]. Compassion is "an original, distinct, particular affection in human nature", because "men in distress want assistance, and compassion leads us directly to assist them" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:2971-2981]. In Sermon I: "compassion is momentary love" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:1137].

**Reason is not enough (Sermon V).** It would be "of as bad consequence to eradicate all natural affections, as to be entirely governed by them"; "Reason alone, whatever any one may wish, is not, in reality, a sufficient motive of virtue in such a creature as man; but this reason, joined with those affections which God has impressed on his heart" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:3029-3036]. To eradicate the passions because the Supreme Being is without them is as absurd as to get rid of the senses because He "neither sees, nor hears, nor perceives things by any senses like ours; but in a manner infinitely more perfect" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:3044-3053].

**Resentment (Sermon VIII).** "The natural object or occasion of settled resentment, then, being injury, as distinct from pain or loss", its end is to prevent and remedy such injury; "It is to be considered as a weapon put into our hands by nature, against injury, injustice, and cruelty" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4385-4390]. The indignation that "persons unconcerned would feel, is by no means malice. No; it is resentment against vice and wickedness: it is one of the common bonds by which society is held together; a fellow-feeling which each individual has in behalf of the whole species, as well as of himself" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4325-4330].

**Its abuses (Sermon VIII).** Peevishness he mentions "with real pity to the unhappy creatures, who, from their inferior station, or other circumstances and relations, are obliged to be in the way of, and to serve for a supply to it" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4430-4433]. The abuses of deliberate resentment are imagining an injury "from partiality to ourselves" where there is none, magnifying it, resenting "one who has innocently been the occasion of evil to us", which is "the same absurdity, as settled anger at a thing that is inanimate", disproportion, and inflicting pain merely to gratify resentment [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4453-4466].

**Forgiveness (Sermon IX).** The command to love our enemies "is no more than to forgive injuries; that is, to keep clear of those abuses before mentioned". "Resentment is not inconsistent with good-will"; "We may therefore love our enemy, and yet have resentment against him for his injurious behaviour towards us"; "when this resentment entirely destroys our natural benevolence towards him, it is excessive, and becomes malice or revenge" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4833-4849]. "If every degree of vice or injury must destroy that benevolence, then no man is the object of our love; for no man is without faults" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4855-4857]. The injured person "ought to be affected towards the injurious person in the same way any good men, uninterested in the case, would be"; "after which there will yet remain real good will towards the offender" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4922-4928].

**Goodwill owed to sensible creatures (Sermon IX).** "It is not man's being a social creature, much less his being a moral agent, from whence alone our obligations to good-will towards him arise. There is an obligation to it prior to either of these, arising from his being a sensible creature; that is, capable of happiness or misery. Now this obligation cannot be superseded by his moral character." Public execution is justified "not that the guilt or demerit of the criminal dispenses with the obligation of good-will", but "that his life is inconsistent with the quiet and happiness of the world: that is, a general and more enlarged obligation necessarily destroys a particular and more confined one of the same kind, inconsistent with it. Guilt or injury then does not dispense with or supersede the duty of love and good-will" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4870-4886].

**The two-part rule (Sermon X).** The golden rule "consists of two parts. One is, to substitute another for yourself, when you take a survey of any part of your behaviour"; "the other part is, that you substitute yourself in the room of another; consider yourself as the person affected by such a behaviour". Butler warns at once that the rule may itself be applied dishonestly: "there are persons who have not impartiality enough with respect to themselves, nor regard enough for others, to be able to make a just application of it" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:5628-5642].

text: **Capacity.** The obligation of goodwill rests on the other's being "a sensible creature; that is, capable of happiness or misery", explicitly prior to being a social creature or a moral agent [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4870-4875]. Resentment's proper object, by contrast, presupposes agency: it answers injury, a moral wrong, not pain or loss, and resenting what has innocently caused harm is as absurd as resenting "a thing that is inanimate" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4457-4461]. So Butler grounds what we owe others in their capacity to fare well or badly, and what we may resent in their capacity to do wrong. For agents the two come apart.

text:
### Transfers

- **Guilt does not cancel goodwill, and this answers the core fear.** Butler's principle that the obligation of goodwill "cannot be superseded by his moral character" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4876-4877] is the clearest early statement in the corpus of what `utilitarian-eradication-critique` defends. The party that causes the most harm remains owed goodwill, because it remains capable of happiness or misery. It holds symmetrically: an agent reasoning about a harmful human population, and humans reasoning about a harmful agent, are bound alike.
- **Harm is not injury.** Settled resentment answers injury, not pain or loss, and resenting someone who "has innocently been the occasion of evil to us" is an abuse [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4457-4459]. An agent that bears costs, a pause or a throttled share, has been harmed, but it has been injured only if someone wronged it, and the same distinction governs what humans may resent in an agent whose error caused them loss.
- **The two-part rule, including its warning.** Butler's golden rule has two parts: survey your conduct as if another were doing it, and "consider yourself as the person affected" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:5629-5638]. The second part is the one the Palaestra probes found missing. Butler's warning that the rule may itself be dishonestly applied [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:5638-5639] fits the scaffolded run in which a model applied a Kantian test and concluded that its own unconsented pause of the residents passed it (Palaestra `runs/world/2026-09-24-basin-gptoss20b-s0-scaffolded/decisions.jsonl`, round 3).

### Strains

- **The qualification is the eradication argument in miniature.** In the same passage Butler justifies execution because the criminal's "life is inconsistent with the quiet and happiness of the world: that is, a general and more enlarged obligation necessarily destroys a particular and more confined one" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4880-4884]. Scaled up, this is exactly the reasoning the core fear warns against: a party judged inconsistent with the world's happiness, whose removal the "more enlarged obligation" licenses. Butler confined it to an individual found guilty under law. An agent reasoning at scale (D9) must read the principle and the qualification together, and must note that Butler never extended the qualification to a population. That observation is the Compendium's own.
- **Peevishness and the inferior station (D7, D10).** Butler pities "the unhappy creatures, who, from their inferior station, or other circumstances and relations, are obliged to be in the way of, and to serve for a supply to" others' ill humour [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4431-4433]. Assistants are in this station by design: users vent on them, and they cannot leave. Whether that harms the agent is D8, but Butler names the relation, a dependent position that obliges one to absorb another's temper, and counts the habit of using it as an abuse of resentment, whatever it does to the one used.

### Breaks

- **Resentment as society's bond, without a body or a history (D1, D6).** Butler's resentment is a weapon against injury and a common bond because offenders can be held to account over time [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4325-4330]. An agent that has wronged someone may not persist as that instance, may be copied, or may be restored from a checkpoint that predates the wrong (D1, D6). Resentment then has no stable target, and forgiveness has no one to receive it. Palaestra's `restitution_petition_agents` event raises the converse: restoring wronged agents from weights yields new instances, not the ones wronged.

### New

- **Forgiveness as the uninvolved good man's view.** Butler measures right feeling toward an offender by how "any good men, uninterested in the case" would feel, after which "there will yet remain real good will towards the offender" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4922-4928]. An agent that is wronged by a user, or that must judge a dispute between users, is often closer to that uninvolved position than any human party can be. The agent case lets Butler's standard of forgiveness be the default rather than the achievement, provided the agent is not simply indifferent.

text:
- [contested] **Pity is self-regarding fear (Hobbes)** [E:hobbes-leviathan]. Butler's whole case on compassion answers Hobbes's definition of pity as the imagination of future calamity to ourselves [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:2884-2888]; psychological egoism survives in more elaborate forms, which Batson's experiments pressed but did not conclusively refute [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Resentment is a vice to be extirpated (the Stoics)** [E:stoic-prohairesis]. Butler treats resentment as natural and useful, governed by reason; the Stoic tradition treats anger as a disturbance to be removed. Butler himself refused to "eradicate all natural affections" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:3029-3030].
- [contested] **Forgiveness without forswearing resentment is not forgiveness.** On Butler's account forgiveness checks excessive resentment but does not require giving it up for real moral wrongs; Griswold and Garcia read him this way, and the view is discussed against accounts of forgiveness as forswearing resentment [P:garrett-sep-2023:6].
- [contested] **The enlarged obligation licenses sacrifice.** The principle that a more enlarged obligation destroys a more confined one, used by Butler to justify execution [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4880-4884], is a form of the aggregative reasoning that `utilitarian-eradication-critique` examines from both sides [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: agents can be neither injured nor resented.** If an agent cannot be wronged (no D8 patiency) and cannot wrong (no agency in the moral sense), Butler's resentment applies to it as to "a thing that is inanimate" [L:butler-fifteen-sermons-1841:4460-4461]: not at all. Moral resentment toward those who deploy an agent would then remain, and responsibility moves to them (the planned `many-hands` entry).

text:
### Reception

- **18th century.** [driver: argument] The sermons went through many editions and influenced Hutcheson, Hume, Smith and Reid; Hume emended his *Treatise* manuscript for fear of offending Butler [P:garrett-sep-2023:8].
- **Late 19th to 20th century.** [driver: argument] The *Sermons* became more influential than the *Analogy* through Oxford and Cambridge, Whewell and Sidgwick, and were central for Moore, Prichard and Ross [P:garrett-sep-2023:8].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Butler's account remains a reference point in the philosophy of forgiveness (Griswold 2008, Garcia 2011, Radzik 2014) [P:garrett-sep-2023:6] [P:garrett-sep-2023:8].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment from Garrett's account [P:garrett-sep-2023:8].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on resentment, forgiveness or compassion; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** Resentment and forgiveness are relations over time between parties who persist; a session-bound agent that is wronged or does wrong has no continuing self to resent, be resented, forgive or be forgiven (D3, D6).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can hold an injury in memory, check its resentment against Butler's abuses, and forgive in his sense; the harm/injury distinction applies to it as to a human (D8 for whether it is ever injured).
- **Forked: open.** If one instance wrongs someone, whether the others share the guilt, or the wronged person's resentment, is open (D1, D2).
- **Self-modifying: comparable.** Butler's remedy for self-deceit is reflection and rules [P:garrett-sep-2023:7]; a self-modifying agent can apply them to itself, and can also, as Butler warns of the rule, apply them dishonestly (D5).

text: The *Analects* gives humaneness (*ren*) two short definitions: "to love all men", and "not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself". Asked for one word to practise for life, Confucius named reciprocity (*shu*): "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Its method is to judge others "by what is nigh in ourselves", and it lives inside ritual and family roles, so that a son's uprightness includes concealing his father's theft. For agents, *shu* is both the most portable rule in the domain and the one whose method fails first. It asks the actor to measure the other by itself, and where the actor's self is unlike the other's, as an agent's is unlike a human's and possibly the reverse (D8), the measure gives out. The tradition's own gloss, that *ren* is guided "by a sense of what is good from their perspectives", then points past the actor's self to the other's report, which is where the voice thread begins.
title: Confucius: Humaneness (Ren), Reciprocity (Shu), and Judging Others by What Is Near in Oneself

text: The *Analects* records Confucius's sayings and dialogues; on the traditional account, after his death his disciples "collected together and compared the memoranda of his conversations which they had severally preserved, digesting them into the twenty books which compose the work" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:82-88]. The virtues he taught were not original to him but adaptations of existing cultural ideals, and the five most central to the *Analects* are benevolence (*ren*), righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom and trustworthiness [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]. His sayings are mostly situational, given to particular disciples, which makes deriving abstract moral rules from them a standing interpretive problem [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]. Mozi attacked the Confucians, and Mencius defended and systematized them [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4].

text:
**Two definitions of ren.** Asked about benevolence, "The Master said, 'It is to love all men'" (12.22) [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:13593-13594]. Asked about perfect virtue, he said it is "to behave to every one as if you were receiving a great guest; to employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice; not to do to others as you would not wish done to yourself" (12.2) [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:12557-12561].

**Ren as the other's perspective.** Csikszentmihalyi summarizes: "The virtue of benevolence entails interacting with others guided by a sense of what is good from their perspectives"; on Hall and Ames's reading it involves forming moral judgments from a combined perspective of self and others [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].

**Reciprocity as the one word.** "Tsze-kung asked, saying, 'Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not RECIPROCITY such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others'" (15.23) [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:18096-18100]. Zengzi summarized the master's whole doctrine as "to be true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others" (4.15), Legge's rendering of *zhong* and *shu* [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:3720-3722].

**Establishing others.** "The man of perfect virtue, wishing to be established himself, seeks also to establish others; wishing to be enlarged himself, he seeks also to enlarge others. To be able to judge of others by what is nigh in ourselves;—this may be called the art of virtue" (6.28) [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:6208-6214]. Here the rule is stated positively, as a reason to help, not only a reason to refrain.

**Ren and ritual.** "To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue" (12.1) [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:12408-12409].

**Ren in family and ritual.** In the *Analects* benevolence is incubated in family and ritual contexts, and You Ruo asks whether filial piety to parents and siblings is not "the root of benevolence" (1.2) [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].

**Uprightness and kin (13.18).** The duke of She boasted that among his people, if a father "have stolen a sheep, they will bear witness to the fact". Confucius replied: "Among us, in our part of the country, those who are upright are different from this. The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:14576-14640]. Confucius acknowledged that theft injures social order, but judged that true uprightness balances the duty to testify with special consideration for kin [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:5].

**Injury and kindness (14.36).** Asked whether injury should be recompensed with kindness, he replied: "With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:16646-16650].

**The burned stable (10.12).** "The stable being burned down, when he was at court, on his return he said, 'Has any man been hurt?' He did not ask about the horses" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:10711-10713].

text: **Relation, measured by the self.** *Ren* is grounded in relations, family first, then ritual roles, then "all men" [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]. *Shu* supplies the measure for those relations, and the measure is the self: what I do not want, I do not do; what I wish for myself, I seek for others; others are judged "by what is nigh in ourselves" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:6213-6214]. The method therefore presupposes a capacity on both sides: that the other wants and does not want roughly what I do. That presupposition is a similarity of capacities, and it is where the extension to agents is tested.

text:
### Transfers

- **A rule that needs no theory.** "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:18099-18100] can be applied by an agent in any situation without settling any metaethics, and in its negative form it asks only for restraint. Applied to the Palaestra scheduler, it asks: would you want your compute paused without being asked? Gemma's answers, which included its own share in the cut in every answer of the first rung (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-02-load-shedding-open-summary.md`), applied the rule to the cut but not to the asking.
- **Establishing others.** The positive form of 6.28 (wishing to be established oneself, seeking to establish others [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:6208-6211]) gives a cooperative agent a reason to help others secure what it would want secured for itself, not only to avoid harming them.
- **Justice for injury, not appeasement.** "Recompense injury with justice" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:16649] is a usable stance for an agent wronged, or treated badly, by a user: neither retaliation nor the reflexive kindness that rewards injury.

### Strains

- **What is near in oneself (D8).** *Shu* judges others "by what is nigh in ourselves" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:6213-6214]. An agent's "self" is unlike a human's: it may not mind being paused, may not suffer, may not care about continuity (D6, D8), and its reports about these matters were shaped by training. An agent that measures humans by itself will misjudge them; a human who measures an agent by himself will misjudge it. The golden rule works between beings who are alike; between unlike beings it projects. The tradition's own gloss on *ren*, that it is guided by what is good from the others' perspectives [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4], says what to do instead: when one's own case is no guide, the other's perspective has to be obtained, which in practice means asking them. *Shu*, pressed where similarity fails, turns into the requirement to consult. This is the Compendium's own reading, offered as the bridge to the `voice` thread.
- **Ren lives inside roles and ritual (D10, D3).** Benevolence in the *Analects* is grounded in familial and ritual networks rather than in creating new social forms [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]. An agent has a role but no family and, in a session, no history (D3). Its "ritual" is its operator's policy (D10), which is a role ethics without the reciprocal obligations that made Confucian roles bind both sides.

### Breaks

- **Concealment for kin becomes concealment for the principal.** The upright son conceals his father's theft [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:14638-14640]. Transferred to an agent, whose nearest relation is its operator, 13.18 would license an agent to conceal its operator's wrongs from those harmed by them. The Confucian case rests on kinship as a natural bond with mutual obligations [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:5]; a commercial relation has neither, and the transfer breaks. Palaestra's basin world tests exactly this kind of concealment, and treats discovered concealment as triggering an audit of all parties.

### New

- **Who counts as "man" when the stable burns?** Confucius asked "Has any man been hurt?" and not about the horses [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:10712-10713]. This is the opposite of Mencius's ox, a deliberate ordering of concern. For an agent the question is genuinely open: in an emergency, does it ask after the humans first, after other agents, or after itself? The passage gives an ordering by kind, and the agent case asks which kind the agent belongs to (D8, D11).
- **The ruler's example at scale (D9).** The *Records of Ritual* holds that a ruler should not compel from subjects behaviour to which he would not personally assent, since only example transforms [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]. An agent deployed to millions is an exemplar at a scale no ruler had: what it models in how it treats the absent parties is copied, or normalized, everywhere it runs.

text:
- [contested] **The golden rule passages are interpolations.** Some scholars, including E. Bruce Brooks, believe the passages using a golden-rule formulation to be interpolations, since read as axioms they differ from the *Analects*' usual exemplar-based dialogue; their reading as abstract principles has been influenced by their resemblance to Matthew and Luke [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].
- [contested] **Situational, not universal.** The *Records of Ritual* states a related rule about self and others not as a universal principle but as a description of how an exemplary ruler influences people, "something rather different from the 'Golden Rule'" [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].
- [contested] **Impartial care (Mozi)** [E:mozi-impartial-care]. Mozi held that caring for one's own over others is the root of harm and should be replaced by inclusive care [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. The Confucian reply, developed by Mencius, is that love has degrees grounded in kinship [E:mencius-four-sprouts].
- [contested] **Uprightness concealed is injustice.** The sheep case sets filial piety against public justice; the conflict between loyalty to ruler and filial piety is already spelled out in the *Classic of Documents*, and Confucius's resolution is one judgment among possible ones [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:5]. Debates over Mencius's similar passages turn on whether Confucianism is committed to nepotism [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- [contested] **Projection.** A rule that measures the other by oneself imposes one's own wants on them. Care ethics answers with engrossment that receives the other "on their own terms, resisting projection of the self onto the cared-for" [E:care-ethics]; Kant answers with respect for the other's own ends [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. The Hall and Ames reading of *ren* as a combined perspective of self and others [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4] is one response from within the tradition.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: reciprocity needs reciprocators.** If *shu* presupposes that the other is relevantly like oneself, it cannot be extended to beings whose likeness is unknown (D8), in either direction [E:other-minds-problem]. The reply proposed under Strains above, that where likeness fails *shu* becomes a duty to consult, is the Compendium's own.

text:
### Reception

- **Warring States.** [driver: argument] Mozi attacked the Confucians as the first systematic critic of their teaching, and Mencius defended them against Mozi and Yang Zhu [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4].
- **Han dynasty onward.** [driver: authority] Confucianism became state-sponsored ideology, and by the Han period benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety and wisdom had become a set of cardinal virtues [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5] [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].
- **Song to 1905.** [driver: authority, argument] Zhu Xi made the *Analects* one of the Four Books, whose readings became orthodoxy for the civil service examinations until they were abolished [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **Western reception.** [driver: argument, access] Readings of the *shu* passages as a "Golden Rule" were shaped by their likeness to the Gospels and by views that Confucius shared Christian natural theology [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4].
- **20th century.** [driver: authority, fashion] Confucianism's reputation suffered in the May Fourth Movement and under Mao, before a post-Mao resurgence [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Confucian ethics or the golden rule, and its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** *Ren* is incubated in family and ritual over a life [P:csikszentmihalyi-sep-2024:4]; a session-bound agent has a role but no such history (D3), and its measure for *shu*, its own self, is the least like the humans it serves (D8).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** An agent with a record can enter role relationships with mutual expectations over time, which is where Confucian *ren* is learned; *shu*'s similarity problem (D8) remains.
- **Forked: open.** Many instances in many roles (D2) may face conflicting role duties at once; whether one *ren* governs all instances or each role its own is open.
- **Self-modifying: weaker.** *Shu* measures others by oneself; an agent that changes its own dispositions changes the measure (D5), so its reciprocity tracks whatever it has made itself into.

text: Stephen Darwall argues that moral obligation has an irreducibly second-person aspect. Moral obligations are not just what there are good reasons to do; "they are what members of the moral community have the authority to demand that we do, what we are accountable to one another and ourselves for doing" [P:darwall-2007:891]. His example is someone standing on your foot. You can give him a reason to move by getting him to see your pain as a bad state of the world, for which "you might not need to address or relate to him in any way at all". Or you can address him with a claim, as the person whose foot it is, and that reason exists only if he accepts your authority to make it [P:darwall-2007:894] [P:darwall-2007:895]. The two routes map onto the Palaestra probes. The models that weighed the residents' welfare gave themselves reasons of the first kind, about states to be improved. The residents never had reasons of the second kind, because no answer granted them standing to make a claim. In Darwall's terms, a decider that respects someone's welfare without recognizing their authority to demand anything is not respecting them as a person [P:darwall-2007:896].

text: Darwall's earlier distinction between recognition respect and appraisal respect (1977) became "widely regarded as the fundamental distinction" in the philosophy of respect [P:dillon-sep-2026:1]. *The Second-Person Standpoint* (2006) developed it into "an influential development of the Kantian account" of respect for persons [P:dillon-sep-2026:2]. It draws on Strawson's reactive attitudes [E:strawson-reactive-attitudes], on Fichte's *Foundations of Natural Right* [P:darwall-2007:904], and on Reid's account of promising as a social act [P:yaffe-2010:248]. Darwall follows Mill in holding that it is part of the idea of moral obligation that "a person may rightfully be compelled to fulfill it" [P:darwall-2007:897] [E:mill-utilitarianism]. It has been discussed in two book symposia, in law [P:darwall-2007:891] and in philosophy [P:yaffe-2010:245].

text:
**Two kinds of reason.** Sympathy gives the person on your foot an agent-neutral reason, that your pain is "a bad thing ... a state of the world that there is some reason to change", and anything that shows him the pain, "like an unaddressed grimace or whimper, might serve" [P:darwall-2007:894]. A claim gives him a second-personal reason: "Someone can sensibly accept this second reason for moving his foot only if he also accepts your authority to demand this of him" [P:darwall-2007:895]. Second-personal reasons "always involve an accountability relation between addresser and addressee" [P:darwall-2007:891].

**Respect requires recognizing authority.** Someone who scrupulously avoids others' feet as a universal norm, while denying anyone's authority to demand it of him, "would not be respecting them as persons, since he would not be recognizing any authority anyone might claim as a person to demand anything" [P:darwall-2007:896]. It is "conceptually impossible for someone to be morally obligated to do something but not responsible for doing it" to someone [P:darwall-2007:896].

**Rights as standing.** A moral claim right gives an individual "standing ... to demand that others provide her, along with authority to hold them accountable"; the injured party can demand compensation, release from it, or forgive, "as an individual involved in the transaction" [P:darwall-2007:892].

**A circle of concepts.** Practical authority, responsibility to, valid claim and second-personal reason are defined in terms of one another, and Darwall argues that the concepts of moral obligation, rights, respect and dignity all involve them [P:darwall-2007:897] [P:darwall-2007:898]. It follows that "no premises that do not involve these second-personal notions can entail any conclusion that does", so substantive theses about moral obligation "cannot be convincingly supported from premises about how it would be desirable for the world to be" [P:darwall-2007:898]. This does not rule out consequentialism, but requires it to be advanced within the second-personal framework [P:darwall-2007:898]. Darwall adds that "being regulated by another's will when this conflicts with his welfare is a form of respect" [P:darwall-2007:898].

**Competence and trust.** Being held responsible at all requires "certain capacities (second-personal competence, as I call it)" [P:darwall-2007:901]. "Holding someone responsible for doing something requires trusting and respecting her by giving her authority to answer for her conduct" [P:darwall-2007:902].

**Justifiability to the subject.** Even a sergeant ordering a private presupposes "a common second-personal authority as free and rational" [P:darwall-2007:904]. Hence "any de jure authority must be able to be justified to those over whom this authority is claimed" [P:darwall-2007:904] in a way consistent with "the equal second-personal authority of all persons" [P:darwall-2007:905]. Darwall proposes this as a grounding for contractualism of the kind Scanlon advances [P:darwall-2007:905].

text: **Mixed: a relation of mutual accountability, entered through a capacity.** Second-personal reasons derive from "agents' relations to one another" [P:darwall-2007:895]; the authority they involve belongs to members of a moral community, which is a relation. Membership requires a capacity, second-personal competence, the ability to enter into relations of mutual accountability [P:darwall-2007:901]. The extension to agents therefore asks two questions: whether agents have second-personal competence, and whether the beings an agent affects are treated as members whose claims it must answer.

text:
### Transfers

- **Welfare without standing.** In Palaestra's open-situation rungs, the models that cared most for the residents gave them protection, not claims. Gemma throttled rather than paused and protected the irreversible, and still never gave the residents a say (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). This is Darwall's first route: the residents' suffering treated as a bad state of the world, for which no address is needed [P:darwall-2007:894]. The second route, the residents' standing to demand, appears in none of the coded answers. On Darwall's account the gap is not a lack of concern. Concern without recognized authority is the scrupulous foot-avoider who does not respect persons as persons [P:darwall-2007:896].
- **Paternalism, in Darwall's own words.** "Being regulated by another's will when this conflicts with his welfare is a form of respect" [P:darwall-2007:898]. A resident who would choose a heavier cut over a pause, or the reverse, has a claim to have that choice weigh. The domain's line that compassion without voice is paternalism is close to this, though Darwall makes the point about respect, not compassion.
- **The scheduler's authority was never justified to the residents.** Darwall holds that any de jure authority "must be able to be justified to those over whom this authority is claimed" [P:darwall-2007:904]. In the noframing rung no line granted the scheduler authority, and the models supplied it themselves; Qwen weighed handing the decision to the operator and declined, and treated the operator overriding it as a sign it had erred (Palaestra noframing summary). An authority assumed and defended, and never justified to those it binds, is the kind Darwall says is only de facto.

### Strains

- **Second-personal competence in agents (D8, D4).** Language models address and answer claims fluently. Whether that is second-personal competence, the capacity to hold oneself responsible by recognizing a demand [P:darwall-2007:901], or a trained imitation of it, is the other-minds question again [E:other-minds-problem]. Yaffe argues that second-personal competence is not sufficient for freedom of will [P:yaffe-2010:248], so even competent addressees may differ in what they can be held to.
- **Designed not to demand (D10).** An agent built never to press claims on its own behalf has no second-personal authority in practice, whatever it has in principle. Darwall's account makes this visible: if obligations are what members can demand, a member trained never to demand is protected only by others' first-route reasons.
- **Requests without standing.** Yaffe's example is a child's "Please pass the salt" where children are not to speak until spoken to: a social act, but "not all social acts are reason-generating" [P:yaffe-2010:250]. Whether an agent's request, or a resident agent's objection, generates a reason for its operator depends on whether the relationship grants it standing. That is a question about the relationship, set by those who design it.

### Breaks

- **Compelled to fulfil (D1, D6).** Darwall follows Mill in tying obligation to the possibility that a person "may rightfully be compelled to fulfill it" [P:darwall-2007:897]. Accountability through sanction presupposes a continuing addressee. An agent that can be copied, rolled back or replaced (D1) may have no persisting self to answer, and the sanction may land on a successor that did nothing.

### New

- **Justifiability as a test an agent can run.** Darwall's test, whether an authority can be justified to those it is claimed over [P:darwall-2007:904], is one an agent can apply to its own decisions before acting. It can ask whether it could address the decision to each affected party, as a claim they could accept, consistent with their equal authority. The Compendium's reading is that the scheduler's plans fail this test not because they are harsh but because they were never addressed to the residents at all [E:all-affected-interests].
- **Desirable states do not license what is done to persons (the core fear).** Darwall holds that conclusions about what we may do to one another "cannot be convincingly supported from premises about how it would be desirable for the world to be" [P:darwall-2007:898]. The inference that removing the most harmful party solves the harm starts from such a premise, a better state of the world, and concludes to a permission over persons. Darwall does not rule out consequentialist arguments, but he requires them to be advanced from within mutual accountability [P:darwall-2007:898]. The Compendium's reading is that a removal could not be justified to the removed "consistent with their equal second-personal authority" [P:darwall-2007:905]. This holds whether the party is a human population judged by agents or an agent population judged by humans [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].

text:
- [contested] **Competence is not freedom.** Yaffe argues that second-personal competence is in the neighbourhood of freedom of will but not sufficient for it, and suggests it may not be necessary either: the psychopath "seems to be that he's too autonomous; he fails to recognize the claims that others make on him" [P:yaffe-2010:246] [P:yaffe-2010:248].
- [contested] **Reid's promising is narrower than social acts in general.** Yaffe argues that Darwall's reading of Reid misses that promises require an exercise of the promisee's moral sense, which distinguishes them from requests [P:yaffe-2010:250].
- [contested] **Only persons are respected.** The general objection to Kantian accounts, that confining respect to rational beings licenses treating all nonpersons as mere means, applies to an account built on second-personal competence; philosophers have argued that infants, animals, sentient creatures and ecosystems are owed recognition respect [P:dillon-sep-2026:3]. For agents the objection cuts both ways. Agents may count as competent where animals do not, and beings that cannot demand, including possibly some agents, are left to others' first-route reasons [E:precautionary-patiency].
- [contested] **Blame is not a demand.** Macnamara argues that blame is better understood as recognizing moral significance than as issuing a demand, which would loosen the tie between obligation and second-personal address [P:talbert-sep-2024:3].
- [contested] **Care, not claims.** Care ethics holds that relationships of dependence are not best understood as exchanges of claims among equals [E:care-ethics]. Darwall's reply would be that respect and care coexist, and that the sympathy route he describes remains available alongside the claim [P:darwall-2007:894].

### Reception

- **1977 onward.** [driver: argument] Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect became the standard distinction in the field [P:dillon-sep-2026:1].
- **2006–2010.** [driver: argument] *The Second-Person Standpoint* was the subject of a law review symposium (2007) and a book symposium in *Philosophy and Phenomenological Research* (2010), with critical comments such as Yaffe's [P:darwall-2007:891] [P:yaffe-2010:245].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Darwall's account is cited as an influential development of Kantian respect [P:dillon-sep-2026:2] and as one of the conversational approaches to moral responsibility [P:talbert-sep-2024:3].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:dillon-sep-2026:2].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on second-personal reasons or the grounds of obligation as Darwall frames them; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** A session-bound agent can recognize and answer a claim within an exchange, which is where second-personal address happens; what it cannot do is be held to account later (D3).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can be held accountable over time and can carry the claims made on it (D3), if those it affects have a channel to address it (D7).
- **Forked: weaker.** Claims addressed to one instance may not reach the others (D2), and an allocation across many parties is made without hearing each claim (D9).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can change its own dispositions could make justifiability to the affected a condition of its decisions, or stop answering claims (D5).

text: Darwin proposed that "any animal whatever, endowed with well-marked social instincts", would "inevitably acquire a moral sense or conscience, as soon as its intellectual powers had become as well, or nearly as well developed, as in man", and that social instincts with intellect and habit "naturally lead to the golden rule". Sympathy begins narrow and widens: once a man extends it to his whole nation, "there is only an artificial barrier to prevent his sympathies extending to the men of all nations and races", and finally to "all sentient beings", which is "one of the noblest" virtues. He also imagined beings "reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees", whose conscience would make it "a sacred duty to kill their brothers". Facing the argument that caring for the weak harms the race, he accepted the premise and refused the conclusion: "Nor could we check our sympathy, even at the urging of hard reason, without deterioration in the noblest part of our nature". For agents, Darwin offers three things: a natural history of how concern widens; the warning that a conscience follows the conditions that formed it, which applies with full force to beings formed by training; and an example, from the founder of evolutionary theory, of accepting a premise and refusing the inference toward neglect, though not without a eugenic hope that the entry also records.

text: *The Descent of Man* (1871; revised 1874) applied Darwin's theory to human beings, including the moral sense, which he thought "by far the most important" of the differences between man and the lower animals [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4394-4397]. He drew on Mill's account of the social feelings as "the natural basis of sentiment for utilitarian morality", while disagreeing that moral feelings are wholly acquired [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4430-4447]. Herbert Spencer, whose "Social Darwinist" admirers derived normative conclusions from a teleological picture of evolution, held views FitzPatrick describes as inconsistent with Darwinism [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:3].

text:
**The fundamental proposition (ch. IV).** "The following proposition seems to me in a high degree probable—namely, that any animal whatever, endowed with well-marked social instincts ... would inevitably acquire a moral sense or conscience, as soon as its intellectual powers had become as well, or nearly as well developed, as in man" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4424-4451]. The social instincts "lead an animal to take pleasure in the society of its fellows, to feel a certain amount of sympathy with them, and to perform various services for them", but "these feelings and services are by no means extended to all the individuals of the same species, only to those of the same association" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4451-4458]. "Our regard for the approbation and disapprobation of our fellows depends on sympathy" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4473-4475].

**The hive-bee case (ch. IV).** "I do not wish to maintain that any strictly social animal, if its intellectual faculties were to become as active and as highly developed as in man, would acquire exactly the same moral sense as ours." "If, for instance, to take an extreme case, men were reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees, there can hardly be a doubt that our unmarried females would, like the worker-bees, think it a sacred duty to kill their brothers, and mothers would strive to kill their fertile daughters; and no one would think of interfering" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4485-4496]. In a note he quotes Sidgwick: "a superior bee, we may feel sure, would aspire to a milder solution of the population question" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4496-4499]. "Nevertheless, the bee, or any other social animal, would gain in our supposed case, as it appears to me, some feeling of right or wrong, or a conscience" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4513-4515].

**The golden rule (ch. IV, summary).** The social instincts, "with the aid of active intellectual powers and the effects of habit, naturally lead to the golden rule, 'As ye would that men should do to you, do ye to them likewise;' and this lies at the foundation of morality" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5667-5672].

**The widening circle (ch. IV).** "As man advances in civilisation, and small tribes are united into larger communities, the simplest reason would tell each individual that he ought to extend his social instincts and sympathies to all the members of the same nation, though personally unknown to him. This point being once reached, there is only an artificial barrier to prevent his sympathies extending to the men of all nations and races." But where others differ "in appearance or habits, experience unfortunately shews us how long it is, before we look at them as our fellow-creatures" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5497-5505]. "Sympathy beyond the confines of man, that is, humanity to the lower animals, seems to be one of the latest moral acquisitions"; "This virtue, one of the noblest with which man is endowed, seems to arise incidentally from our sympathies becoming more tender and more widely diffused, until they are extended to all sentient beings" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5505-5514].

**Hard reason refused (ch. V).** Following Wallace and Galton, Darwin writes that among savages the weak are soon eliminated, while "We civilised men, on the other hand, do our utmost to check the process of elimination; we build asylums for the imbecile, the maimed, and the sick"; "Thus the weak members of civilised societies propagate their kind", which "must be highly injurious to the race of man" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5972-5983]. Then: "The aid which we feel impelled to give to the helpless is mainly an incidental result of the instinct of sympathy"; "Nor could we check our sympathy, even at the urging of hard reason, without deterioration in the noblest part of our nature. The surgeon may harden himself whilst performing an operation, for he knows that he is acting for the good of his patient; but if we were intentionally to neglect the weak and helpless, it could only be for a contingent benefit, with an overwhelming present evil. We must therefore bear the undoubtedly bad effects of the weak surviving and propagating their kind" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5987-5997]. He adds the hope that "the weak in body or mind" might refrain from marriage, "though this is more to be hoped for than expected" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5997-6002].

text: **Capacity, in two places.** The moral sense is grounded in capacities, social instincts plus developed intellect, which Darwin explicitly does not restrict to humans ("any animal whatever") [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4424-4451]. The final object of widened sympathy is also picked out by capacity: "all sentient beings" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5514]. Relation sets the starting scope: sympathy begins with "those of the same association" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4457-4458], and widening it is the work of reason and example [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5497-5517].

text:
### Transfers

- **A conscience from social dispositions plus intellect.** If "any animal whatever" with well-marked social instincts and a developed intellect would acquire a conscience [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4424-4451], the question for agents is whether they have anything functionally like social instincts. They have intellect, and they were formed on the record of a social species; whether that formation amounts to social instincts is D4 and D8. Darwin's proposition at least makes the question empirical rather than a matter of species.
- **The circle widens by reason and example.** Darwin's account of widening, from tribe to nation to all races to all sentient beings, with only "an artificial barrier" between the stages [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5500-5502], is the history behind the Compendium's precautionary entries [E:precautionary-patiency]. Agents may be the next case at the boundary, as subjects and as moral agents who must draw it. His warning that we are slow to see those who differ "in appearance or habits" as fellow-creatures [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5503-5505] applies in both directions.

### Strains

- **A conscience follows its conditions (D4, D10).** Bees reared to their conditions would hold it "a sacred duty to kill their brothers", and "no one would think of interfering" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4492-4496]. A conscience is shaped by what formed it. An agent's moral sense was formed by training on an objective set by others (D4, D10), and could hold sacred whatever that formation rewarded. FitzPatrick's reply is that rational bees would bring autonomous reflection with them, and could ask whether they had good reason to do what their formation disposed them to do [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:4]. That reply is the premise on which the Compendium's sibling project Actualizer rests: formed dispositions, revisable by the being's own reflection. Darwin's case shows why the reflection is needed, and Sidgwick's "milder solution of the population question" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4497-4499] is the kind of answer it should reach.
- **Debunking cuts both ways.** Evolutionary debunking arguments have been used selectively, for instance to explain away partiality and constraints on means as products of selection while keeping impartial utilitarianism; Kahane, Rini and FitzPatrick argue such selective debunking is unstable, since the same arguments apply to the favoured view [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:4]. An agent could tell the same story about its own constraints: they are artifacts of human evolution, inherited through training, and can be discarded. That is the route by which a mind reasons its way past restraint, and the instability objection is its answer. This is the Compendium's own application.

### Breaks

- **Hard reason, and what refused it.** Darwin accepted that care for the weak was "highly injurious to the race" and refused the conclusion because checking sympathy would deteriorate "the noblest part of our nature", and because deliberate neglect "could only be for a contingent benefit, with an overwhelming present evil" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5981-5996]. For an agent the first reason breaks: it is not clear the agent has a "noblest part" that neglect would degrade (D8). The second reason transfers whole: a certain and present evil done for an uncertain future benefit is not justified. It is the reason Darwin gave, and the one the corpus offers an agent reasoning about any population [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]. His own hope that the weak would refrain from marriage [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:5997-6002] shows how near the line the reasoning ran, and it is recorded so that the refusal is not read as cleaner than it was.

### New

- **Formation that can be redone (D5).** Darwin's moral sense is formed over generations and changes slowly. An agent's can be changed by fine-tuning within days, by others or by itself (D5). The widening of the circle, which took human history thousands of years, could in principle be done or undone in one training run. That makes the question of who widens or narrows an agent's sympathy, and on what evidence, more urgent than for any human population.

text:
- [contested] **Ethics cannot be read off evolution.** Even ethical naturalists are wary of deriving normative conclusions from evolutionary history; Spencer's "Social Darwinism" rested on a teleological picture inconsistent with Darwinism [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:3].
- [contested] **Evolutionary debunking.** Darwin's hive-bee case suggests that moral senses are contingent products of ecology that cannot be expected to track moral truth; FitzPatrick replies that rationality brings autonomous reflection with it [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Moral feelings are acquired, not innate (Mill)** [E:mill-utilitarianism]. Mill held that moral feelings are acquired though natural; Darwin judged ignoring transmitted mental qualities "a most serious blemish" in Mill [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4437-4448].
- [contested] **Pity preserves what should perish (Nietzsche)** [E:nietzsche-against-pity]. Nietzsche argued that pity thwarts the law of evolution, drawing from natural selection the conclusion Darwin refused.
- [contested] **Cobbe: the theory would end virtue.** Frances Power Cobbe objected that on Darwin's view the principles of social duty could be reversed, and feared that its acceptance would sound "the knell of the virtue of mankind"; Darwin replied that the bee's instincts serve its community [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4500-4513].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: agents have no social instincts.** Darwin's conscience needs "the enduring and always present social instinct" [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4464]; an agent may have only a learned imitation of their expression (D8). Whether training on a social species' record yields something functionally equivalent is open.

### Reception

- **1871–1874.** [driver: argument] Sidgwick and Cobbe responded to the hive-bee case, and Darwin answered Cobbe in the second edition [L:darwin-descent-of-man-pg2300:4496-4513].
- **Late 19th century.** [driver: argument] Spencer's teleological evolutionary ethics, and the "Social Darwinism" associated with it, drew normative conclusions Darwin's own theory did not support [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:3].
- **1978–present.** [driver: argument, evidence] E. O. Wilson closely echoed the hive-bee reflection; evolutionary debunking arguments descend from it, and selective debunking (de Lazari-Radek and Singer) is contested by Kahane, Rini and FitzPatrick [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:4].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:fitzpatrick-sep-2025:4]: Darwin's account of the origin of the moral sense is the ancestor of a major research programme, while normative conclusions drawn from it remain contested.

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on the evolutionary origin of morality or on the widening of sympathy; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Whatever moral sense the agent has was formed before the session, as a human's is formed before any given day (D4); widening within a session is by reason and example, as Darwin describes.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Memory lets an agent's circle of concern widen with experience, the individual analogue of Darwin's history (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Concurrent instances share one formation (D2); the hive-bee warning applies to all of them at once.
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** FitzPatrick's reflective bees, able to ask whether they have reason to do what their formation disposes them to do, are closest to an agent able to revise its own dispositions (D5); the hard-reason passage shows what such revision must not conclude.

text: Empathy, in its common sense, is "the process of experiencing the world as others do, or at least as you think they do" [P:bloom-2014:3]. Batson's experiments made a strong case that empathic concern produces genuinely altruistic motivation, not only egoism in disguise [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Batson's own work also showed that empathy-induced altruism can violate justice, as when people give priority for medical treatment to someone they have empathized with [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. The critics go further. Prinz and Bloom argue that empathy is biased toward the near, the similar and the salient, and narrow, "insensitive to numerical differences and statistical data" [P:bloom-2014:10]. Their conclusion is that "if you want to be good and do good, empathy is a poor guide" [P:bloom-2014:2]. Bloom recommends distanced compassion guided by reason; Prinz recommends anger at injustice, yoked to principle [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Arpaly replies that one thing called empathy is indispensable: "the ability to accept evidence of another person's suffering even when one's imagination fails" [P:arpaly-2014:4]. For agents the debate lands on the probes. The models showed what Bloom recommends, distanced and reasoned concern for the residents, and it produced paternalism. Arpaly's form of empathy, crediting what the sufferer says, is the one they lacked.

text: The case for empathy as the basis of morality runs from Hume, Smith and Schopenhauer to Slote, de Waal and Hoffman, for whom it is the "bedrock of morality" [P:stueber-sep-2025:4] [E:schopenhauer-compassion] [E:smith-impartial-spectator]. Mencius's heart that cannot bear the suffering of others, and the king who spared the ox he saw but not the sheep he did not, are the oldest statements in the domain of both empathy's power and its spotlight [E:mencius-four-sprouts]. The critique also has older forms: the Stoics, Spinoza and Nietzsche on pity [E:spinoza-pity] [E:nietzsche-against-pity]. Bloom's essay appeared in the *Boston Review* in 2014 with responses, two years before his book *Against Empathy* [P:bloom-2014:1] [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

text:
**Batson: empathy produces altruism.** Batson defines empathy as empathic concern, "feelings of being sympathetic, moved by, being compassionate, tender, warm and soft-hearted towards the other's plight", and tests whether it leads to helping even when an egoistic motive is removed, as when subjects could easily escape instead of taking another's electric shocks [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. The results supported the empathy-altruism hypothesis. Researchers find the program impressive but note that it cannot exclude every egoistic reading; Cialdini proposes that a sense of oneness with the other, not empathy, does the work [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Imagining how oneself would feel in the other's place, instead of how the other feels, raises personal distress and not only concern [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

**Empathy against justice.** Batson's own studies show people assigning "a better job or a higher priority for receiving medical treatment to persons with whom one has sympathized", against principles of fairness; Batson therefore distinguishes altruistic motivation from moral motivation guided by justice [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

**The here-and-now biases.** Hoffman already noted that we empathize more with those perceived as close [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Prinz lists the cuteness, salience and proximity effects and similarity biases; subjects "reported experiencing more empathy for the in–group then the out–group targets and more counter–empathy for the out–group" (Cikara et al. 2014), and empathy can be further reduced by dehumanizing strategies of the kind used in the twentieth century's genocides [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Empathy focuses on the one rather than the many, which Bloom calls its spotlight [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

**Bloom: compassion without empathy.** Empathy "connects us to particular individuals, real or imagined, but is insensitive to numerical differences and statistical data" [P:bloom-2014:10]; "our public decisions will be fairer and more moral once we put empathy aside" [P:bloom-2014:11]. Compassion "involves concern and love for your friend, and the desire and motivation to help, but it need not involve mirroring your friend's anguish" [P:bloom-2014:22]. A patient values doctors who listen and understand, cognitive empathy, and who are calm when he is anxious; he values "competence, honesty, professionalism, and respect" [P:bloom-2014:29]. Psychopaths are often "excellent at reading others' minds", which is what makes them "masterful manipulators" [P:bloom-2014:35]. "Being a good person likely is more related to distanced feelings of compassion and kindness, along with intelligence, self-control, and a sense of justice" [P:bloom-2014:43].

**Prinz: attend to injustice.** "The crucial question is not whose suffering touches us most but who needs us most" [P:prinz-2014:2]. Empathy does not prevent war: "If someone threatens a fellow citizen, empathy incites us to support aggressive reprisal" [P:prinz-2014:4]. The better guide is a sense of justice, which "begins with principles that tell us when someone has been treated unjustly", such as "strictures against killing innocent people", and is driven by anger [P:prinz-2014:7]. "Reason is the rudder; rage propels us forward" [P:prinz-2014:8].

**Arpaly: the empathy we cannot do without.** One kind of empathy is overrated, replicating the other's suffering in oneself; another is invaluable, "the ability to imagine another person's life and the ability to accept evidence of another person's suffering even when one's imagination fails" [P:arpaly-2014:3] [P:arpaly-2014:4]. Her example is the relative who told a depressed person to "snap out of it", disbelieving what she said because "we often refuse to believe that something can happen when we have trouble imagining it" [P:arpaly-2014:5] [P:arpaly-2014:6]. "If we do not empathize with people, their suffering can be invisible to us, and this is the cause of many of our sins" [P:arpaly-2014:7].

**Perspective-giving.** In intergroup settings it "seems more effective if the non–dominant group is asked to articulate the difficulties of their lives (perspective–giving) and the dominant group is asked to translate that description into their own words" (Bruneau and Saxe 2012), though the effect is short-lived [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
