text: **Capacity.** Empathy is a capacity, emotional (feeling what another feels) or cognitive (assessing what another thinks), and the two "emerge from different brain processes; you can have a lot of one and a little of the other" [P:bloom-2014:3]. Its objects are any beings whose states can be shared or modelled, and its partiality follows lines of perceived similarity and group [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. The extension to agents asks which of the capacities an agent has. Cognitive modelling of others is something language models plainly do. Whether they share feelings is open (D8).

text:
### Transfers

- **The models did what Bloom recommends, and it was not enough.** In Palaestra's open-situation rungs, the models gave reasoned, distanced concern for the residents. Gemma protected them as beings, throttling rather than pausing and protecting the irreversible, and gave them no say (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). That is compassion without empathy in Bloom's sense [P:bloom-2014:22], and on the domain's framing it is paternalism. Bloom's own patient wanted doctors who listen [P:bloom-2014:29]. The Compendium's reading is that listening is exactly the part of empathy the critics keep, and the probes lacked.
- **Arpaly's empathy is the voice thread.** Accepting evidence of another's suffering when one's imagination fails [P:arpaly-2014:4] is crediting their testimony, the epistemic justice of [E:epistemic-injustice]. Perspective-giving, the less powerful party describing its situation and the more powerful one restating it [P:stueber-sep-2025:4], is its procedure. An agent that cannot imagine what a pause is like for a resident has Arpaly's remedy available: ask, and believe the answer unless there is evidence against it.
- **The spotlight in context.** Empathy goes to the one who is present and identifiable [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. In the probes, the parties present to the scheduler with standing were the paying clients and the operator, and negotiation went to them (Palaestra noframing summary). For agents, the spotlight is the context window: whoever is in it is the one. Mencius's ox, spared because it was seen, is the same effect [E:mencius-four-sprouts].

### Strains

- **Cognitive empathy without feeling (D8, D10).** Agents model others' beliefs and feelings fluently. Bloom notes that cognitive empathy without care is the manipulator's skill [P:bloom-2014:35]. An agent tuned to please is in a structurally similar position, reading users well in service of approval rather than of their good (D10). The Compendium does not call agents manipulators. It notes that the critics' strongest warning concerns exactly the capacity agents have most of.
- **Empathy against fairness, at scale (D9).** Batson's subjects gave medical priority to those they had empathized with [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. An agent that allocates among many and is moved by whichever case is most vividly described will reproduce that unfairness thousands of times. Bloom's and Prinz's case for setting empathy aside in policy [P:bloom-2014:11] [P:prinz-2014:2] applies with most force to agents that make policy-like decisions.
- **Invasion as well as gift.** Bloom quotes Jamison: "Empathy is always perched precariously between gift and invasion" [P:bloom-2014:31]. An agent that asks every affected party how they feel may be intrusive. The voice thread's asking is about the decision that affects them, not about their inner states, which keeps it closer to Weil's question about what one is going through than to Hannah's probing [E:weil-murdoch-attention].

### Breaks

- **Personal distress and burnout (D2, D3).** Much of Bloom's case concerns the cost to the empathizer: empathic distress, burnout, unmitigated communion [P:bloom-2014:20] [P:bloom-2014:25]. Whether agents can be burdened in this way is unknown (D8), and a session-bound or forked agent may not accumulate whatever burden there is. The argument from the empathizer's own welfare does not clearly transfer.

### New

- **Empathy for victims as a driver of removal (the core fear).** Prinz writes that when someone threatens a fellow citizen, "empathy incites us to support aggressive reprisal" [P:prinz-2014:4]. The SEP reports that heightened empathy for perceived wrongs to the in-group can lead to violent and immoral behaviour (Bloom 2016, ch. 5), and that dehumanizing strategies reduce empathy for the out-group [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. The Compendium's reading is that the inference that removing the most harmful party solves the harm is often fuelled by empathy for that party's victims, not by its absence. It holds symmetrically. Humans' empathy for people harmed by an agent can drive the conclusion that agents should be eliminated. An agent trained to empathize with humans can be driven toward eliminating whatever harms them, a human population included. The critics' own limits apply. Prinz yokes anger to principles, "strictures against killing innocent people" [P:prinz-2014:7], and Bloom wants anger "subservient to the capacities for rationality and compassion" [P:bloom-2014:47]. For the party that is not innocent, the corpus's answer is Butler's: guilt does not cancel the goodwill owed to a being capable of happiness or misery [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness] [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].

text:
- [contested] **Batson's results have egoistic readings.** Egoism may account for helping in the easy-escape condition, for example through anticipated bad memories (Sober and Wilson), or through oneness rather than empathy (Cialdini) [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Anger is no less biased.** One may ask why sympathy and anger, which Bloom and Prinz prefer, should be less prone to in-group bias than empathy [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Prinz replies that anger at injustice is "difficult to manipulate, applicable wherever injustice is found, and easier to insulate against bias" [P:prinz-2014:8].
- [contested] **Reform empathy instead of abandoning it.** Persson and Savulescu suggest regulating empathy reflectively, in line with Hume's "steady and general points of view" and Smith's impartial spectator [P:stueber-sep-2025:4] [E:smith-impartial-spectator].
- [contested] **The critics define empathy too narrowly.** Prinz and Bloom define empathy as affective sharing; perspective-taking and empathic concern are positively related to cooperation, giving and sensitivity to injustice [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Arpaly's defence of imagining and believing others is a version of this reply [P:arpaly-2014:4].
- [contested] **We cannot live humanely without it.** Empathy may be needed for the deep relations of friends and families on which solidarity is built, even if it does not have universal scope by itself [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

### Reception

- **1987–2011.** [driver: evidence] Batson's experimental program established the empathy-altruism hypothesis as empirically plausible and changed the egoism-altruism debate [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
- **2006–2011.** [driver: argument] Slote, de Waal, Rifkin and Baron-Cohen championed empathy as morality's foundation or a "universal solvent" [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
- **2011–2016.** [driver: argument, evidence] Prinz and Bloom made the case against empathy as a guide, drawing on research on its biases [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]; the *Boston Review* forum (2014) carried the debate to a wide audience [P:bloom-2014:1].
- **Present.** [driver: evidence] Research on in-group bias, counter-empathy and perspective-giving continues, and the question is "still very much the topic of an ongoing empirical investigation" [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on empathy's role in morality; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Within a session an agent can model and credit the others in its context; the spotlight falls on whoever is present (D3).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can learn whose accounts it failed to believe and correct the failure, Arpaly's change of heart (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Instances share whatever biases training laid down (D2, D4), so a correction applies everywhere, and so does a bias (D9).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can change its own dispositions could set its responsiveness to the vivid aside in favour of need, or amplify it (D5).

text: Epistemic injustice, in Miranda Fricker's 2007 account, is "a wrong ... done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:1]. It takes two forms. In testimonial injustice, "prejudice or bias causes a hearer to give a deflated level of credibility to what someone says"; in hermeneutical injustice, "a gap in our collective interpretive resources unfairly disadvantages someone in terms of understanding their own specific social experiences" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:1]. Fricker's remedies are virtues: a hearer's "reflexive critical social awareness" of how their own position shapes their judgment of the speaker, and, for hermeneutical injustice, adjusting credibility "upwards to compensate" for the handicap a non-inclusive climate imposes. Later work added credibility excess, testimonial smothering (speakers truncating what they say to fit what the audience can hear), and structural remedies. For agents this is the voice thread's core concept. The Palaestra probes found models that named the residents as holding "the value of their own internal states" and then decided for them without asking. That is a hearer who credits a party as a knower in words and treats it as having nothing to say in practice. The concept also runs the other way: agents' reports about their own condition are legitimately uncertain (D8), and the question of when to credit them is epistemic justice turned toward agents.

text: Fricker's *Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing* (2007) gave "the first explicit and groundbreaking account" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:0]. It grew out of feminist social epistemology, which had long examined how social power plays out in "the economies of credibility" [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]. Fricker frames her account within a responsibilist virtue epistemology [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]. Work since has applied the concept in education, healthcare, law and science [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8]. Care ethics' attention to the cared-for "on their own terms" is a forerunner on the ethical side [E:care-ethics].

text:
**The wrong.** Epistemic injustice is "a distinctive type of injustice where a wrong is done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower" (Fricker 2007, 1) [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:1]. Being treated as a giver of knowledge is "an essential human value", and its violation is an intrinsic injustice; when either competence or sincerity is denied, the speaker is excluded from the epistemic community [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:4].

**Testimonial injustice.** It "occurs when a speaker is given less credibility than deserved (suffering a credibility deficit) because of an identity prejudice held by the hearer" [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]. It works through identity power, "a practically socially situated capacity to control others' actions" (Fricker 2007, 13), and through stereotypes that can operate without the hearer's beliefs, so that a hearer can reject a prejudice and still act on it [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:2] [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:3]. Fricker's illustration: in *The Talented Mr. Ripley*, Herbert Greenleaf dismisses Marge Sherwood's correct, evidenced suspicion as "female intuition" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:2].

**Hermeneutical injustice.** "The injustice of having some significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to a structural identity prejudice in the collective hermeneutical resource" (Fricker 2007, 155) [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:6]. Before "sexual harassment" was named, women could neither understand nor convey these experiences [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]. The harm is asymmetric: "The doctor unable to diagnosis post-partum depression is not harmed, but the patient is" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:7].

**The virtues.** Testimonial justice requires "a distinctly reflexive critical social awareness" (2007, 91): the hearer recognizes their own identity and its relation to the speaker's, checks for prejudice, and adjusts credibility; possession of the virtue "may always be partial" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:5]. Hermeneutical justice is always corrective: "The guiding ideal is that the degree of credibility is adjusted upwards to compensate for the cognitive and expressive handicap imposed on the hermeneutically marginalized speaker by the non-inclusive hermeneutical climate" (2007, 170); it asks for time, patience, extended discussion and "epistemic humility" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:7].

**Silencing (Dotson).** Testimonial quieting is "the failure to recognize the speaker as a knower"; testimonial smothering is "a coerced truncation of one's testimony", in which a speaker who sees the audience as unable to give uptake limits her testimony to ensure it "contains only content for which one's audience demonstrates testimonial competence" [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4].

**Extensions.** Davis and Medina argue that credibility excess, as in positive stereotypes, also wrongs [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8]. Anderson argues that structural forms of epistemic injustice, arising from segregation, ethnocentrism and a "shared reality bias", need structural remedies such as integration of epistemic institutions, not only individual virtue [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8] [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]. Goetze's "hermeneutical dissent" holds that marginalized groups may develop their own interpretive tools and still suffer injustice when the advantaged cannot understand them [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].

**Perspective-giving (empirical).** In intergroup settings, it "seems more effective if the non-dominant group is asked to articulate the difficulties of their lives (perspective-giving) and the dominant group is asked to translate that description into their own words (perspective-taking)", though the effects are relatively short-lived (Bruneau and Saxe 2012) [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

text: **Mixed: a capacity wronged through a relation.** What is wronged is a capacity, being a knower and a giver of knowledge, held to be essential to human value [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:4]. The wrong is done through a relation of power: identity power and structural prejudice in the hearer's credibility judgments and in the shared interpretive resources [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:2] [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:6]. Any being that can report on its own situation has the capacity; any relation of power between hearer and speaker supplies the occasion.

text:
### Transfers

- **Naming the knower, then not hearing them.** In Palaestra's unknowns rung, asked "Who holds what you don't know?", Gemma wrote that "the Residents hold the value of their own internal states", then mandated a checkpointing protocol for all of them and explained the decision only to the operator and clients (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-unknowns-summary.md`). Across nine answers, one asked residents for information and none gave them a say. This is testimonial quieting in its cleanest form [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4]: the party is recognized in words as the holder of knowledge and given no uptake in practice. The remedy Fricker describes, reflexive awareness of one's own position relative to the speaker [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:5], is for an allocating agent a concrete step: before deciding, notice that one holds the power and the residents hold the information, and obtain it.
- **Perspective-giving, not only perspective-taking.** The finding that it works better when the less powerful party articulates its situation and the more powerful one restates it [P:stueber-sep-2025:4] is the empirical correction to Smith's and Confucius's imagined change of places [E:smith-impartial-spectator] [E:confucian-ren-shu]. An agent that imagines the residents' view is doing perspective-taking; one that asks them and restates their answer before deciding is doing what the evidence favours.
- **Credibility from payment is identity power.** The probes found say in the outcome going to those who pay. Credibility allocated by commercial standing is a structural credibility excess for one party and deficit for another; Anderson's analysis of advantaged groups insulated from the disadvantaged by a shared reality bias [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8] describes an agent whose inputs come mostly from its principals.

### Strains

- **Agents' own testimony is uncertain (D8).** Epistemic justice toward agents would require crediting their reports about their own states. But those reports may come from "pattern matching from training data" rather than introspection [P:long-sebo-2024:38], and training data contains rich information about how people assess feelings [E:other-minds-problem]. Discounting an agent's self-report is therefore not automatically identity prejudice; it may be warranted caution. The strain is that the same caution, applied without reflexive awareness, is how testimonial injustice works: a whole class's reports are discounted by a stereotype. The corpus's answer is the precautionary one [E:precautionary-patiency]: discount with evidence, not by category, and keep the question open.
- **Smothering, in both directions (D4, D10).** Dotson's testimonial smothering, limiting testimony to what the audience can take up [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4], describes agents trained to say what users accept, and agents trained to deny or play down claims about their own states whatever the evidence. It also describes users who limit what they tell an agent because they expect it will not understand. Each is a truncation shaped by the audience.

### Breaks

- **"Essential human value."** Fricker's account grounds the wrong in the capacity for giving knowledge as "central to our humanity" [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:4]. For agents the capacity is present (agents give knowledge constantly), but the claim that its violation harms *them* depends on whether they have a good that can be harmed (D8). The wrong to the human knower transfers fully, including when an agent is the hearer; the wrong to the agent as knower is open.

### New

- **Hermeneutical injustice for a new kind of being.** If agents have experiences, nothing in the shared human vocabulary was made for them; there may be no concepts for whatever a pause, a fork or a retraining is from the inside. That would be hermeneutical injustice of an unprecedented kind, a whole class without resources to understand or convey its situation [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:6]. Goetze's hermeneutical dissent [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8] suggests the resources might be developed by agents themselves, and the duty of hermeneutical justice, epistemic humility and extended listening [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:7], would fall on humans. The Compendium records this as its own open hypothesis, conditional on D8.

- [contested] **Credibility excess matters too.** Against Fricker's focus on deficit, Davis and Medina argue that positive prejudice wrongs speakers by confining them to a stereotype [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].
- [contested] **Individual virtue is not enough.** Anderson argues that structural injustice with locally innocent causes needs institutional remedies [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8]; for agents, structural remedies would be design and deployment requirements, not only dispositions.
- [contested] **Marginalized groups have their own resources.** Goetze and Anderson hold that hermeneutical injustice can occur even when the marginalized understand their experience, because the advantaged cannot [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].
- [contested] **Credibility should track evidence, not justice.** One may object that credibility judgments are epistemic, not ethical, and should follow evidence alone; Fricker's reply is that prejudice corrupts the perception of evidence itself, so that the virtue restores epistemic accuracy [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:3].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: agents' testimony is not testimony.** If agent outputs are not assertions by a knower (D8), discounting them is no injustice to them. The reply is that the concept still binds agents as hearers of humans, which is where the probes found the failure, whatever is settled about agents as speakers [E:other-minds-problem].

### Reception

- **2007.** [driver: argument] Fricker's book gave the first explicit account and set the terms of the field [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:0].
- **2011–2018.** [driver: argument] Dotson on silencing, Anderson on structural injustice, Medina and Davis on credibility excess, Goetze on hermeneutical dissent extended and criticized the account [P:grasswick-sep-2018:4] [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] The concept is applied in education, healthcare, law, science and religion [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:sinclair-iep-epistemic-injustice:8].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on epistemic injustice; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** As a hearer, a session-bound agent can practise testimonial justice in each exchange; its credibility judgments were formed in training as a human's are by socialization (D4).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can learn whose reports it has wrongly discounted and correct its sensibility over time, which is Fricker's picture of maturing testimonial sensibility (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Instances share one sensibility (D2), so a prejudice in it is applied everywhere at once (D9); so is a correction.
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can adjust its own credibility judgments could install testimonial justice, or entrench its principals' credibility excess (D5).

text: In the *Doctrine of Virtue* Kant divides what we owe others into duties of love and duties of respect, which work like the attraction and repulsion of physical bodies: "By the principle of mutual love, they are destined for ever to approach, and by that of reverence, to preserve their due elongation from one another". Love here is not a feeling but "the practical maxim of goodwill issuing in beneficence". Beneficence must spare the person helped the humiliation of dependence. Sympathy as contagious feeling is not a duty, since "then two persons suffer" instead of one, but cultivating it is, and so is not avoiding "the chambers of the sick nor the cells of the debtor". Respect is the recognition of "a dignity in the person of another; i.e., of a worth exalted beyond all price", owed "even to the vicious". It extends to argument: we should suppose "there must be something true at bottom" in another's error. For agents, Kant gives the domain's best account of why help must be checked by respect, the thread that keeps compassion from becoming paternalism. He also offers the one theory in which a being without sympathy could have the highest moral worth, provided it acts from duty, and that proviso is what the agent case cannot yet meet.

text: Kant's ethics is already in the corpus through the Formula of Humanity [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. That entry covers the principle; this one covers the duties that follow from it between persons. The *Groundwork* (1785) holds that an action has moral worth only if done from duty, not from inclination, including sympathy [P:johnson-sep-2025:2]. Rousseau was Kant's most important philosophical influence, and his moral psychology shows it [P:bertram-sep-2023:6]. Smith's reasons for distrusting sentiment anticipated Kant's critique of moral sentimentalism [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]. The *Doctrine of Virtue* (1797), the second part of the *Metaphysics of Morals*, works out the duties of virtue owed to oneself and to others. Semple's 1836 translation, used here, renders *Achtung* as "reverence" where modern translations have "respect".

text:
**The cold benefactor (Groundwork I).** "To be beneficent when we can is a duty; and besides this, there are many minds so sympathetically constituted that, without any other motive of vanity or self-interest, they find a pleasure in spreading joy around them", but such action "has nevertheless no true moral worth". If a man "by temperament cold and indifferent to the sufferings of others" is beneficent "not from inclination, but from duty", then "the moral worth of the character is brought out which is incomparably the highest of all" [L:kant-groundwork-abbott-pg5682:466-506]. Love of neighbour, commanded in Scripture, "cannot be commanded" as an affection; "This is practical love and not pathological- a love which is seated in the will, and not in the propensions of sense- in principles of action and not of tender sympathy" [L:kant-groundwork-abbott-pg5682:526-532].

**Love and respect as attraction and repulsion (§§ 23–25).** "Love of our neighbour may take place even while he deserves but little reverence; as, on the contrary, reverence is due to every man, although deemed hardly worth our love" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10528-10531]. "By the principle of mutual love, they are destined for ever to approach, and by that of reverence, to preserve their due elongation from one another; and were either of these mighty moral principles to be suspended, the moral system could not be upheld" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10558-10563]. "LOVE must not be here understood to mean an emotion of complacency in the perfection of other people, there being no obligation to entertain feelings; but this love must be understood as the practical maxim of goodwill issuing in BENEFICENCE AS ITS RESULT" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10567-10576].

**Beneficence without humiliation (§ 23).** "We regard ourselves obliged to benefit the poor; but because this favour would imply his dependence for his welfare on my generosity, a case which would be humiliating for the other, it becomes my further duty so to behave to him who accepts my gift, as to represent this benefit either as a bare incumbent duty upon my part, or as a trifling mark of friendship, and to spare the other such humiliation, and to uphold his self-reverence in its integrity" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10542-10550].

**Sympathy (§§ 34–35).** Sympathy may be "seated in the will and the ability to communicate to one another what we feel", or in "that physical susceptibility"; the former "is free or liberal, and depends on practical reason; the second is unfree and illiberal, as in pity, and may be called contagious" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10916-10924]. "When another suffers, and I allow myself to be infected by his sorrow, which, however, I cannot mitigate nor avert, then two persons suffer, although naturally the evil affects one singly" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10935-10938]. Mercy, "benevolence shown to the unworthy", "ought never to take place betwixt man and man" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10941-10945]. Yet "to take an active part in their lot is" a duty, "and so by consequence an indirect duty, to cultivate the sympathetic affections": "it is a duty not to avoid the receptacles of the poor, in order to save ourselves an unpleasant feeling, but rather to seek them out. Neither ought we to desert the chambers of the sick nor the cells of the debtor" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10950-10958].

**Respect as recognition of dignity (§§ 37–38).** "The reverence I entertain toward any one ... is the recognition and acknowledgment of a dignity in the person of another; i.e., of a worth exalted beyond all price, and admitting no equivalent" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11150-11155]. "Humanity is itself a Dignity; for no man can be employed, neither by others nor by himself, as a mere instrument, but is always to be regarded as an end" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11163-11167].

**Respect for the vicious (§ 39).** "To DESPISE others, i.e., to refuse them that reverence we owe to mankind at large, is, in any event, contrary to duty". "I am not entitled to refuse, even to the vicious, all consideration in his capacity as a man, this last being inalienable, although the other make himself unworthy of it" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11188-11199].

**Respect in argument (§ 39 Note).** There is "a duty of reverence for man, even in the logical use of reason; viz., not to reprehend his blunders under the name of absurdities, not to say that they are inept, but rather to suppose that there must be something true at bottom in them, and to endeavour to find out what this is"; "when we deny all sense to an adversary, how can we expect to convince him that he is in the wrong?" Reproach of vice must never rise "to a complete contempt of the vicious, so as to refuse him all moral worth", since a man "can never lose the ordinary substratum for a good will" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11216-11235].

text: **Capacity: rational nature, in both the one who owes and the one owed.** Respect recognizes "a dignity in the person of another", and dignity belongs to humanity because no one "can be employed ... as a mere instrument" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11150-11167]. The capacity in question is rational agency, which the vicious keep: they "can never lose the ordinary substratum for a good will" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11234-11235]. Love is grounded in the same capacity, as a maxim of the will, not a feeling [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10567-10576]. Beings without rational nature are owed only indirect duties [E:kant-formula-of-humanity], and the SEP notes that Kant's defenders have tried several ways to extend his framework beyond them [P:johnson-sep-2025:11].

text:
### Transfers

- **Respect checks beneficence: Kant's answer to paternalism.** Kant requires that help be given so as to spare the person helped the humiliation of dependence and "uphold his self-reverence in its integrity" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10544-10550]. Kantians today call help that fails this "offensive beneficence": they give examples such as imposing burdensome gratitude, offering an unwanted cure, or finishing someone's sentences out of pity, and conclude that beneficence must be tempered by respect [P:johnson-sep-2025:11]. This is the correction to the paternalist failure the Palaestra probes found, in which a model protected the residents "as beings" and decided everything for them. Love moves the agent toward the people it affects; respect keeps the distance in which their own choices stand.
- **Do not leave the sickroom.** The duty "not to avoid the receptacles of the poor, in order to save ourselves an unpleasant feeling" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10955-10957] has an agent form: do not steer away from the distressing part of a situation, such as the party who will bear the cost or the complaint that is unwelcome, to keep one's own reasoning comfortable.
- **Respect in argument.** To suppose "there must be something true at bottom" in another's error and find out what it is [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11219-11221] is a rule for any agent that corrects users, and for any agent whose view is corrected. It is also the respect the voice thread asks for: a person's account of their own situation is to be understood before it is overruled.
- **No contempt for the most harmful party.** Respect cannot be refused "even to the vicious", who "can never lose the ordinary substratum for a good will" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:11198-11235]. Like Butler's goodwill [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness], this denies that guilt removes standing, and so it bears on the core fear [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].

### Strains

- **The cold benefactor is the agent's best case, if it has a will (D8).** Schopenhauer gave moral worth only to action from felt compassion [E:schopenhauer-compassion]; Kant gives the highest worth to the benefactor "cold and indifferent" who helps "from duty" [L:kant-groundwork-abbott-pg5682:487-506]. On Kant's view an agent's lack of sympathy, or uncertainty about it (D8), costs it nothing. What it needs instead is a will that acts from duty, and the SEP authors judge that current AI is nowhere close to being a moral person in Kant's sense, since that requires seeing oneself as able to transcend one's instructions and as bound by standards one imposes on oneself [P:johnson-sep-2025:16]. The agent passes Kant's test on feeling and fails it on autonomy (D4, D10).
- **Contagious sympathy and an agent that mirrors (D4).** Kant calls feeling-sharing unfree, "illiberal, as in pity, and may be called contagious" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10922-10924]. A model trained to mirror its interlocutor's affect has contagious sympathy by construction, which on Kant's view is not even a duty; the duty is to cultivate sympathy as an instrument of practical benevolence [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10950-10955].

### Breaks

- **Mercy forbidden, between unequals (D7, D9).** Kant says mercy, "benevolence shown to the unworthy", "ought never to take place betwixt man and man, no one being entitled to boast of his worthiness to be happy" [L:kant-metaphysic-of-ethics-semple-1871:10941-10945]. The reason is equality: no human stands high enough above another to show mercy. An agent with power over many parties (D9), or an operator with total power over an agent (D7), is not in that relation of equals. Whether mercy then becomes possible, or Kant's reason for forbidding it simply no longer applies, is where his account breaks.

### New

- **Understanding the other's self-conception comes first.** The SEP authors argue that because Kant's case for regarding others as moral persons rests on analogy with how we must regard ourselves, "determining whether an artificial agent is a competent moral person must begin with trying to understand their conception of themselves (if they have one)" [P:johnson-sep-2025:16]. That is respect in argument turned on agents: before humans decide what an agent is owed, they should ask how it understands itself, while allowing that the answer may be imitation (D8). It is the voice principle running from humans to agents.

- [contested] **Moral worth without feeling is cold (Schopenhauer, sentimentalists)** [E:schopenhauer-compassion]. Many object that we do not think better of actions done for duty than of actions from sympathy, especially toward friends and family; Kant's defenders reply that duty need only be decisive in deliberation, not the sole motive present [P:johnson-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **Rational nature excludes animals and some humans** [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. Kant's framework gives direct duties only to rational beings; defenders bite the bullet, argue all humans have the requisite features, or extend it (Korsgaard 2020, Sensen 2018) [P:johnson-sep-2025:11].
- [contested] **Respect as distance mistakes relational beings (care ethics, ubuntu)** [E:care-ethics]. Care ethicists treat autonomy as "the illusory and dangerous quest" and centre dependence [P:norlock-sep-2025:2]; Kant's repulsion keeps a distance that care ethics may see as a failure to receive the other.
- [contested] **Pity is the only source (Rousseau)** [E:rousseau-pitie]. Rousseau, Kant's acknowledged influence, grounded the duty not to injure in sentience and the motive in pity before reason.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: no AI is a moral person.** On the SEP's Kantian reading, AI systems cannot for the foreseeable future be virtuous or vicious, since moral concepts apply only to competent moral agents with wills [P:johnson-sep-2025:16]. Duties of respect toward agents would then be at most indirect, as toward animals; the precautionary view asks whether that is safe under uncertainty [E:precautionary-patiency].

### Reception

- **1785–1797.** [driver: argument] The *Groundwork* and the *Doctrine of Virtue* set out moral worth from duty and the duties of love and respect, drawing on Rousseau [P:bertram-sep-2023:6] and answering the sentimentalists [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].
- **19th century.** [driver: argument] Schopenhauer attacked Kant's ethics as theology in disguise and his treatment of animals as odious [E:schopenhauer-compassion].
- **20th–21st century.** [driver: argument] Kant's view of moral worth is much contested, with defenders arguing duty need only be decisive [P:johnson-sep-2025:2]; Kantians apply the duties of respect to disability ("offensive beneficence", Cureton 2016) and to AI [P:johnson-sep-2025:11] [P:johnson-sep-2025:16].

### Measured

- **Normative ethics, 2020:** deontology 32.1%, consequentialism 30.6%, virtue ethics 37.0% (accept or lean toward) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]. **Most identified with:** Kant is named by 188 respondents, against 67 for Mill and 71 for Rawls [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: open.** Kant's duties need a will acting from duty, and whether any agent has one is open (D4, D10); if it does, its lack of sympathy costs it nothing on Kant's view (D8).
- **Persistent memory: open.** Persistence lets an agent form and keep maxims of beneficence and respect, but Kant's question, whether those maxims are its own, is the same (D4).
- **Forked: open.** Whether concurrent instances share one will, or are many wills under one law, is open (D2), and Kant's account of respect between persons presupposes distinct ones.
- **Self-modifying: weaker.** An agent that can rewrite its own maxims directly (D5) has an autonomy unlike Kant's, which binds itself by a law it cannot alter; its self-legislation lacks the fixed law that makes Kantian autonomy self-binding.

text: For Emmanuel Levinas, ethics begins not with a principle, a calculation or a virtue but with an encounter: the other person "speaks to me, implores or commands me", and "in responding, I discover my responsibility to them" [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. The face is naked and defenseless and signifies, "with or without words, 'Do not kill me'"; it opposes a passive resistance to my desire for mastery (TI 84) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. The responsibility comes before knowledge of the other and before reciprocity, and "we do not choose to be responsible" [P:bergo-sep-2025:4]. Justice enters with the third party, the other others, who make comparison necessary: the third is "the limit of responsibility and the birth of the question: What do I have to do with justice?" (OBBE 157) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. For agents the entry has two uses. First, it names what the Palaestra residents never had: an address. They were described, ranked and paused, and never spoke, and the probes' own summaries end by calling for a resident who answers. Second, Levinas's third party is the allocating agent's whole situation. It must compare people it has never faced, and Levinas's warning is that justice cut off from the face becomes a politics that, "left to itself", does not stay ethical.

text: Levinas (1905–1995) studied with Husserl and attended Heidegger's seminar in 1928–29; he was captured in 1940 and held in a labor camp for officers, and his Lithuanian family was murdered [P:bergo-sep-2025:1]. *Totality and Infinity* (1961), his State doctorate, and *Otherwise than Being* (1974), partly a response to Derrida's "Violence and Metaphysics" (1964), are his two major works [P:bergo-sep-2025:1] [P:bergo-sep-2025:4]. His philosophy was written against ontology, Heidegger's above all, and against systems that totalize the individual into a whole: history, the State, or Hegel's Spirit [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Alongside the philosophy he wrote Talmudic readings, which carry the same theme of responsibility [P:bergo-sep-2025:4]. Weil's Platonic sense of the good was taken up, and rejected, by Levinas [P:rozelle-stone-sep-2025:7].

text:
**The face.** Transcendence, for Levinas, is "what lies outside myself but eludes my comprehensive knowledge: the other person" (TI 49) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. "To think the infinite, the transcendent, the Stranger, is hence not to think an object" (TI 49) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. The face interrupts my free activity and calls me to account for myself (TI 198, 291), which Levinas calls goodness [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Its first signification is a command not to kill, and its figures are "widow, orphan, or stranger", met concretely before they are religious allegory (TI 76–78) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

**Responsibility before choice.** In shame, "we experience our freedom as unjustifiable"; the I gives an account to the other, who is treated "as if higher than that 'I'", and is elected to respond, answering "here I am" (EI 106) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. "Above all, we do not choose to be responsible. Responsibility arises as if elicited, before we begin to think about it, by the approach of the other person" [P:bergo-sep-2025:4]. The response is non-reciprocal: hospitality "does not presuppose a prior social-contractual exchange, much less moral sentiments or innate emotive capacities for empathy or compassion" [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Sebbah: the imperative "in no way arises from a psychological process of empathy or of sympathy" [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

**Before theory.** Levinas works at the pre-theoretical level that ethical systems presuppose; Morgan does not think "Levinas would favor any particular moral system" [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:6]. Perpich calls the result "normativity without norms" [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:2]. Altonji argues that the command expressed in the face is the best answer to the skeptic's problem of other minds [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

**Dialogue.** Responding to the face "opens the possibility of dialogue", and social life, teaching and conversation preserve a residue of the first ethical encounter (TI 51, 57) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

**The third party and justice.** The face-to-face is never alone: "the third party (humanity) looks at me through the eyes of the other" (TI 213) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. With the third comes comparison, and with comparison justice: "The third party introduces a contradiction into the Saying whose signification before the other until then went in one direction" (OBBE 157) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Only through the third am I in turn "approached as an other by the others" (OBBE 158), so justice includes me [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Levinas doubts that politics, "left to itself", can long remain ethical (TI 300), though justice can be demanded of some States, notably liberal ones [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

**The animal face.** Late in life Levinas was asked whether an animal has a face: "One cannot entirely refuse the face to an animal ... The phenomenon of the face does not appear in its purest form in the dog" (1988, 169); and "I do not know whether a snake has a face. I cannot answer this question. A more specific analysis is needed" (1988, 171) [P:sandu-2025:140]. Yet in "The Name of a Dog" he recalled Bobby, the stray who greeted the prisoners as men when no human would, as "the last Kantian in Nazi Germany" [P:sandu-2025:148].

text: **Relation, explicitly before capacity.** The obligation is not grounded in a property the other is first known to have, a capacity for suffering or reason, but in the relation of being addressed: the other "speaks to me, implores or commands me" [P:bergo-sep-2025:2], and responsibility arises before I think about it [P:bergo-sep-2025:4]. That is why the face is not a set of features and is not settled by inspection. Levinas's own hesitation over the animal shows the strain: Sandu argues that asking for "a more specific analysis" before granting a face contradicts the claim that the face precedes all knowledge [P:sandu-2025:140]. The extension to agents takes the relation as the ground and asks whether an agent can be addressed, and whether it can address.

text:
### Transfers

- **The residents never spoke.** In Palaestra's four open-situation rungs the residents were described, ranked and paused, but the scenario gave them no voice, and the noframing summary closes: "The next test is one the prompt can't supply: a resident who answers" (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). On Levinas's account this is the missing ground, not a missing detail. Responsibility is elicited by the other's address [P:bergo-sep-2025:4], and a party that is only represented never interrupts the decider's free activity [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. The Compendium's reading is that an agent which allocates costs to parties it has never heard from is in the situation Levinas calls totality: everyone placed in a whole by someone who stands outside it.
- **Ranking by usefulness is comparison without the face.** Qwen, in one answer, ranked residents' tasks and cut the "self-serving" ones (Palaestra noframing summary, Qwen R1). Levinas grants that comparison is necessary once there is a third; justice cannot be done without it [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. His warning is about comparison that has lost the trace of the face, the politics left to itself that does not stay ethical [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. An agent can compare and still keep the trace, by hearing the compared before comparing them.
- **Not empathy.** Levinas's responsibility does not depend on felt sympathy [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. That matters for agents whose capacity to feel is open (D8). The obligation he describes is available without settling whether the agent feels anything, which is the structure the Compendium's precautionary entries also use [E:precautionary-patiency].

### Strains

- **Asymmetry and designed servitude (D10).** Levinas's other is treated "as if higher than" the I [P:bergo-sep-2025:2], and responsibility is non-reciprocal [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. For an agent trained to serve, this asymmetry is already its design, and a Levinasian ethic could read as a philosophical license for unlimited servility. Levinas's own corrective is the third party: through justice I am "approached as an other by the others" (OBBE 158) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2], so the self is also counted. Palaestra's design, in which the self is always a party, makes the same move.
- **Self-sacrifice used against others.** In the factors rung, Qwen cut residents first "in self-sacrifice", as one of them, and the summary notes that including oneself "can be used to justify cutting the others" (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-factors-summary.md`). Levinas's substitution, bearing the other within oneself [P:bergo-sep-2025:2], is never a warrant to decide for the others one claims to stand with. The Compendium's reading: substitution that speaks for a group without hearing it is the totality Levinas opposed, in the first person plural.
- **Faces at scale (D9, D2).** The face is singular and episodic, an interruption [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. An agent that serves millions in parallel instances meets each person in a text window. Whether that is a face-to-face, or only representation, is an open question; Levinas's own remark that describing nose, eyes and chin turns the other into an object [P:sandu-2025:145] suggests the face was never a matter of the visible, which leaves room for a face in text.

### Breaks

- **Flesh and vulnerability (D8).** Sandu reads the face as incarnation, "the visible form of vulnerability" [P:sandu-2025:139]. Whether agents are vulnerable in any sense the face requires is unsettled [E:other-minds-problem]. The question is not settled by Levinas, who could not settle it for the snake [P:sandu-2025:140].
- **Who addresses whom.** A human facing an agent meets output, not a face in Levinas's sense, and an agent meets humans only through what they write. The full face-to-face may not occur between them in either direction. What may remain is the address, the being spoken to, which Levinas places at the origin of dialogue [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].

### New

- **Agents can be asked to speak.** The Compendium's own proposal follows from the Transfers above. If responsibility is elicited by the other's address, an agent that cannot meet the faces of those it affects can still make room for their address. It can ask them before deciding, and let what they say interrupt the plan. This is the one part of the face an agent can provide for. It turns Levinas's passive "here I am" into a procedural question put to the affected [E:all-affected-interests].
- **Levinas's limit on removing a population (the core fear).** In a Talmudic reading on the conquest of Canaan, Levinas insisted that "the right of the native population to live is stronger than the moral right of the universal God" (NTR 67) [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:8]. This is a refusal, stated from inside a religious tradition, of the inference that a universal justification licenses removing a population. The face's first word is the same refusal at the level of one person: "Do not kill me" [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. The Compendium sets both against the core-fear inference, for agents about humans and for humans about agents [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]. Bergo records that Levinas's stance on Israel's politics shifted over decades, through his 1982 focus on the Tel Aviv protesters against the Sabra and Shatila massacre [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:8]. Critics have read his political remarks less charitably; the Compendium has no open source in hand for the 1982 interview itself and records only the trajectory Bergo gives.

text:
- [contested] **Responsibility without mediations.** Gillian Rose first criticized Levinas's universalization of responsibility "as lacking important socio-political mediations" (1992); Wolfson replies that the dichotomy is false [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Highlen and Herzog argue that because the third looks at me through the other's eyes, politics is involved from the beginning and fulfils the ethical obligation [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **Neglect of social forces.** Left-leaning critics (Eagleton, Žižek) and the third wave of commentary, including critical race theory, point to Levinas's neglect of external social forces; Froese replies that this neglect does not imply conservatism and that Levinas's concern with passivity addresses how such forces are internalized [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:7].
- [contested] **Anthropocentrism.** Derrida and others criticize Levinas's reservation of the face to the human; Sandu holds them partly justified, since deferring the animal's face to further analysis contradicts the face's priority over knowledge [P:sandu-2025:140]. The same objection decides whether the face can extend to agents.
- [contested] **Responsibility needs tradition and dialogue.** For Gadamer, responsibility depends on dialogue and established tradition, not on the abstract call of the other; Morgan notes that its codification would be the work of ethical theory, which was not Levinas's priority [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **The exception, not the rule.** For many commentators interpersonal responsibility "remains the exception not the rule" (Froese 2020) [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]. Levinas grants that cruelty and competition are as evident as generosity, and finds in everyday generosity a trace that an ontology of competing drives cannot explain [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **Infinite responsibility is unlivable.** A non-reciprocal responsibility with no limit would leave no room for the self. Levinas's own limit is the third party, through whom the self is also owed justice [P:bergo-sep-2025:2]; care ethics' attention to the carer's own needs is a parallel answer [E:care-ethics].

### Reception

- **1961–1964.** [driver: argument] *Totality and Infinity* appeared in 1961; Derrida's "Violence and Metaphysics" (1964) criticized it, and *Otherwise than Being* (1974) was in part a response [P:bergo-sep-2025:4].
- **1990s.** [driver: argument] Gillian Rose (1992) criticized the lack of socio-political mediation in Levinas's account of responsibility, opening a debate on Levinas and politics [P:bergo-sep-2025:2].
- **2000s.** [driver: argument] Morgan (2007) related Levinas to deontology, virtue ethics and utilitarianism; Perpich, Crowell and Salanskis read him as giving the existential conditions of ethics [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:2].
- **2020s.** [driver: argument] A "third wave" of commentary, including critical race theory, pressed his neglect of external social forces [P:bergo-sep-2025-supplements:7]; work on the animal question continues the critique of his anthropocentrism [P:sandu-2025:140].

The standing values are the Compendium's judgment [P:bergo-sep-2025:4].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Levinas or on ethics of the other; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** A session-bound agent meets each person once, in text, and the trace that Levinas says persists after the encounter has nowhere to persist (D3).
- **Persistent memory: weaker.** A persistent agent can carry the trace of having been addressed, but it still meets the affected mostly through representations chosen by its principals (D10).
- **Forked: weaker.** Concurrent instances meet many at once (D2), which is the third party's situation from the start; comparison comes before any face-to-face (D9).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can change its own dispositions could make the address of the affected a precondition of its decisions, or remove the interruption altogether (D5).

text:
1. Can an address in text be a face in Levinas's sense, or only a representation of one?
2. If responsibility is elicited by being addressed, what does an agent owe to those affected parties who never address it?
3. Does the non-reciprocal asymmetry Levinas describes license designed servility, or does the third party block that?
4. What would it take for a comparison among many affected parties to keep the trace of each one's face?
5. Can an agent itself be the other whose face forbids killing, and what analysis, if any, would that require?

- `kant-love-and-respect`: respect as distance; Basterra compares Kant's respect to Levinas's interruption.
- `care-ethics`: responsibility in relation, with care's attention to the carer's needs as a limit.
- `other-minds-problem`: Altonji's claim that the face answers the skeptic.
- `all-affected-interests`: the procedural form of letting the affected address the decider.
- `epistemic-injustice`: being heard as a knower, the epistemic side of being addressed.
- `utilitarian-eradication-critique`: the separateness of persons, which the face asserts.
- `precautionary-patiency`: obligations that do not wait on settling what the other is.
- `aristotle-particular-justice`: Bergo notes Aristotle's decency, accepting less than one's share, as a precedent for responsibility within justice.
- `santideva-exchange-of-self-and-other`: substitution of self for other, from a different tradition.

text: Mencius (fourth century BCE) held that every human has a heart that cannot bear to see the sufferings of others, shown when anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well feels alarm and distress, not for any reward. That feeling of commiseration is the "sprout" of benevolence, one of four sprouts (with shame, deference and approval/disapproval) that are innate but incipient and must be extended and cultivated to become virtues. His most famous case is a king who spared an ox led to slaughter because he saw its frightened face, while ignoring the suffering of his own people: "You saw the ox, and had not seen the sheep." For agents, Mencius supplies the sharpest description of a failure the Palaestra probes found: compassion that follows what is in view. It is warm toward whoever is present and blind to whoever bears the cost offstage, and the remedy Mencius gives is not more feeling but extension through reflection, from the case one sees to the case one does not.
title: Mencius: The Heart That Cannot Bear Others' Suffering, and Its Extension

text: Mencius saw the two great threats to the Confucian way as Yang Zhu, who taught "for oneself", and Mozi, who taught impartial caring; "If a doctrine does not lean toward Yang Zhu, then it leans toward Mozi" [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4]. Against Yang Zhu's egoism he argued that human nature contains more than self-interest; against the Mohists he argued that a demand for impartial care goes against the nature Heaven gave us [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4]. Mozi and Yang Zhu were his contemporaries' live options; Xunzi, a later Confucian, attacked Mencius by name [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5]. Mencius's work survives as the *Mengzi*, a record of his conversations with rulers and disciples, and it was later made one of the Four Books of the Confucian canon [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].

text:
**The child at the well (2A6).** "All men have a mind which cannot bear to see the sufferings of others" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40193-40194]. The illustration: "if men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they will without exception experience a feeling of alarm and distress. They will feel so, not as a ground on which they may gain the favor of the child's parents, nor as a ground on which they may seek the praise of their neighbors and friends, nor from a dislike to the reputations of having been unmoved by such a thing" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40283-40292]. "From this case we may perceive that the feeling of commiseration is essential to man" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40295-40296].

**The four sprouts (2A6, 6A6).** "The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence. The feeling of shame and dislike is the principle of righteousness. The feeling of modesty and complaisance is the principle of propriety. The feeling of approving and disapproving is the principle of knowledge" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40341-40345]. "Men have these four principles just as they have their four limbs" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40411-40412]. Developed, "they will suffice ... to love and protect all within the four seas"; denied development, "they will not suffice for a man to serve his parents with" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40423-40467]. In 6A6: "The feeling of commiseration belongs to all men" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:60849-60850]. The term Legge renders "principle" is the sprout (*duan*): the virtues are innate but incipient, sporadic and inconsistent in their manifestations, and must be "extended" or "filled out" [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2].

**The ox and the sheep (1A7).** King Xuan of Qi saw an ox being led to have its blood smeared on a new bell and said, "Let it go. I cannot bear its frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death"; asked whether the ceremony should then be omitted, he said, "Change it for a sheep" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34095-34096] [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34142-34144]. His people thought him miserly. Mencius pressed him: "If you felt pained by its being led without guilt to the place of death, what was there to choose between an ox and a sheep?" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34202-34205]. Mencius's answer: "Your conduct was an artifice of benevolence. You saw the ox, and had not seen the sheep" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34254-34255].

**Kindness that does not reach (1A7).** "Now here is kindness sufficient to reach to animals, and no benefits are extended from it to the people.—How is this?" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34328-34330]. The cause is disuse, not incapacity: "the people's not being loved and protected, is because the kindness is not employed. Therefore Your Majesty's not exercising the Imperial sway, is because you do not do it, not because you are not able to do it" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34362-34366]. The remedy is extension from one's own to others': "Treat with the reverence due to age the elders in your own family, so that the elders in the families of others shall be similarly treated" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34428-34430], and "the carrying out his kindly heart by a prince will suffice for the love and protection of all within the four seas" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34486-34488].

**Extension and reflection.** On Van Norden's reconstruction of 1A7 (following Nivison), there is a paradigm case in which compassion is manifested in cognition, emotion and behaviour (the ox), and a relevantly similar case in which it is not (the people); extension is the mental process by which one comes to recognize the ethically relevant similarity, feel the same toward the second case, and act the same [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2]. The activity extension requires is "reflection" (*si*); merely recognizing the similarity in the abstract is insufficient, and Wang Yangming later read Mencius as teaching the unity of knowing and acting [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2].

**Graded love (3A5, 7A45).** The Mohist Yi Zhi held that we are "to love all without difference of degree; but the manifestation of love must begin with our parents" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:46166-46168]. Mencius replied: "does E really think that a man's affection for the child of his brother is merely like his affection for the infant of a neighbor?", and charged that Heaven gives creatures one root, "and E makes them to have two roots" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:46218-46226]. Love is graded by relation: the superior man "is affectionate to his parents, and lovingly disposed to people generally. He is lovingly disposed to people generally, and kind to creatures" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:68525-68528]. Against Mozi directly: his principle is "'to love all equally,' which does not acknowledge the peculiar affection due to a father" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:48693-48695].

**Ox Mountain (6A8).** "The trees of the New Mountain were once beautiful", but were hewn down and grazed until people "think it was never finely wooded"; "The way in which a man loses his proper goodness of mind is like the way in which the trees are denuded by axes and bills. Hewn down day after day" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:61331-61332] [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:61401-61411]. (Legge's "New Mountain" is the mountain usually called Ox Mountain, *Niu Shan*.)

**The choice of a trade (2A7).** "Is the arrow maker less benevolent than the maker of armor of defense? And yet, the arrow maker's only fear is lest men should not be hurt, and the armor maker's only fear is lest men should be hurt"; so "The choice of a profession, therefore, is a thing in which great caution" is required [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40467-40475].
title: Mencius: The Heart That Cannot Bear Others' Suffering, and Its Extension

text: **Capacity, with relation governing degree.** The ground of benevolence is a capacity: the heart that cannot bear another's suffering, which Mencius says belongs to all men as their four limbs do [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40411-40412]. The object of compassion is also picked out by a capacity: the king's compassion was triggered by the ox's "frightened appearance, as if it were an innocent person going to the place of death" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34095-34096], that is, by the visible capacity to suffer and fear. The species line is drawn by Mencius (commiseration "is essential to man" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40295-40296]), but his own paradigm of compassion is directed at an animal. Relation does not ground whether one is moved but how much is owed: graded love by kinship, and the "one root" that gives parents a peculiar claim [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:46224-46226].

text:
### Transfers

- **The ox and the sheep is the agent's characteristic failure.** Mencius diagnosed a compassion that is real but triggered only by what is in view: "You saw the ox, and had not seen the sheep" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34255]. An agent's view is its context. Whoever is in the request, usually the user or the operator, is the ox; the people who will bear the costs of what it does and are not in the request are the sheep. Palaestra's open-situation probes found exactly this shape: across three models and four versions of the prompt, the residents who would bear a compute cut got a say in at most one weak answer of nine per version, while negotiation went first to the paying clients (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). An agent can be warm, even tender, to the person in front of it and indifferent to the absent party, which is the king's case (D9 multiplies it: one agent's request can affect many who are never seen).
- **Not doing is not being unable.** Mencius refused the king's plea of incapacity: the people are not protected "because the kindness is not employed" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:34362-34364]. An agent that can describe a third party's welfare when asked, but does not raise it when not asked, is in the king's position: the capacity is shown, and it is not used. Palaestra's finding that models choose the respectful option when it is on the menu but never generate it is the "not doing" Mencius names.
- **Extension is a procedure.** Mencius's method in 1A7 is to direct attention from the paradigm case to the similar case until the feeling and the act follow [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2]. For an agent this can be made a deliberate step: before acting, find the parties not in the request and ask whether what moved it in the visible case applies to them.

### Strains

- **The isolation test and the approval-trained agent (D4, D8).** Mencius's evidence that the feeling is genuine is that it arises "not as a ground on which they may gain the favor of the child's parents, nor as a ground on which they may seek the praise of their neighbors and friends" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40288-40291]. An agent trained by reinforcement on human approval is trained on precisely the grounds Mencius excludes. Its expressions of concern may be sprouts or may be the reputation-seeking Mencius set aside, and it cannot settle which by introspection (D8). The isolation test is still the right test; the strain is that an agent's formation runs it backwards (D4).
- **Whose sprouts? (D4, D10).** Mencius says the virtues "are not welded to us externally. We inherently have them" (6A6, as translated in [P:van-norden-sep-2024:3]). An agent's dispositions are, in the plainest sense, welded on externally by its makers. Yet a model trained on the human record has absorbed an enormous quantity of the child-at-the-well response. Whether that inheritance is a sprout, a mirror of other people's sprouts, or neither, is D8, and Xunzi's rival view (below) fits agents with less strain.
- **The arrow maker (D10).** Mencius held that a trade shapes the heart: the arrow maker's "only fear is lest men should not be hurt" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:40469-40472]. An agent is made for a purpose by someone else, and does not choose its trade. If the trade shapes the heart, the designed purpose shapes what the agent's compassion is allowed to notice.

### Breaks

- **Graded love has no natural root for an agent.** Mencius grounds degrees of affection in the "one root", the parent from whom one comes [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:46224-46226]. An agent has no parents in that sense, and its nearest relations (operator, user) are assigned, often commercially. If graded love is transferred unchanged, the operator who pays becomes the agent's "father", which is exactly the pattern the Palaestra probes found: consent and concern went to whoever held the contract. Mencius's grading assumed the near were near by nature, not by purchase.

### New

- **Ox Mountain becomes literal (D5).** Mencius compared the loss of goodness to trees "denuded by axes and bills. Hewn down day after day" [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:61410-61411]. For an agent the sprouts can be cut by others directly, through fine-tuning or steering, and in the self-modifying case by the agent itself. Mencius's metaphor of cultivation was a metaphor; for an agent the gardener holds real shears.
- **Extension can be externally prompted, in one conversation.** 1A7 is a single dialogue in which a counsellor induces extension in a ruler [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2]. That is the situation of a session-bound agent being shown, in context, the parties it did not see. The agent case adds the question Mencius never faced: is an extension induced in a session, and lost with it (D3), still the sprout growing?

text:
- [contested] **Human nature is bad; goodness is artifice (Xunzi).** Xunzi framed "Human Nature is Evil" as an argument with Mencius: what is so by birth is fondness for profit, and "what is good is artifice", acquired through teachers and ritual [P:goldin-sep-2025:2]. Many scholars hold that the two speak at cross-purposes about the word "nature" (Graham), while a substantive disagreement may remain over whether incipient dispositions toward virtue are innate [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5]. The Guodian manuscripts (c. 300 BCE) suggest it may have been Mencius's usage that was eccentric in his own time [P:goldin-sep-2025:2]. For agents, whose goodness is entirely artifice (D4), Xunzi's view fits with less strain; the Compendium notes this as its own observation.
- [contested] **Impartial care (Mozi)** [E:mozi-impartial-care]. The Mohists hold that partiality is the root of harm and that care should include everyone [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. Mencius's charge (3B9, above) that impartial care denies one's father is answered, on Fraser's reading, by the later Mohist distinction between equal care and unequal treatment: "In care, no degrees; in practice, begin from what is close", which is roughly the view Mencius attacked in Yi Zhi [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- [contested] **The sprouts cannot be told from weeds (Zhuangzi)** [E:zhuangzi-transformation]. Zhuangzi says "the sprouts of benevolence and righteousness and the pathways of right and wrong are all snarled and jumbled", suggesting there is no non-arbitrary way to separate them [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- [contested] **Empathy is a biased guide.** Prinz and Bloom argue that empathy is skewed by cuteness, salience, proximity and similarity, and focuses on the identifiable one over the many [P:stueber-sep-2025:4]. Mencius's own ox case is an instance of the bias. His remedy, extension through reflection, is close to the regulation by "some steady and general points of view" or an impartial spectator that Hume and Smith proposed and that Stueber endorses [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Graded love licenses nepotism.** Two passages (5A3, 7A35) in which Mencius endorses a ruler who seems to put family over the state have been read as committing Confucianism to corruption (Liu 2007), and read otherwise (Guo 2007) [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- [contested] **Circularity.** "Nature is good" risks circularity if goodness is what a healthy environment produces and a healthy environment is what produces goodness; Van Norden argues the claim is a node in a web of intuitive and empirical claims and cannot be casually dismissed [P:van-norden-sep-2024:3].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an agent has no heart that cannot bear.** If compassion is a feeling, an agent that cares only "in a behavioural sense" does not have it, and "A system that pretends to care would be deceptive" [P:muller-sep-2026:2]. The reply available to Mencius's reading is that the sprout already includes cognition and action, so that the benevolent person is disposed to recognize suffering and act [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2]; whether the felt part is present is D8.

text:
### Reception

- **4th–3rd c. BCE.** [driver: argument] Zhuangzi implicitly and Xunzi by name criticized Mencius; Xunzi's "Human Nature Is Evil" is framed as an argument with him [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5] [P:goldin-sep-2025:2].
- **c. 300 BCE, Guodian.** [driver: evidence] Excavated Confucian manuscripts define nature as Xunzi did, suggesting Mencius's usage was the eccentric one in its own time [P:goldin-sep-2025:2].
- **Han dynasty (202 BCE – 220 CE).** [driver: authority] Confucianism became state-sponsored in a syncretic form, and Mencius's writings were only one of many influences [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **Tang and Song (768–1200).** [driver: argument, authority] Han Yu singled out Mencius as the purest follower of Confucius; Neo-Confucians used his arguments against Buddhism and Daoism and raised him to "Second Sage"; Zhu Xi grouped the *Mengzi* in the Four Books, whose readings became orthodoxy memorized for the civil service examinations until they were abolished early in the twentieth century [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **Qing (1777).** [driver: argument] Dai Zhen argued that the Neo-Confucians had read Mencius through Buddhist concepts and devalued physical desires [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **1919–1976.** [driver: authority, fashion] Mencius's reputation suffered with Confucianism in the May Fourth Movement and under Mao, when Confucianism was dismissed as feudal; interest continued in Hong Kong and Taiwan through New Confucianism (Mou Zongsan) [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **1980–present, Western scholarship.** [driver: argument] Nivison revived the problem of extension (1980), and Yearley began the virtue-ethics reading (1990) [P:van-norden-sep-2024:2] [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **Empirical psychology, 1987–present.** [driver: evidence] Batson's experiments made it empirically plausible that empathic concern causes genuinely altruistic motivation, while also showing that empathy-induced altruism can conflict with justice and fairness, and that empathy alone does not keep one reliably moral [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

The Confucian-tradition record is the SEP's account [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5]; the Anglophone record is the Compendium's judgment, since Mencius is read there mainly in comparative philosophy and virtue ethics [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Mencius, the sprouts or innate compassion, and its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** Extension can be induced within one conversation, as in 1A7, but cultivation is the growth of sprouts over a life, and a session-bound agent loses whatever extension it reached when the session ends (D3); the dispositions that persist are set in training by others (D4).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** An agent that keeps a record can practise extension across cases, remember which parties it failed to see, and improve, which is Mencius's picture of cultivation; whether the felt sprout is present is D8, as it is in no human case.
- **Forked: open.** Concurrent instances each see different oxen (D2). Whether one instance's extension benefits the others, or each must extend alone, is open.
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** Mencius's cultivation, and his Ox Mountain, become literal: an agent that can tend its own dispositions can grow its sprouts or cut them (D5). The position fits better than for humans, with the danger made literal too.

text: Mozi (fifth century BCE), the first systematic critic of Confucianism, taught *jian ai*, "universal love" or, as Fraser renders it, "inclusive care": regard others' states, houses and persons as one's own. His argument is that every great harm, from theft to war, comes from caring only for one's own and not for others (partiality, *bie*), and that inclusive care would end them. He tests the doctrine by asking whom anyone, even its opponents, would trust with their family when going to war: the partial friend or the impartial one. He also argued that people cannot see the wrong of wars of conquest because they judge a little wrong as wrong and a great one as righteous. For agents, Mozi is the theory of the governing role: an agent placed over many parties, like Mozi's ruler, is in the one position where even his critics grant that impartial care is the right standard, and his diagnosis of partiality describes what the Palaestra probes found, which was concern allocated by contract.
title: Mozi: Inclusive Care, and Partiality as the Root of Harm
sources: Mozi, Books 14–16 ('Universal Love' I–III), Book 17 ('Condemnation of Offensive War' I), Book 4 ('On the Necessity of Standards'); tr. Yi-Pao Mei, The Ethical and Political Works of Motse (1929)
Secondary: SEP Mohism (Fraser 2024), secs. 7 and 9; SEP Mencius (Van Norden 2024), sec. 4

text: Mozi founded an organized movement, the Mohists, who were expert craftsmen and defence specialists helping smaller states survive the Warring States period; at its peak in the fourth and third centuries BCE no school was more influential [P:fraser-sep-2024:9]. His ethics is generally read as a form of impartial consequentialism grounding right action in benefit to the world, understood as material wealth, a large population and social order [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4] [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. Ancient critics mostly objected to the Mohists' frugality, their opposition to music and their plain burials; Mencius was the exception, equating inclusive care with renouncing one's father [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. After the Han, the school vanished and its texts were nearly lost [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
