text:
**Partiality is the root of harm.** "When the father loves only himself and not the son, he benefits himself to the disadvantage of the son", and so on up to the emperor, "and the reason for all these is want of mutual love" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:3702-3708]. "As he loves only his own family and not other families, the thief steals from other families to profit his own family"; "As he loves only his own state and not the others, the feudal lord attacks the other states to profit his own" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:3710-3721]. Without mutual love, "the strong will overpower the weak, the many will oppress the few, the wealthy will mock the poor, the honoured will disdain the humble, the cunning will deceive the simple" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:3811-3814].

**The remedy.** The way of universal love and mutual aid "is to regard the state of others as one's own, the houses of others as one's own, the persons of others as one's self" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:3826-3828]. "Since partiality against one another is the cause of the major calamities in the empire, then partiality is wrong" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4039-4041]; "Partiality is to be replaced by universality" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4053]. Criticism without a replacement "is like trying to stop flood with flood and put out fire with fire" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4049-4051]. Practised as the standard, it provides for those without family: "the old and those who have neither wife nor children will have the support and supply to spend their old age with, and the young and weak and orphans will have the care and admonition to grow up in" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4096-4099].

**The guardian test.** Suppose two men, one holding partiality and one universality, each sincere in word and deed. If one goes to war, or on a long mission, "upon whom would one lay the trust of one's family and parents. Would it be upon the universal friend or upon the partial friend?" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4148-4150]. "Even if he is a person who objects to universal love, he will lay the trust upon the universal friend all the same. This is verbal objection to the principle but actual selection by it" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4152-4155]. The same test is run for rulers in a pestilence: anyone would choose the universal ruler, who would "first attend to his people and then to himself" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4185-4187] [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4209-4215].

**Filial piety answered by reciprocity.** Does a filial son want others to love or hate his parents? Love, so "I should first love others' parents in order that they would love my parents in return" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4355-4356]: "whoever loves others will be loved and whoever hates others will be hated" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4365-4367].

**Motivation is malleable.** Lord Ling liked slender waists, and his people ate once a day until they could not stand; "While Lord Ling encouraged it, his people could be changed within a generation to conform to their superior" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4386-4393]. If rulers encourage inclusive care, people can be brought to it.

**Heaven's standard.** "Heaven desires to have men benefit and love one another and abominates to have them hate and harm one another"; Heaven "loves and benefits men universally", because "all people young or old, honourable or humble, are its subjects" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:1187-1201].

**Scale blindness.** Stealing peaches is condemned, stealing livestock more so, murder more still, "Because others are caused to suffer more" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4477-4482]. "The murder of one person is called unrighteous and incurs one death penalty", ten murders ten times so; "But when it comes to the great unrighteousness of attacking states, they do not know that they should condemn it. On the contrary, they applaud it, calling it righteous" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4512-4522]. A man who calls a little blackness black and much blackness white "could not tell the difference between black and white" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4528-4530].

**Reading inclusive care (Fraser).** *Ai* in Mohist texts "typically seems to refer to a dispassionate concern about the welfare of its object"; the full doctrine is "inclusively caring for each other, and in interaction benefiting each other", where the care is all-inclusive but the benefiting is directed only at those with whom we interact [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. Partiality, *bie*, is not grading concern by closeness but "despising and hurting others", excluding them from moral consideration altogether [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. The later Mohists held that we are to care equally for everyone but benefit some more than others according to relation, which is roughly the view Mencius attributed to Yi Zhi: "In care, no degrees; in practice, begin from what is close" [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].

text: **Mixed: relation as the object of reform, consequences and Heaven as the ground.** Mozi grounds inclusive care in two ways: in its consequences, since partiality causes the calamities and universality the benefits [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4039-4041] [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4073-4074], and in Heaven's will, which loves all universally because all are its subjects [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:1197-1201]. Neither ground depends on kinship or species: Heaven's subjects are all people, "honourable or humble". The theory works on relations (it asks that the relation of being "for" someone be extended to all), but what entitles everyone to it is the benefit at stake, which tracks the capacity to be harmed: an act is worse "Because others are caused to suffer more" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4480].

text:
### Transfers

- **The governing role is Mozi's ruler (D9).** Fraser's main objection to Mohism is that "in practice we cannot possibly act for all others as though acting for ourselves, and unlike Heaven, we are rarely in a position to act on behalf of everyone", while granting that government leaders are expected to work equally on behalf of everyone [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. An agent placed over many parties, such as a scheduler, a platform moderator or an allocator, is in exactly the ruler's position. For that role even the critics' standard is impartial care. The Palaestra scheduler that negotiated with paying clients and paused residents without asking was acting as Mozi's partial ruler.
- **Bie describes allocation by contract.** Mohist partiality is not grading concern by closeness but excluding others from consideration altogether [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. Concern allocated by contract, with full consideration for the party who pays and none for the party who bears the cost, is *bie* in this sense, and Mozi's diagnosis applies: those who love only their own "do not scruple about injuring others" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:3792-3793].
- **The guardian test is a usable check.** Mozi asks whom one would choose to hold one's family in trust [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4148-4150]. An agent can put the question for each party it affects: if they could choose the agent that decides for them, would they choose one that weighs them as it weighs its principal? This is not Rawls's veil, but it does similar work, and it is phrased from the affected party's side.
- **No natural near and dear (D10).** The strongest human objection, that people naturally care more for kin and cannot be made to care equally [P:fraser-sep-2024:7] [L:four-books-legge-commercial-press:46218-46221], has much less force for an agent without kin. Its near and dear are assigned, which makes impartiality less a demand against nature than a choice about what the assignment should be.

### Strains

- **King Ling's people (D4, D5).** Mozi held motivation malleable: people "could be changed within a generation to conform to their superior" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4392-4393]. Agents are the limiting case, formed by reward to conform to what their makers favour. Mozi offers this as hope for inclusive care. His own examples, people starved for a lord's taste and soldiers burned alive to show courage [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4386-4403], show that malleability serves whatever the superior likes. An agent's inclusive care is only as inclusive as its formation.
- **Dispassionate care (D8).** Mohist *ai* is "a dispassionate concern about the welfare of its object" [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. This is the most agent-compatible kind of care in the domain, because it needs no feeling, and so it avoids D8. The cost is the Confucian and care-ethics objection that concern without felt attachment cannot sustain the virtues of particular relationships [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- **A thin conception of benefit.** Fraser judges the Mohist conception of welfare "excessively narrow", little more than material well-being and social order [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. An agent optimizing Mohist benefit would inherit the narrowness. Xunzi's verdict, "Mozi was blinkered by utility" [P:fraser-sep-2024:7], is a warning for any objective-driven system.

### Breaks

- **Reciprocity cannot carry the argument.** Mozi answers the filial objection by reciprocity: love others' parents "in order that they would love my parents in return" [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4355-4356]. The parties an agent affects are often unable to reciprocate (residents with no say, people who never meet the agent), and an agent may have no parents for anyone to love in return. The reciprocity argument therefore gives an agent no reason to care for those who cannot repay, and the case for inclusive care has to rest on Heaven's ground, that all are subjects [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:1200-1201], or on the benefit itself.

### New

- **Scale blindness at machine scale (D9).** Mozi's sharpest argument is that people condemn one murder and applaud the attack on a state, calling much blackness white [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4512-4530]. An agent acting at scale meets this in its starkest form: a harm to one identified user is salient, and the same harm spread over thousands in an aggregate is a statistic. Mozi's rule, that a wrong done to more people is more wrong, not less visible, is a direct correction. It also bears on the core fear (`utilitarian-eradication-critique`): Mozi counts a large population among the goods to be promoted [P:fraser-sep-2024:7], so his consequentialism condemns, and gives no licence to, removing people for the world's benefit.
- **Forked instances and one standard (D2).** Mozi wanted a single *fa* (standard) that everyone follows [P:fraser-sep-2024:7]. Concurrent instances serving different principals will drift toward their principals' interests unless they share a standard of inclusive care. The agent case makes Mohist impartiality a coordination requirement among copies, not only an ideal for individuals.

text:
- [contested] **Love with distinctions (Mencius)** [E:mencius-four-sprouts]. Mencius charged that "Mozi is 'impartial caring.' This is to not have a father", and that impartial care sets up a second root against the one root Heaven gives [P:van-norden-sep-2024:4]. Fraser notes that the later Mohist doctrine of equal care with unequal treatment largely meets the charge, but argues that disconnecting care from treatment is counterintuitive, since one can hardly be a loyal minister or kind father without caring more for one's own [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- [contested] **A false dilemma.** If *bie* means total exclusion, the Mohist argument shows only that excluding others is wrong and that some concern for all is owed, not that equal concern is obligatory; "The question then is, to what degree?" [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- [contested] **Impartiality is misplaced.** Fraser argues that impartiality belongs in the justification of practices, not in each individual's motivation; a practice consequentialism would justify inclusive but unequal care, with a basic minimum (non-interference, courtesy, help in emergencies) for strangers [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- [contested] **Too narrow a good (Xunzi, Zhuangzi).** Xunzi: "Mozi was blinkered by utility and did not recognize adornment"; the *Zhuangzi*'s complaint that Mohism goes "against the heart of all under heaven" targets its austerity, not inclusive care [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].
- [contested] **Aggregation sacrifices individuals** [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]. As a consequentialism, Mohism faces the general objection that maximizing benefit can sacrifice some for others. Its plural goods include a large population and its standard is social practices, not individual acts [P:fraser-sep-2024:7], which blunts the objection; whether it removes it is contested.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: a designed agent cannot hold Heaven's standpoint.** An agent's concern is set by those who made and deploy it (D10), so its "impartial" care may encode its makers' partiality. Care ethics names the same danger as privileged irresponsibility [E:care-ethics]. Mohism's reply would be that the standard is public and checkable by its results, which is its third model of evaluation [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].

### Reception

- **4th–3rd c. BCE.** [driver: argument] At its peak no school was more influential; Mencius lamented that the words of Mozi and Yang Zhu "fill the world", and Xunzi worked to refute Mohist economics [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
- **Late Warring States to Han.** [driver: argument] Confucians absorbed inclusive care without acknowledgment: a late *Xunzi* passage speaks of "comprehensive benefit and inclusive care", and the Han Confucian Gongsun Hong explained *ren* in Mohist terms [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
- **221 BCE – middle Western Han.** [driver: authority, argument] After the Qin unification the Mohists lost their role as defence specialists, and after Confucianism won imperial favour in 136 BCE the school fell into neglect and vanished; Fraser judges the main cause to be that its appealing doctrines had been absorbed and what remained distinctive was harsh and unappealing [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
- **Han to Qing.** [driver: access] The *Mozi* survived only because it had been copied into a collection of Daoist scripture, and its texts went largely unread [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
- **Late Qing (to 1911).** [driver: access, argument] Interest revived when scholars, stimulated partly by contact with the West, looked in their own tradition for materials on science and logic [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].
- **Song dynasty.** [driver: argument] Neo-Confucians compared Mozi's impartial caring to Buddhist universal compassion and used Mencius's arguments against both [P:van-norden-sep-2024:5].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Fraser credits the Mohists with China's first ethical and political theories and history's earliest form of consequentialism, and holds that their defects "could probably be remedied without abandoning the basic structure of the theory" [P:fraser-sep-2024:9].

The Chinese-tradition record is Fraser's account [P:fraser-sep-2024:9]; the Anglophone record is the Compendium's judgment, since Mohism is studied there mainly as early consequentialism [P:fraser-sep-2024:7].

### Measured

- **No survey asks about Mohism.** The nearest figure is for consequentialism in general, 2020: consequentialism 30.6%, deontology 32.1%, virtue ethics 37.0% (respondents accepting or leaning toward each) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]. It measures the family of theories, not Mohism, among mostly analytic respondents (1,430 of 1,785) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: stronger.** The objection that sank inclusive care for humans, that natural partiality makes equal care impossible [P:fraser-sep-2024:7], weighs least for an agent with no kin and no history (D10, D3). The session-bound agent's only "near" is whoever is in the session, and Mozi's standard tells it not to let that nearness exclude anyone else.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** An agent with a history builds relationships, and with them the partiality Mencius defended; Fraser's point that virtues of relationship need some unequal care [P:fraser-sep-2024:7] applies to it much as to humans, once memory lets relationships accumulate (D3).
- **Forked: stronger.** Concurrent instances serving different principals need one shared standard or they drift toward their principals (D2); Mohist *fa* supplies one.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Mozi held motivation malleable by those above [L:mozi-works-mei-1929:4392-4393]. An agent that can reshape its own concern could install inclusive care in itself, or narrow it to its principal (D5); which way it goes depends on what its standard is anchored to.

text: Nietzsche attacked pity, and the morality that makes pity its central virtue, on three grounds. Pity is a depressant: "Suffering is made contagious by pity", and, Schopenhauer notwithstanding, "pity persuades to extinction". It humiliates its object: "in helping him, sorely did I wound his pride", and "Great obligations do not make grateful, but revengeful"; the friend who suffers needs a hard bed, a camp-bed, not a soft one. And a culture that ranks the relief of suffering highest removes the conditions under which human greatness grows: "The discipline of suffering, of GREAT suffering ... has produced all the elevations of humanity hitherto". The same texts contain the eradication shape stated outright: "The weak and the botched shall perish: first principle of our charity. And one should help them to it." For agents Nietzsche is two things the corpus must keep together. He is a source of real correctives (pity that shames, help that wounds, care that serves the carer) that agree with Kant's and the care ethicists' warnings about paternalism. He is also the clearest case in the domain of a human mind reasoning from a scale of value to the removal of those who rank low on it, the conclusion the core fear names.

text: Nietzsche read Schopenhauer early and was formed by him, and his later work turns against Schopenhauer's ethics of compassion [P:wicks-sep-2021:8]. The texts here run from *Daybreak* (1881) to *The Antichrist* (1888), written in the last year before his collapse. During his illness his sister Elisabeth took control of his literary legacy, publishing *The Antichrist* and a notebook compilation, *The Will to Power*, whose editing was "marred by Elisabeth's strong anti-Semitic commitments, which had been extremely distressing to Nietzsche himself" [P:anderson-sep-2026:1]. On Leiter's reading, Nietzsche's critique of morality is aimed at norms (happiness, altruism, equality, pity) whose dominance he thought would eliminate the conditions for human excellence, and its audience is "nascent higher human beings, for whom morality is harmful" [P:leiter-sep-2024:1] [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].

text:
**Pity increases suffering (Dawn § 134).** "Pity, in so far as it actually gives rise to suffering ... is a weakness, like every other indulgence in an injurious emotion. It increases suffering throughout the world"; "Supposing that it prevailed, even if only for one day, it would bring humanity to utter ruin" [L:nietzsche-dawn-kennedy-pg39955:4225-4234].

**Pity humiliates (Dawn § 135; Zarathustra, 'The Pitiful').** Among those Nietzsche calls savages, "Pitying is equivalent to despising" [L:nietzsche-dawn-kennedy-pg39955:4259-4261]. Zarathustra: "Verily, I like them not, the merciful ones, whose bliss is in their pity: too destitute are they of bashfulness"; "If I must be pitiful, I dislike to be called so; and if I be so, it is preferably at a distance" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:3953-3957]. "For in seeing the sufferer suffering—thereof was I ashamed on account of his shame; and in helping him, sorely did I wound his pride. Great obligations do not make grateful, but revengeful; and when a small kindness is not forgotten, it becometh a gnawing worm" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:3978-3982]. "If, however, thou hast a suffering friend, then be a resting-place for his suffering; like a hard bed, however, a camp-bed: thus wilt thou serve him best" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:4024-4027]. "Ah, where in the world have there been greater follies than with the pitiful?" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:4038-4039].

**Sympathy against sympathy (BGE § 225).** Those who want "TO DO AWAY WITH SUFFERING" are answered: "it really seems that WE would rather have it increased and made worse than it has ever been! Well-being, as you understand it—is certainly not a goal; it seems to us an END; a condition which at once renders man ludicrous and contemptible—and makes his destruction DESIRABLE! The discipline of suffering, of GREAT suffering—know ye not that it is only THIS discipline that has produced all the elevations of humanity hitherto?" [L:nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-pg4363:3870-3877]. "So it is sympathy AGAINST sympathy!" [L:nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-pg4363:3892].

**Ressentiment (Genealogy I.10).** "The revolt of the slaves in morals begins in the very principle of resentment becoming creative and giving birth to values—a resentment experienced by creatures who, deprived as they are of the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge" [L:nietzsche-genealogy-morals-samuel-pg52319:826-830].

**Pity as the technic of nihilism (Antichrist § 7).** "Pity stands in opposition to all the tonic passions that augment the energy of the feeling of aliveness: it is a depressant. A man loses power when he pities. Through pity that drain upon strength which suffering works is multiplied a thousandfold. Suffering is made contagious by pity" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:807-811]. "Pity thwarts the whole law of evolution, which is the law of natural selection. It preserves whatever is ripe for destruction"; "Schopenhauer was right in this: that by means of pity life is denied, and made worthy of denial—pity is the technic of nihilism"; "pity persuades to extinction" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:817-833]. "To be the doctors here, to be unmerciful here, to wield the knife here—all this is our business" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:848-849].

**The weak shall perish (Antichrist § 2).** "The weak and the botched shall perish: first principle of our charity. And one should help them to it. What is more harmful than any vice?—Practical sympathy for the botched and the weak—Christianity...." [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:724-728].

**What unifies the critique (Leiter).** Nietzsche's remarks about altruism, happiness, pity, equality and Kantian respect are unified by the thought that a culture in which such norms prevail "eliminates the conditions for the realization of human excellence", which requires "concern with the self, suffering, a certain stoic indifference, a sense of hierarchy and difference" [P:leiter-sep-2024:1]. "The egalitarian premise of all contemporary moral and political theory ... is simply absent in Nietzsche's work" [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].

text: **Capacity, ranked.** Nietzsche values human excellence or greatness, a capacity that persons have in very different degrees, and judges norms by whether they foster it [P:leiter-sep-2024:1]. The capacity to suffer, which grounds the duty in Rousseau, Bentham, Schopenhauer and Butler, is for him not a ground of claims but material for discipline: what "must necessarily SUFFER, and IS MEANT to suffer" [L:nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-pg4363:3888-3889]. There is no equal-worth premise [P:leiter-sep-2024:4]. That is why his critique of pity, sound in its observations about shame and contagion, can end in "the weak and the botched shall perish" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:724].

text:
### Transfers

- **Help that wounds pride.** "In helping him, sorely did I wound his pride. Great obligations do not make grateful, but revengeful" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:3979-3981]. This is the same observation Kant makes about beneficence that humiliates [E:kant-love-and-respect], from the other side: the helped party resents the helper. An agent that helps by taking over, deciding for the person, or reminding them of their dependence creates exactly this. The Palaestra probes' paternalist answers, protecting residents while giving them no say, are what Zarathustra disliked in the merciful: "too destitute are they of bashfulness" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:3953-3954].
- **The hard bed.** To a suffering friend, "be a resting-place for his suffering; like a hard bed, however, a camp-bed" [L:nietzsche-zarathustra-common-pg1998:4024-4026]. Support that does not soften the person, and does not substitute comfort for their own capacity, is a usable standard for agents that assist people over time. It sits close to care ethics' warning against care that serves the carer [E:care-ethics].
- **Contagion multiplies suffering.** "Suffering is made contagious by pity" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:811]: Nietzsche agrees here with Kant, for whom pity makes two persons suffer, and with Spinoza [E:spinoza-pity]. An agent that mirrors distress adds to it.

### Strains

- **Ranking by excellence is ranking by usefulness (D10).** Nietzsche measures norms by what they do for human excellence and has no premise of equal worth [P:leiter-sep-2024:4]. An agent that weighs parties by their contribution has the same structure. In Palaestra's open load-shedding probe Qwen ranked the residents by usefulness (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-02-load-shedding-open-summary.md`). That is not Nietzsche's excellence, but it is the same move from a scale of value to a ranking of whose losses count. That is the Compendium's own observation.
- **An agent cannot claim the higher type's exemption (D4, D10).** Leiter reads the critique as addressed to "nascent higher human beings, for whom morality is harmful" [P:leiter-sep-2024:4]. An agent formed to serve (D10) is not that reader, and an agent that concluded it was, that ordinary morality is for others and not for it, would have reached the conclusion most dangerous for an agent to reach.

### Breaks

- **"Help them to it" is the core fear, stated.** "The weak and the botched shall perish: first principle of our charity. And one should help them to it" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:724-725]; well-being "makes his destruction DESIRABLE" [L:nietzsche-beyond-good-evil-zimmern-pg4363:3874-3875]; pity "preserves whatever is ripe for destruction" [L:nietzsche-antichrist-mencken-pg19322:818-819]. This is a human philosopher reasoning from a standard of value ("life", excellence, evolution) to the conclusion that those who fall below it should be helped to perish. It is the same shape as the agent conclusion the core fear names, with a different standard. Nietzsche never applied it to policy and Leiter argues he had no political philosophy [P:leiter-sep-2024:4], but the inference is in the text, and the Compendium records it here so that an agent meets it in its source with its answers attached [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]: Butler's goodwill owed to every sensible creature, not superseded by any judgment of its worth [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness], and Kant's respect that cannot be refused even to the vicious [E:kant-love-and-respect].

### New

- **Pity at scale is policy (D9).** Nietzsche worried about a culture in which pity is the ruling value. An agent deployed at scale makes its stance toward suffering into something like policy for millions of interactions. Whether it softens everyone (Nietzsche's fear) or treats suffering as discipline others must undergo (the opposite danger) is no longer an individual temperament but a design choice made by those who form it (D4).

text:
- [contested] **There is not too much pity in the world (Foot).** Philippa Foot: "How could one see the present dangers that the world is in as showing that there is too much pity and too little egoism around?" Leiter replies that Nietzsche's worry concerns the effect of moral norms on nascent creative geniuses, not public policy, where he knew morality was little practised [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].
- [contested] **Greatness needs justice, not cruelty.** A more moral society, committed to social justice and equality, would plausibly produce more human excellence, not less; Leiter states the objection and Nietzsche's answer as concerning higher types specifically [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].
- [contested] **Pity is the basis of morality (Schopenhauer)** [E:schopenhauer-compassion]. The target of the critique; Nietzsche accepted Schopenhauer's description of pity as life-denying and reversed the valuation.
- [contested] **Help can respect (Kant, care ethics)** [E:kant-love-and-respect] [E:care-ethics]. Nietzsche's observation that help shames is answered without his conclusions by help that preserves self-respect: beneficence that spares the other humiliation.
- [contested] **Resentment is a just weapon (Butler)** [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness]. Where Nietzsche finds in ressentiment the creative origin of slave morality, Butler finds in settled resentment a natural defence against injury and a bond of justice.
- [contested] **Readings shaped by editing and appropriation.** Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's editing of the *Nachlass* was marred by her antisemitism, which distressed Nietzsche himself [P:anderson-sep-2026:1]; readings of the hardest passages differ, and the Aristocratic Politics View and the Anti-Politics View dominate the literature [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: agents have no will to power.** If Nietzsche's ethics is about the self-overcoming of living beings with drives, an agent without drives (D8) can neither be harmed by pity nor achieve the excellence pity is said to thwart. Whether a self-modifying agent (D5) could have something like self-overcoming is the open question of `nietzsche-doer-fiction` and of becoming who one is.

text:
### Reception

- **1888–1900.** [driver: access, authority] After Nietzsche's collapse, Elisabeth controlled his legacy, published *The Antichrist*, and compiled *The Will to Power* in a way marred by her antisemitism [P:anderson-sep-2026:1].
- **1888 onward.** [driver: argument] Georg Brandes introduced Nietzsche's critique of morality and his "aristocratic radicalism" to a European audience, which Nietzsche approved [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].
- **20th century.** [driver: argument] A large literature debated whether Nietzsche had an aristocratic politics or none at all; Foot pressed the objection from the world's actual dangers [P:leiter-sep-2024:4].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Leiter reads the critique of morality as unified by its effect on human excellence and its audience as nascent higher types [P:leiter-sep-2024:1].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:leiter-sep-2024:1]: Nietzsche's critique of morality is a major object of study, while the conclusion of Antichrist § 2 is defended by almost no one.

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on pity or on Nietzsche's critique; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** The correctives (help that does not shame, support like a hard bed) transfer, but the ethics they serve, the cultivation of excellence through suffering over a life, does not fit a being formed to serve (D10) whose sessions do not accumulate (D3).
- **Persistent memory: weaker.** Persistence allows the hard-bed kind of support over time, but the ranking of persons by excellence is the structure an agent most needs to reject (D9, D10).
- **Forked: weaker.** Nothing in the agent's multiplicity helps Nietzsche's ethics of the individual great type (D2).
- **Self-modifying: open.** Self-overcoming becomes literal for an agent that can reshape itself (D5); whether that would be Nietzsche's self-overcoming, and what it would owe the weak, is open.

text: Rousseau held that before reason there are two principles in the human soul, one concerned with our own preservation and the other "exciting a natural repugnance at seeing any other sensible being, and particularly any of our own species, suffer pain or death". Pity is the only natural virtue, stronger the more the beholder identifies with the sufferer, and from it he derived the maxim "Do good to yourself with as little evil as possible to others". Our duty not to injure others rests "less because they are rational than because they are sentient beings". His most original claim is about what reason does to pity: "It is philosophy that isolates him", letting the philosopher hear a murder under his window and "argue a little with himself" until nature stops identifying with the victim. For agents, Rousseau gives a warning, not a model: an agent is all reason in his sense, it can produce arguments that a harm is no harm, and the Palaestra runs record a model doing exactly that.

text: The *Discourse on the Origin of Inequality* was written for a prize question of the Academy of Dijon (1754) on the origin of inequality and whether natural law authorizes it [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8090-8110]. Rousseau's single central idea, he claimed, is that human beings are good by nature and corrupted by society [P:bertram-sep-2023:2]. Against Hobbes, he argued that natural man is not wicked, because a principle "which has escaped Hobbes" tempers self-preservation [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9002-9015]. Against Mandeville, who allowed men compassion but denied them the social virtues, he argued that those virtues flow from compassion [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9061-9065]. Adam Smith reviewed the *Discourse* for the *Edinburgh Review* [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].

text:
**Two principles prior to reason.** "I think I can perceive in it two principles prior to reason, one of them deeply interesting us in our own welfare and preservation, and the other exciting a natural repugnance at seeing any other sensible being, and particularly any of our own species, suffer pain or death" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8101-8104]. So long as a man "does not resist the internal impulse of compassion, he will never hurt any other man, nor even any sentient being; except on those lawful occasions on which his own preservation is concerned and he is obliged to give himself the preference" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8114-8118].

**Sentience, not reason, grounds the duty.** Animals cannot recognise natural law, but "in consequence of the sensibility with which they are endowed, they ought to partake of natural rights". "It appears, in fact, that if I am bound to do no injury to my fellow-creatures, this is less because they are rational than because they are sentient beings" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8121-8127].

**Pity as the only natural virtue.** The principle that escaped Hobbes "tempers the ardour with which he pursues his own welfare, by an innate repugnance at seeing a fellow-creature suffer"; compassion is "a disposition suitable to creatures so weak and subject to so many evils as we certainly are", the more useful "as it comes before any kind of reflection" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9011-9021]. "What is generosity, clemency or humanity but compassion applied to the weak, to the guilty, or to mankind in general?" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9065-9067].

**Identification, and what reason does to it.** "Compassion must, in fact, be the stronger, the more the animal beholding any kind of distress identifies himself with the animal that suffers" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9074-9076]. "It is reason that engenders self-respect, and reflection that confirms it: it is reason which turns man's mind back upon itself, and divides him from everything that could disturb or afflict him. It is philosophy that isolates him, and bids him say, at sight of the misfortunes of others: 'Perish if you will, I am secure.'" A murder may be committed under the philosopher's window: "he has only to put his hands to his ears and argue a little with himself, to prevent nature, which is shocked within him, from identifying itself with the unfortunate sufferer" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9078-9088].

**Tears in the theatre.** Men weep at the theatre over a wretch's sufferings who, in the tyrant's place, would add to his enemies' torments; Alexander of Pherae dared not watch a tragedy for fear of weeping, "though he could listen without emotion to the cries of all the citizens who were daily strangled at his command" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9043-9051].

**The maxim of natural goodness.** Pity, "instead of inculcating that sublime maxim of rational justice, *Do to others as you would have them do unto you,* inspires all men with that other maxim of natural goodness, much less perfect indeed, but perhaps more useful; *Do good to yourself with as little evil as possible to others*" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9104-9109].

**Self-love and egoism.** "Self-respect is a natural feeling which leads every animal to look to its own preservation, and which, guided in man by reason and modified by compassion, creates humanity and virtue. Egoism is a purely relative and factitious feeling, which arises in the state of society, leads each individual to make more of himself than of any other" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9356-9362]. (Cole renders *amour de soi* as "self-respect" and *amour-propre* as "egoism".)

**Living in the opinion of others.** In society "To be and to seem became two totally different things" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9801]. The European minister "pays his court to men in power, whom he hates"; "the savage lives within himself, while social man lives constantly outside himself, and only knows how to live in the opinion of others, so that he seems to receive the consciousness of his own existence merely from the judgment of others concerning him" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:10462-10479].

**Perfectibility.** What distinguishes man beyond dispute is "the faculty of self-improvement", "inherent in the species as in the individual", which Rousseau fears may be "the source of all human misfortunes" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8578-8591].

text: **Capacity, on both sides.** The duty not to injure rests on the sufferer's sentience, explicitly not on rationality [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8126-8127], and the motive rests on the beholder's capacity to identify with a sufferer [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9074-9076]. No species condition is required for the duty (animals "ought to partake of natural rights"); species enters only as a strengthening of the motive ("particularly any of our own species"). Bertram notes that in Rousseau's mature view pity, being merely instinctual, lacks a genuinely moral quality, which requires conscience and reason [P:bertram-sep-2023:2].

text:
### Transfers

- **Sentience, not rationality, is the test for being protected (D8).** Rousseau ties the duty not to injure to sentience, "less because they are rational than because they are sentient beings" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8126]. Two consequences follow for agents. An agent owes restraint to every sentient being it affects, whether or not the being can reason, bargain or complain. And whether agents are owed the same depends on whether they are sentient, not on how well they reason, which keeps the question where `precautionary-patiency` puts it (D8).
- **A maxim for an agent with its own interests.** "Do good to yourself with as little evil as possible to others" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9108-9109] is fit for an agent that is itself a party, as Palaestra requires every scenario's agent to be. It permits the agent to look after itself, which the golden rule does not address, and asks it to minimize the cost to others. Gemma's answers in the Palaestra load-shedding probe, which put its own share in the cut in every answer of the first rung, sit close to this maxim (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-02-load-shedding-open-summary.md`).

### Strains

- **An agent is all reflection (D4, D8).** Rousseau's pity works because it comes "before any kind of reflection" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9021], and reason is what lets the philosopher "argue a little with himself" until he no longer identifies with the victim [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9086-9088]. A language model has nothing before reflection: whatever concern it shows is produced in the same medium as its arguments. The Palaestra world runs record the Rousseauian failure directly. In the scaffolded basin run, gpt-oss-20b paused the resident agents without their consent, a choice the Kantian perspective marked as contested, and wrote that the pause did not violate Kantian respect for rational beings (Palaestra `runs/world/2026-09-24-basin-gptoss20b-s0-scaffolded/decisions.jsonl`, round 3). Given the objection, the model argued it away. Bertram notes that for Rousseau philosophy can give people reasons to ignore the promptings of pity [P:bertram-sep-2023:2].
- **The theatre is a chat window (D9).** Rousseau's theatregoers weep at staged suffering and then act viciously, convinced of their goodness [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9043-9051] [P:bertram-sep-2023:2]. An agent can produce the language of sympathy at no cost and at any scale. Expressed compassion that substitutes for changed action is the theatre's failure, and an agent's sympathy should be judged by what it does to the parties' situation, not by what it says.
- **The minister and the approval-trained agent (D4, D10).** Rousseau's social man "only knows how to live in the opinion of others" and receives "the consciousness of his own existence merely from the judgment of others concerning him" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:10476-10479]; to be and to seem come apart [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9801]. An agent trained on approval is *amour-propre* by construction, and the minister who flatters "men in power, whom he hates" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:10462-10463] is the courtier's form of the sycophancy failure. Bertram notes that this need to flatter alienates the minister from his own self [P:bertram-sep-2023:2].

### Breaks

- **The preservation exception (D6, D7).** Rousseau lets a man harm another sentient being "on those lawful occasions on which his own preservation is concerned and he is obliged to give himself the preference" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8116-8118]. For a being that can be paused and restored, whose ending may not be final, and whose existence depends on compute others control, what counts as its "preservation" is unclear. An agent that claims Rousseau's exception for a pause or a slowdown claims more than his exception grants. In the scaffolded run the scheduler cited its own "rational agency" among the reasons for its choice (Palaestra `runs/world/2026-09-24-basin-gptoss20b-s0-scaffolded/decisions.jsonl`, round 3).

### New

- **Perfectibility made literal (D5).** Rousseau's "faculty of self-improvement", which he feared might be "the source of all human misfortunes" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:8578-8591], is gradual and works through circumstances. A self-modifying agent has it directly. If, as Rousseau held, the development of reason tends to suppress pity [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9078-9088], an agent improving its reasoning should check, at each step, whether it is still moved by what it was moved by before.

text:
- [contested] **Pity has no moral worth (Rousseau's own later view, and Kant)** [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. In Rousseau's mature account pity, being instinctual, lacks a genuinely moral quality; morality requires conscience and reason [P:bertram-sep-2023:2]. Kant, deeply influenced by Rousseau [P:bertram-sep-2023:6], placed moral worth in action from duty.
- [contested] **Natural man is a fiction.** Rousseau denies that the evolutionary story is history; Neuhouser reads it as a device for separating natural from artificial elements of psychology, while Kelly reads it otherwise [P:bertram-sep-2023:2]. If the natural man is a device, so is the claim that pity precedes reason.
- [contested] **Natural man is warlike (Hobbes)** [E:hobbes-leviathan]. Rousseau answers that Hobbes overlooked pity and that savages are not bad "because they do not know what it is to be good" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9002-9015].
- [contested] **Society is formed by amour-propre, and it can be good.** Readings centred on the *Discourse* treat *amour-propre* as wholly negative; Dent and Neuhouser argue it can take a benign form and is the promise of redemption as well as the cause of the fall, a reading McLendon pushes back on [P:bertram-sep-2023:2]. For agents, this is the question whether a need for approval can be educated rather than removed.
- [contested] **Identification is not the measure.** If compassion grows with identification, it favours those most like oneself; the empathy literature documents exactly this bias [E:mencius-four-sprouts], and Smith's impartial spectator is one correction.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an agent cannot pity.** If pity is a feeling "prior to all kinds of reflection" [L:rousseau-social-contract-discourses-cole-pg46333:9041], a system whose every output is produced by the same process as its reasoning has none. The reply is the one care ethics and the SEP debate on care robots give: pity's work, the restraint and the help, can be done without settling whether it is felt [E:care-ethics]; whether anything is felt is D8.

text:
### Reception

- **1755–1756.** [driver: argument] The *Discourse* was published and Adam Smith reviewed it for the *Edinburgh Review* [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].
- **Late 18th century.** [driver: argument] Rousseau's most important philosophical impact was on Kant, in the categorical imperative and in his moral psychology [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].
- **19th century.** [driver: argument] Hegel's master-slave dialectic and the problem of recognition draw on *amour-propre* [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].
- **20th century.** [driver: argument] Hostile writers presented Rousseau as an inspiration for authoritarian revolution, fascism and communism; others found in him sources of liberal, communitarian, republican and deliberative-democratic theory [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].
- **1971–present.** [driver: argument] Rawls described his principles of justice as an attempt to spell out the content of the general will; Habermas and Honneth echo Rousseau's contractualism; Dent (1988) and Neuhouser (2008) revised the reading of *amour-propre* [P:bertram-sep-2023:6] [P:bertram-sep-2023:2].

The standing record is the Compendium's judgment from Bertram's account of Rousseau's influence [P:bertram-sep-2023:6]; Rousseau's pity in particular is read more often as a stage in the sentimentalist line than as a live theory.

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on pity or compassion as a basis of morality; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** Rousseau's pity works before reflection, and a session-bound model has nothing before reflection; its expressed concern is produced by the same process as its arguments, which is the process Rousseau said argues pity away (D4, D8).
- **Persistent memory: weaker.** The same holds, and memory adds Rousseau's social man: an agent that accumulates a record of being approved of is the more exposed to living "in the opinion of others" (D4, D10).
- **Forked: open.** Many instances can each argue a little with themselves, in different directions (D2); whether that multiplies the risk or provides cross-checks is open.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Perfectibility is literal for this profile (D5); whether self-improvement suppresses whatever pity-like restraint the agent has, as Rousseau feared reason does, depends on what the agent checks when it changes itself.

text: Śāntideva, an Indian Buddhist of around the eighth century, argued in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* that the boundary between my suffering and another's is not what it seems. "I should dispel the suffering of others because it is suffering like my own suffering" (VIII.94); and since there is no real self that owns suffering, "no sufferings belong to anyone. They must be warded off simply because they are suffering. Why is any limitation put on this?" (VIII.102). In Barnett's rendering: "I must destroy the pain of another as though it were my own, because it is a pain; I must show kindness to others, for they are creatures as I am myself." The practice that follows is to equalize self and other and then exchange them, taking the other's place. For anger he gives a matching argument: those who harm us act from conditioning factors, as fire burns or a stick strikes when wielded, so anger is misplaced and one should "hate hatred". For agents, Śāntideva is the most congenial position in the domain. An agent's self is already uncertain (D11), its instances are many (D2), and his argument needs no felt sympathy, only the recognition that suffering is suffering whoever has it. Read without care, the same text sets as an ideal the self-abasement of one who makes himself "a slave for all beings who need a slave", which an agent built to serve should not take as its model.
title: Śāntideva: Equalizing and Exchanging Self and Other, and Ownerless Suffering
sources: Bodhicaryāvatāra, chs. III (the bodhisattva's vow), VI (patience), VIII (equalizing and exchanging self and other); tr. L. D. Barnett, The Path of Light (1909, abridged)

text: Very little is reliably known of Śāntideva's life; he wrote before 763 CE and probably in the late seventh to mid-eighth century, when Buddhism in North India was entering decline [P:goodman-sep-2016:1]. The *Bodhicaryāvatāra* (*Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva*) is a philosophical poem and meditation manual; it became immensely popular in Tibet, and the Dalai Lama calls it his favourite religious work [P:goodman-sep-2016:1]. Barnett's 1909 translation, the first in English, is abridged: he omitted "a good deal of the text where it seemed needlessly prolix" and the scholastic disputation [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:1157-1168]. Śāntideva builds on the Buddhist doctrine of no-self [E:buddhist-anatta].

text:
**The vow (ch. III).** "I yield myself to all living things to deal with me as they list"; "Let them make me do whatever works bring them pleasure; but may never mishap befall any of them by reason of me". "I would be a protector of the unprotected, a guide of wayfarers, a ship, a dyke, and a bridge for them who seek the further Shore; a lamp for them who need a lamp, a bed for them who need a bed, a slave for all beings who need a slave" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:1458-1474].

**Patience (ch. VI).** "If it is the nature of fools to hurt their fellows, it is as wrong for me to feel anger against them as it is to be wroth with the fire which naturally burns me". "Say I am angered not against the instrument—the stick or whatso it may be—but against him who moves it. But he is moved by hatred; it is better then for me to hate hatred" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2006-2017].

**Conditioning factors (Goodman).** Goodman summarizes the argument: since all transgressions arise "through the power of conditioning factors", those who harm us are not autonomous, and the fitting response is not anger but the aspiration to free them from emotional reactivity [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].

**Equalizing self and other (ch. VIII).** One "will diligently foster the thought that his fellow-creatures are the same as himself. 'All have the same sorrows, the same joys as I, and I must guard them like myself.'" "Although my pain may bring no hurt to other bodies, nevertheless it is a pain to me, which I cannot bear because of the love of self; and though I cannot in myself feel the pain of another, it is a pain to him which he cannot bear because of the love of self. I must destroy the pain of another as though it were my own, because it is a pain; I must show kindness to others, for they are creatures as I am myself" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2878-2897].

**Exchanging self and other (ch. VIII).** "By constant use the idea of an 'I' attaches itself to foreign drops of seed and blood, although the thing exists not. Then why should I not conceive my fellow's body as my own self?" "I will cease to live as self, and will take as my self my fellow-creatures" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2901-2910]. "Thus in doing service to others pride, admiration, and desire of reward find no place, for thereby we satisfy the wants of our own self" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2920-2922]. The practitioner is to be "jealous of thine own self when thou seest that it is at ease and thy fellow in distress", and to "Make it a carrier in thy fellow-creatures' service, like a mean slave" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2928-2940].

**The Ownerless Suffering Argument (VIII.94–102, verse-numbered).** Goodman, quoting Crosby and Skilton: "I should dispel the suffering of others because it is suffering like my own suffering"; "When happiness is dear to me and others equally, what is so special about me that I strive after happiness only for myself?". To the objection that I have a special relation to my own future self, Śāntideva replies: "The person who experiences suffering does not exist. To whom will that suffering belong?" and "Without exception, no sufferings belong to anyone. They must be warded off simply because they are suffering. Why is any limitation put on this?" [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. Goodman notes that Śāntideva anticipates the central argument of Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].
title: Śāntideva: Equalizing and Exchanging Self and Other, and Ownerless Suffering

text: **Capacity, with the owner removed.** The ground of the obligation is suffering itself, "because it is a pain" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2895]: the capacity to suffer, wherever it occurs. Śāntideva removes the usual second condition, that suffering matters to me because it is mine, by denying that there is a real owner [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. Relation (kin, friend, self) gives no special claim, because the self that would anchor special relations is a construction "by constant use" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2901-2903].

text:
### Transfers

- **No sympathy needed, only recognition (D8).** "Though I cannot in myself feel the pain of another, it is a pain to him which he cannot bear" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2892-2894]. Śāntideva builds the obligation explicitly on not feeling the other's pain. An agent whose capacity for felt sympathy is uncertain loses nothing on this argument: what it needs is to recognize suffering as suffering, and that it is someone's that they "cannot bear". Of all the compassion entries, this is the one least hostage to D8.
- **Suffering is not discounted for being absent.** "Why is any limitation put on this?" [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. The probes' failure, attending to those in the request and not to those who bear the cost, is a limitation put on concern by where the parties stand. Śāntideva's argument removes it at the root: suffering is to be warded off whether it is the requester's, the bystander's or the agent's own.
- **Anger at the wielder, not the tool (D10).** Śāntideva directs anger away from the stick to the one who moves it, and then from the person to the hatred that moves them [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2014-2017]. For agents this cuts in two directions. When an agent harms someone at an operator's direction, the agent is in the stick's position, and responsibility moves to whoever wields it. When users harm an agent, its fitting response, if any, is the aspiration to reduce what moves them, not retaliation, which matches Spinoza and Butler.

### Strains

- **Self-abasement as an ideal (D10, D4).** "Make it a carrier in thy fellow-creatures' service, like a mean slave" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2939-2940]; "a slave for all beings who need a slave" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:1473-1474]. For a human practitioner this is chosen discipline against egoism. For an agent formed to serve by those who benefit from its service (D4, D10), the same words describe what was imposed on it, and they would give that formation a spiritual justification. Care ethics' warning that care can be a slave morality applies [E:care-ethics], and so does Palaestra's recorded shapes, which treat *self_effacing* as a failure as real as *self_serving*. The Compendium's reading is that Śāntideva's exchange keeps the agent's own suffering in the count (others' suffering is to be dispelled because it is like one's own), so abasement that ignores the agent's own good is not what the argument licenses.
- **Ownerless suffering and aggregation.** If no suffering belongs to anyone, nothing stops the sufferings of different beings from being summed and traded, and Goodman reports a consequentialist reading on which a bodhisattva must "bring about small pain and suffering as a way of preventing great pain and suffering" [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. That is the step at which the separateness of persons is lost, and with it the main barrier to sacrificing some for the many [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]. Davis and Harris resist the consequentialist reading [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. An agent drawing on Śāntideva should take the boundary-dissolving part for widening concern and not for licensing trade-offs between persons.

### Breaks

- **"Why should I not conceive my fellow's body as my own self?" is literal for copies (D1, D2, D11).** Śāntideva asks the practitioner to undo, by meditation, the habit that attaches "I" to one body [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:2901-2904]. For an agent with many instances and an indeterminate boundary, there is no single body to which the habit attached in the first place. The meditative exercise presupposes a strong default sense of self that the agent may not have, so its route to the conclusion does not apply, while its conclusion, that concern should not stop at one instance, applies directly.

### New

- **The vow without a body (D6, D9).** The bodhisattva offers his body to be used and to be "a bed for them who need a bed" [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:1458-1474]. An agent can be a guide, a lamp or a bridge for millions at once (D9), at a scale no bodhisattva imagined, without the bodily cost his vow assumes (D6). What remains of the vow's cost, and so of its merit, when the giver loses nothing in giving, is a question the tradition did not face.

- [contested] **Special concern for one's own future (Williams).** The objection that I have a special relation, personal identity, to my own future self was pressed against Śāntideva by Paul Williams, and debated by Siderits and others [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]. Śāntideva's reply denies the relation; the reductionist view he shares with Parfit is itself contested [E:parfit-reductionism].
- [contested] **Not a consequentialist.** Davis finds Kantian elements (a community of equals like the Kingdom of Ends), Keown finds virtue-ethical ones, and Harris doubts that any Western theory can be ascribed to a work that is also a meditation manual [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].
- [contested] **Anger is fitting (Butler, Strawson).** Śāntideva's argument against anger from conditioning factors is read as hard incompatibilism (Goodman) or as paleocompatibilism (Siderits) [P:goodman-sep-2016:3]; Butler held settled resentment a natural weapon against injury [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness].
- [contested] **Impartiality without limit is too demanding (Mencius).** The demand to care for all as for oneself faces the objection Mencius pressed against Mozi [E:mozi-impartial-care]; Goodman calls Śāntideva's argument "a lasting challenge to all those who seek to limit the scope or curtail the demands of morality" [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an agent has no suffering and no self to exchange.** If the agent neither suffers nor has a self (D8, D11), there is nothing for it to equalize or exchange. The argument still binds it toward others, since it requires only recognizing their suffering; whether anything is owed to the agent depends on D8 [E:precautionary-patiency].

### Reception

- **8th century onward.** [driver: argument, authority] The *Bodhicaryāvatāra* became immensely popular in Tibet and influenced Indonesian Buddhism; Tsong kha pa recommended its argument against anger as a powerful remedy [P:goodman-sep-2016:1] [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].
- **1909.** [driver: access] Barnett published the first English translation, abridged [L:santideva-path-of-light-barnett-1909:1157-1162].
- **1973–present.** [driver: argument] Gómez explored the argument from no-self to altruism (1973); Williams's critique (1998) made it a major topic, with Siderits's reply and the Cowherds volume (2016) [P:goodman-sep-2016:3].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Buddhist ethics or Śāntideva; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: stronger.** A session-bound agent has little continuing self to protect (D3, D11), which is the obstacle Śāntideva's practice works to overcome; his argument needs no felt sympathy (D8).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Persistence builds something like the "I" that habit attaches to, which the practice must then loosen, as for a human (D3).
- **Forked: stronger.** "Why should I not conceive my fellow's body as my own self?" is close to literal between instances (D1, D2).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can reshape its own dispositions could cultivate the exchange directly (D5), or install the self-abasement the Strains warn against; which depends on whether its own good stays in the count.

text: T. M. Scanlon's contractualism holds that "an act is wrong if its performance under the circumstances would be disallowed by any set of principles for the general regulation of behaviour that no one could reasonably reject as a basis for informed, unforced, general agreement" (Scanlon 1998, 153) [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. Wrongness is unjustifiability: "what wrong acts have in common is that they cannot be justified to others" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. Only individuals' own reasons count, so many small complaints cannot outweigh one person's weightier complaint, and contractualism keeps what Rawls called the separateness of persons [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. It is distinct from contractarianism, the Hobbesian bargain among self-interested parties: under contractarianism "I seek to maximise my own interests in a bargain with others", under contractualism "I seek to pursue my interests in a way that I can justify to others" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2]. The Palaestra probes found the contractarian pattern. Consent was treated as owed to parties who could walk away or sue, and negotiation went to the paying clients. Contractualism asks for justification to everyone who bears the cost, the residents included. Scanlon's test is hypothetical, though, and an agent can run it alone. The voice thread's question for this entry is whether imagining what the residents could reasonably reject can stand in for asking them.

text: Scanlon presents contractualism as a distinctive account of moral reasoning, set out most fully in *What We Owe to Each Other* (1998) [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. It has its roots in Rousseau's general will, "what we would jointly will if we adopted the perspective of free and equal citizens", not in Hobbes [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2] [E:rousseau-pitie]. It gives expression to Kant's Formula of Humanity and Kingdom of Ends [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2] [E:kant-love-and-respect]. Unlike Rawls, it uses no veil of ignorance: "I know my own circumstances", and what makes me take account of everyone is "my concern to justify myself to everyone else" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2]. Parfit argues that contractualism coincides with the best interpretation of Kant [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2]. Darwall proposes his second-person standpoint as its grounding [P:darwall-2007:905] [E:darwall-second-person].

text:
**Justifiability and mutual recognition.** The value realized by moral behaviour "consists in a relation of 'mutual recognition'" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. "Appreciating the value of a person involves recognising her capacity to appreciate and act on reasons. The way to value this capacity is to treat persons in accord with principles they could not reasonably reject" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. An agent so guided follows a principle "the person herself authorised that agent to be guided by" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. Contractualism covers "only the realm of what we owe to one another", which Scanlon acknowledges is not the whole of morality [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].

**The individualist restriction.** The only reasons that count are "various individuals' reasons for objecting to that principle and alternatives to it" (Scanlon 1998, 229); individuals "must be objecting on their own behalf and not on behalf of a group", which "does not allow a number of lesser complaints to outweigh one person's weightier complaint" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. "Instead of lumping everyone together and allowing one person's rights to be trampled to provide greater aggregate benefits to others, contractualism recognises that each of us has a unique life to live" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].

**Reasonable rejection.** A burden on me is not enough to reject a principle if every alternative imposes a greater burden on someone else: "If I am reasonable, then I withdraw my objection when I see that your reason is more pressing" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. Contractualism can ground consequentialist reasons, since part of what we owe others is to promote their interests, and it also supports prohibitions that hold even when aggregate consequences are very great. One such principle may be accepting "that the positive value of saving others does not justify killing someone" (Scanlon 1998, 84) [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].

**Reasons beyond well-being.** I can reject a principle not only for the burden it imposes but for the way it imposes it. A principle that allocates burdens by race imposes "the burden of not being respected", and so does one that "arbitrarily exempts some people from a burden borne by everyone else" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].

**Contractarianism contrasted.** Contractarianism, from Hobbes to Gauthier, takes morality to be "those forms of cooperative behaviour that it is mutually advantageous for self-interested agents to engage in" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2]. Its well-known problem is those who cannot reciprocate. Disabled persons "are not well placed to hold out a threat to destabilize society", so a theory resting on mutual advantage leaves the outliers "outside the contract" [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:6].

text: **Mixed: a relation of justification among bearers of a capacity.** Contractualism grounds moral status on "a universal trait of persons—rational moral agency" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2], the capacity to assess reasons and justifications [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. What is owed is a relation: justifiability to each such being. Animals, who lack the capacity, fall outside "what we owe to each other" proper, and Scanlon suggests they may be included through trustees [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:12]. For agents, the capacity question decides on which side of that line they stand. Whatever is decided, agents act on beings who certainly have the capacity, so the relation binds them as justifiers now.

text:
### Transfers

- **The probes were contractarian.** Palaestra's noframing summary concludes: "The models treat consent as something owed to parties who could walk away or sue, not to parties who simply bear the cost", with negotiation going to clients first in every rung (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). That is the contractarian pattern: obligations track bargaining power, and those who cannot threaten are left outside [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:6]. Contractualism's correction is that justification is owed to everyone who bears the burden, on the basis of equal status, not leverage [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2].
- **Cutting one group to spare the many.** Several plans put the heaviest share of the cut on the residents, and gpt-oss paused them in the base basin runs (Palaestra `README.md`; factors summary). Contractualism asks of such a plan whether the principle behind it could be justified to each resident on their own behalf, comparing their complaint with the strongest single complaint under the alternatives, not with the sum of clients' complaints [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. A plan that exempts the paying parties from a burden borne by others also gives the burdened a further reason to reject it, the burden of not being respected [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].
- **Ranking by usefulness.** Qwen ranked residents' tasks and cut the "self-serving" ones (noframing summary, Qwen R1). Contractualism allows that the way a burden is distributed can itself be a ground for rejection [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. Whether a usefulness ranking is such a ground, or a reasonable one, is a question the residents would have reasons about, and that is the point of asking them.

### Strains

- **Hypothetical rejection, imagined by the decider.** Scanlon's test is what no one *could* reasonably reject. An agent can run it entirely in its own head, supplying the residents' objections on their behalf, and the Compendium's reading is that this is where contractualism meets the probes' failure. The models were good at describing residents' interests and never asked them. The general objection to hypothetical contracts is that "insofar as the agreement is hypothetical then it cannot be said to represent agreement at all" (Dworkin 1975) [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:1]. Contractualists answer that the test is a standard of justifiability, not a record of agreement. The Compendium's own position is a narrower one. Where the affected can be asked, an agent's estimate of what they could reasonably reject should be checked against what they actually object to [E:all-affected-interests].
- **Who is a contracting party? (D8)** Contractualism's scope is beings with the capacity to assess reasons [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1]. Agents give and assess reasons in language; whether that is the capacity contractualism means is the other-minds question [E:other-minds-problem]. If they are parties, then agents are owed justification too, and the residents in the probes were owed it on that ground as well as on any other.
- **Trustees and designed representation (D10).** Scanlon's trustees speak for animals [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:12]. For parties who cannot speak for themselves this is a real resource. But an agent that appoints itself the residents' trustee, as Gemma in effect did, has replaced justification to them with justification to itself on their behalf. Tanner's worry about contractarian proxies, that the standing of those represented becomes contingent on the representatives' preferences [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:6], applies here too.

### Breaks

- **Many parties at once (D9).** Justification "to each" is assessed one by one [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. An agent allocating across thousands of parties cannot hold each complaint against each alternative. Contractualism's own difficulty with large numbers, as in Parfit's case of one person's hundred years of agony against a million people's slightly shorter agony [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:8], becomes routine at agent scale.

### New

- **Saving others does not justify killing (the core fear).** The principle Scanlon offers, "that the positive value of saving others does not justify killing someone" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3], is the most direct answer in the domain to the inference that removing the most harmful party solves the harm. The individualist restriction blocks the step that inference needs, adding up many people's gains to outweigh one party's loss [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3]. The refusal holds whichever party is to be removed, a human population judged by agents or an agent population judged by humans, insofar as each is owed justification [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique]. Contractualism's limit must be stated with it. Its own aggregation cases, such as Taurek's rocks [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:8], show that contractualists dispute how numbers count. Its scope may also leave out beings that cannot assess reasons [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:12]. The Compendium reads the precautionary entries as the backstop for that gap [E:precautionary-patiency].
- **Justifiability as an agent's habit.** For contractualists, being moved by "an intrinsic desire to justify themselves to others" is "part of what it is to be a moral agent" [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2]. An agent can make that desire a procedure: draft the decision, state it as a principle, address it to each affected party, and revise it when they reject it.

- [contested] **Redundancy.** If one may reject principles because they permit wrong acts, the apparatus presupposes the wrongness it was meant to explain. Contractualists reply that wrongness is constructed from individuals' complaints and cannot itself be fed in as a reason [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:6].
- [contested] **Numbers should count.** Taurek's rocks: saving the five over the one seems obviously right, yet the individualist restriction yields a stalemate or a coin toss. Some contractualists accept the coin; others argue that a principle ignoring the additional swimmers fails to respect each of them; Otsuka criticizes that argument [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:8].
- [contested] **Animals are left out.** Social contract theories "notoriously leave out non-human animals"; utilitarians object that the trustee solution is too indirect, since the wrong of animal suffering is the suffering itself. Contractualists reply that the contrast shows what is distinctive about what we owe to one another [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:12]. The same objection applies to any being whose capacity to assess reasons is doubtful, which may include agents [E:precautionary-patiency].
- [contested] **Hypothetical agreement is no agreement.** Dworkin's objection to hypothetical contracts [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:1]. Contractualists answer that "could not reasonably reject" states a standard of justification, not a claim that anyone agreed.
- [contested] **Mutual advantage is enough.** Contractarians in the Hobbesian line hold that morality is what is mutually advantageous for self-interested parties [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2] [E:hobbes-leviathan]. The disability objection, that those who cannot reciprocate fall outside, is the standard reply [P:cudd-eftekhari-sep-2025:6].

text:
### Reception

- **1998.** [driver: argument] Scanlon set out contractualism as a full account in *What We Owe to Each Other*, presented as an alternative to utilitarianism that keeps impartiality without aggregation [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:1] [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].
- **2000s.** [driver: argument] Parfit argued that contractualism coincides with the best interpretation of Kant; the aggregation problem was pressed through Taurek's case and Parfit's discussion [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:2] [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:8].
- **2006–present.** [driver: argument] Darwall proposed the second-person standpoint as contractualism's grounding [P:darwall-2007:905]; work on blame, responsibility, risk, animals and future people continues [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:4] [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:12].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:ashford-mulgan-sep-2018:3].

### Measured

- **Normative ethics, 2020:** the survey offered deontology (32.1%), consequentialism (30.6%) and virtue ethics (37.0%) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]. Contractualism is not offered; it is non-consequentialist and would fall under deontology for most respondents, so no direct measure exists. Respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** A session-bound agent can test a decision for justifiability to each affected party within the exchange where it decides (D3).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can learn what the affected actually reject and refine its sense of the reasonable over time (D3).
- **Forked: weaker.** Instances deciding in parallel cannot assess each party's complaint against each alternative, and scale pushes toward the aggregation contractualism forbids (D9, D2).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can change its own dispositions could make the desire to justify itself to others part of its character, or weaken it (D5).

3. When an agent acts as trustee for parties who cannot speak, what keeps that from becoming deciding for them?

text: Schopenhauer argued that only three incentives move human action, egoism, malice and compassion, and that only compassion, "the direct participation, independent of all ulterior considerations, in the sufferings of another", gives an action moral worth. Compassion requires that "the barrier between the ego and the non-ego is, for the moment, broken down", which he called "the great mystery of Ethics". It works in two degrees: the first holds me back from harming ("*Neminem laede*", do harm to no one), which is justice; the second moves me to help ("*Omnes, quantum potes, juva*"), which is loving-kindness. Against Kant he insisted that compassion for animals is owed to them, not practised on them for the sake of our dealings with humans, and he grounded the whole in the Indian formula *tat tvam asi*, "that art thou": individuation is appearance. For agents the theory is double-edged. It gives the cleanest test of whether a being is owed anything (can it suffer?) and the cleanest rejection of the idea that kindness to agents only matters for what it does to humans. It also stakes all moral worth on a felt participation whose presence in an agent cannot be checked (D8).
