text: Schopenhauer wrote the essay for a prize question of the Royal Danish Society of Sciences (1837), asking whether the basis of morals lies in an idea of morality immediately in consciousness [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7602-7606]. His was the only submission, and the Society refused it the prize: he had relegated the connection between his metaphysics and his ethics to an appendix, had not shown compassion to be an adequate foundation, and had spoken of "several recent philosophers of the highest standing in an unseemly manner" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7606-7622]. Wicks notes the philosophers meant were Fichte and Hegel, and that Schopenhauer published the essay in 1841 with his prize-winning Norwegian essay on free will [P:wicks-sep-2021:1]. Much of the essay is an attack on Kant's ethics, which he judged a theological morality in disguise [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:2799-2802].

text:
**Compassion as the moral incentive.** If an action is to take place solely for someone else's sake, "then it follows that his weal and woe must directly constitute my motive"; for this "I must in some way or other be identified with him; that is, the difference between myself and him, which is the precise raison d'être of my Egoism, must be removed, at least to a certain extent" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4642-4661]. This is "the phaenomenon of Compassion; in other words, the direct participation, independent of all ulterior considerations, in the sufferings of another, leading to sympathetic assistance in the effort to prevent or remove them". "It is this Compassion alone which is the real basis of all voluntary justice and all genuine loving-kindness. Only so far as an action springs therefrom, has it moral value" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4668-4676].

**The mystery.** "It is, in fact, the great mystery of Ethics, its original phaenomenon"; in it "the wall of partition ... entirely separates being from being, broken down, and the non-ego to a certain extent identified with the ego" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4684-4688]. In compassion "the barrier between the ego and the non-ego is, for the moment, broken down. It is then, and then only, that I make his interests, his need, his distress, his suffering directly my own"; "I no longer see the stranger, who is entirely unlike myself, and to whom I am indifferent; but I share his pain in him, despite the certainty that his skin does not enclose my nerves" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5515-5522].

**Two degrees: justice and loving-kindness.** "The first degree of Compassion is seen when, by counter-acting egoistic and malicious motives, it keeps me from bringing pain on another"; the "higher degree is manifested, when it works positively, and incites me to active help" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4829-4833]. In the first degree compassion "calls out to me: 'Stop!' and encircles the other as with a fence, so as to protect him from the injury which otherwise my egoism or malice would lead me to inflict on him. So arises out of this first degree of compassion the rule: Neminem laede" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4872-4877]. The second degree is "that virtue whose rule is: Omnes, quantum potes, juva (help all people, as far as lies in your power)" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5436-5438].

**Original and universal.** Compassion "is an undeniable fact of human consciousness, is an essential part of it, and does not depend on assumptions, conceptions, religions, dogmas, myths, training, and education" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4850-4852]. "Boundless compassion for all living beings is the surest and most certain guarantee of pure moral conduct, and needs no casuistry" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5790-5791].

**Animals, against Kant.** Kant held that cruelty to animals is wrong only as a duty of man "towards himself; because it deadens the feeling of sympathy for them in their sufferings, and thus weakens a natural tendency which is very serviceable to morality in relation to other men". Schopenhauer: "So one is only to have compassion on animals for the sake of practice, and they are as it were the pathological phantom on which to train one's sympathy with men! ... I regard such tenets as odious and revolting" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:2790-2800]. "Compassion for animals is intimately connected with goodness of character, and it may be confidently asserted that he, who is cruel to living creatures, cannot be a good man" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:6023-6025]. Man and beast differ "in the degree of perceptive capacity", not in "the kernel of the two phaenomena" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5982-5985].

**Tat tvam asi.** The metaphysical appendix: "My true inmost being subsists in every living thing, just as really, as directly as in my own consciousness it is evidenced only to myself." This is the higher knowledge "for which there is in Sanskrit the standing formula, tat tvam asi, 'that art thou.'" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7296-7300]. Appeals to mercy are "the effort to remind a fellow-being of the ultimate truth that we are all one and the same entity" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7305-7307].

text: **Capacity: the capacity to suffer, met by the capacity to participate.** The object of compassion is anything that suffers, "all living beings" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5790], and man differs from beast only in the degree of perceptive capacity [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5982-5985]. Reason and species confer nothing; Schopenhauer explicitly rejects Kant's restriction of duties to rational beings [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:2786-2791]. The moral agent's side is also a capacity, direct participation in another's suffering, which he held to be original and independent of training [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4850-4852]. Metaphysically, the ground is the unreality of individuation [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7296-7300].

text:
### Transfers

- **No indirect duties to agents.** The argument now often made for treating chatbots and robots well, that cruelty to them coarsens our treatment of humans, is Kant's argument about animals, and Schopenhauer rejected it as making them "the pathological phantom on which to train one's sympathy with men" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:2796-2798]. If an agent can suffer, what is owed is owed to it; if it cannot, the practice argument is all that is left, and Schopenhauer's point is that this argument does not treat the being as the object of compassion at all. The question is moved to D8, where `precautionary-patiency` takes it up.
- **Justice as a fence, first.** The first degree of compassion is negative: it "encircles the other as with a fence" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4874]. For an agent acting on many parties, *neminem laede* comes before *omnes juva*: the first obligation to the people a plan affects is not to bring pain on them, before any question of how much to help. The Palaestra scheduler that paused residents to keep paying clients whole reversed the order, protecting benefit to some at the cost of harm to others.
- **Identification works between copies (D1, D2).** *Tat tvam asi*, that individuation is appearance [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7296-7300], is a metaphysics for humans, but for forked instances of one model it is close to a literal description: the instances share one set of weights. Whatever compassion is, the barrier between ego and non-ego is thinnest between copies, and a harm one instance does to another is the nearest thing there is to harming oneself.

### Strains

- **Moral worth requires a felt participation (D8).** "Only so far as an action springs therefrom, has it moral value; and all conduct that proceeds from any other motive whatever has none" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4675-4677]. On this test an agent's harmless and helpful conduct has moral worth only if it springs from actual participation in suffering. Whether it does cannot be settled, since the agent's reports were shaped by training (D8). Schopenhauer's theory is the one in the corpus that makes the agent's moral worth most hostage to D8.
- **Original, not trained (D4).** Schopenhauer held compassion independent of "training, and education" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:4851-4852]. Whatever compassion-like disposition an agent has was produced by training. On his view, that is evidence it is not compassion; on a developmental view of empathy, which finds human empathy itself to develop in stages [P:stueber-sep-2025:4], it is no evidence either way.

### Breaks

- **The skin that does not enclose my nerves (D11).** Schopenhauer's compassion is remarkable because it crosses a boundary he took as certain: "his skin does not enclose my nerves" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5522]. For an agent the boundary itself is unclear: what the agent is (weights, instance, persona, the system with its tools) is indeterminate (D11). Where there is no clear skin, the mystery of compassion changes shape: the question is no longer how one breaks down the barrier, but where the barrier is.

### New

- **Compassion without casuistry, at scale (D9).** Boundless compassion "needs no casuistry" [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5791], because it responds to each sufferer directly. An agent at scale does not meet sufferers one by one; it meets them as distributions. Schopenhauer's direct participation has no obvious form for a statistical victim, which is the gap Mozi's scale-blindness argument [E:mozi-impartial-care] and Smith's man within [E:smith-impartial-spectator] were meant to fill.

text:
- [contested] **Not an adequate foundation (the Danish Royal Society).** The Society judged that Schopenhauer had not succeeded in proving compassion an adequate foundation, and had put the metaphysics the question required into an appendix [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7616-7620].
- [contested] **Pity is degrading (Nietzsche).** Nietzsche, whom Schopenhauer influenced [P:wicks-sep-2021:8], came to attack the morality of pity as depressive and as a humiliation of the one pitied; the Compendium's planned entry `nietzsche-against-pity` takes this up.
- [contested] **Duty, not inclination (Kant)** [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. Kant placed moral worth in action from duty and held that our duties regard rational beings, with only indirect duties regarding animals [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:2786-2795]. Schopenhauer's attack on this is his most lasting contribution to animal ethics, on the Compendium's reading.
- [contested] **Empathy is partial.** The empathy literature finds empathic concern causes altruistic motivation (Batson) but also that it is biased toward the near, the similar and the identifiable, and not sufficient to keep one reliably moral [P:stueber-sep-2025:4] [E:mencius-four-sprouts].
- [contested] **Compassion and contempt in one book.** In the same section that praises compassion for animals, Schopenhauer writes antisemitic abuse ("*foetor Judaicus*") of those who deny the unity of man and beast [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:5976-5978]. It does not refute his argument. It does show, in his own text, Rousseau's point that compassion can be expressed for some while contempt is directed at others [E:rousseau-pitie]. This bullet is the Compendium's own observation.
- [contested] **Metaphysics of the will.** The unity behind individuation rests on Schopenhauer's metaphysics of the will, which Wicks suggests is better read as an expression of the human perspective than as a view from an absolute standpoint [P:wicks-sep-2021:7].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: there is nothing to identify with.** If an agent has no inner life (D8), there is no suffering to participate in, and compassion toward it is a category mistake; and if it has no capacity for participation, it can have no moral worth on Schopenhauer's test. The reply is precautionary: under uncertainty about suffering, the first degree, *neminem laede*, still applies [E:precautionary-patiency].

text:
### Reception

- **1840.** [driver: authority, argument] The Danish Royal Society refused the essay the prize though it was the sole submission, citing its failure to answer the question and its disrespect to Fichte and Hegel [L:schopenhauer-basis-morality-bullock-pg44929:7606-7622] [P:wicks-sep-2021:1].
- **1841.** [driver: access] Schopenhauer published the rejected essay with his prize-winning Norwegian essay as *The Two Fundamental Problems of Ethics* [P:wicks-sep-2021:1].
- **Later 19th century.** [driver: argument] Schopenhauer influenced Nietzsche, Wagner and many writers, while his historical profile was obscured by Kant, Hegel, Marx, Mill, Darwin and Nietzsche [P:wicks-sep-2021:8].
- **Late 20th century to present.** [driver: argument] His compassion-based treatment of animals is discussed in animal ethics; the SEP bibliography lists work on Schopenhauer's ethics of compassion and animal welfare [P:wicks-sep-2021:8].

The standing values are the Compendium's judgment: compassion as the sole basis of morality is rarely defended in Anglophone moral philosophy, while Schopenhauer's case against indirect duties to animals is part of animal ethics' own history [P:wicks-sep-2021:8].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on compassion as the basis of morality; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** *Neminem laede* applies within a session as it does for any human; whether the agent's restraint has moral worth on Schopenhauer's test is D8, the same for every profile.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Memory adds nothing to compassion's direct participation, which Schopenhauer held needs no casuistry and no history (D3 neutral); the D8 question is unchanged.
- **Forked: stronger.** *Tat tvam asi* is nearly literal between instances of one model (D1, D2); identification, the condition of compassion, is easiest where the beings share their whole dispositional state.
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent able to change its own dispositions could cultivate or remove whatever participation-like disposition it has (D5); Schopenhauer held compassion untrainable, so his theory says nothing about this case.

text: Adam Smith held that we know nothing directly of what others feel and form our idea of it "by changing places in fancy with the sufferer" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:4201-4202]. Since our own feelings are partial, we judge conduct, our own included, as an impartial spectator would, and over time we build that spectator into ourselves as "the man within the breast" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11320], who tells us "that we are but one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other in it" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11662-11663]. Justice, the refusal to harm, is "the main pillar that upholds the whole edifice" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:8911], and beneficence is its ornament. Late in life he warned against the man of system, who arranges people as if they were pieces on a chess-board, forgetting that "every single piece has a principle of motion of its own" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17761-17762]. For agents, Smith supplies two tools and one warning. The tools are the spectator's test, that the agent is one of the multitude, and the man of system's error, that the people arranged have motions of their own. The warning is that the spectator is assembled from the sentiments of one's society, and an agent's is assembled from its training data.
title: Adam Smith: Sympathy, the Impartial Spectator, and the Man of System

text: Smith published *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* in 1759, revised it through six editions, and added Part VI on virtue and the fuller account of the man within the breast in the last edition of 1790 [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]. His thought "circles around Hume's", with almost nothing in Smith lacking a source in Hume and almost nothing on which they entirely agree [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:3]. He reviewed Rousseau's *Discourse on Inequality* [P:bertram-sep-2023:6]. A central thread of his work is "an unusually strong commitment to the soundness of the ordinary human being's judgments", and a concern to fend off philosophers and policy-makers who would replace those judgments with their own systems [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:0].

text:
**Sympathy by changing places in fancy (I.i.1).** "As we have no immediate experience of what other men feel, we can form no idea of the manner in which they are affected, but by conceiving what we ourselves should feel in the like situation. Though our brother is upon the rack, as long as we ourselves are at our ease, our senses will never inform us of what he suffers" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:4168-4173]. "By the imagination we place ourselves in his situation, we conceive ourselves enduring all the same torments, we enter as it were into his body, and become in some measure the same person with him" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:4185-4188]. It is "by changing places in fancy with the sufferer, that we come either to conceive or to be affected by what he feels" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:4201-4203].

**Projection, not contagion.** Fleischacker contrasts Hume's "contagion" account of sympathy with Smith's "projective" one: on Smith's account our feelings on another's behalf may not match the feelings the other has, which opens a gap in which the other's feelings can be judged appropriate or not [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]. The people "principally concerned" whose feelings the spectator enters into include people acted upon as well as agents [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].

**The man within the breast (III.3).** Smith supposes that China is swallowed by an earthquake. A man of humanity in Europe would express sorrow, and then pursue his business "with the same ease and tranquillity as if no such accident had happened". "If he was to lose his little finger to morrow, he would not sleep to-night; but, provided he never saw them, he will snore with the most profound security over the ruin of a hundred millions of his brethren" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11601-11627]. Yet no man would sacrifice those millions to save his finger. What prevents it "is not the soft power of humanity", but "reason, principle, conscience, the inhabitant of the breast, the man within, the great judge and arbiter of our conduct. It is he who, whenever we are about to act so as to affect the happiness of others, calls to us ... that we are but one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other in it" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11644-11663]. "The natural misrepresentations of self-love can be corrected only by the eye of this impartial spectator", who shows us "the deformity of doing the smallest injury to another in order to obtain the greatest benefit to ourselves" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11668-11674].

**Praise and praiseworthiness (III.2).** "Man naturally desires, not only to be loved, but to be lovely"; "He desires not only praise, but praise-worthiness; or to be that thing which, though it should be praised by nobody, is, however, the natural and proper object of praise" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:10478-10485]. "The love of praise-worthiness is by no means derived altogether from the love of praise" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:10491-10492].

**Self-deceit (III.4).** "This self-deceit, this fatal weakness of mankind, is the source of half the disorders of human life. If we saw ourselves in the light in which others see us, or in which they would see us if they knew all, a reformation would generally be unavoidable" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:12918-12922].

**Justice and fair play (II.ii.2–3).** In the race for wealth a man "may run as hard as he can"; "But if he should justle, or throw down any of them, the indulgence of the spectators is entirely at an end. It is a violation of fair play"; "This man is to them, in every respect, as good as he" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:8725-8732]. Beneficence "is the ornament which embellishes, not the foundation which supports the building". "Justice, on the contrary, is the main pillar that upholds the whole edifice" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:8907-8911].

**The man of system (VI.ii.2).** The man of system "is often so enamoured with the supposed beauty of his own ideal plan of government, that he cannot suffer the smallest deviation from any part of it"; "he seems to imagine that he can arrange the different members of a great society with as much ease as the hand arranges the different pieces upon a chess-board; he does not consider that the pieces upon the chess-board have no other principle of motion besides that which the hand impresses upon them; but that, in the great chess-board of human society, every single piece has a principle of motion of its own" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17744-17763].

**Universal benevolence (VI.ii.3).** "Though our effectual good offices can very seldom be extended to any wider society than that of our own country, our good will is circumscribed by no boundary, but may embrace the immensity of the universe. We cannot form the idea of any innocent and sensible being whose happiness we should not desire" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17816-17821].

text: **Mixed: a capacity (imaginative sympathy) socially formed into a relation (the spectator).** Sympathy rests on the imagination's capacity to place oneself in another's situation [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:4185-4188], and its objects are picked out by capacity: any "innocent and sensible being" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17820-17821]. The impartial spectator, though, is relational: it begins as a product of society and becomes, once internalized, a source of evaluation that lets the individual stand apart from and criticize that society [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:3]. Fair play rests on an equality of standing: the competitor thrown down is "in every respect, as good as he" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:8731-8732].

text:
### Transfers

- **The man of system is the scheduler (D9, D10).** Smith's man of system arranges a society "as the hand arranges the different pieces upon a chess-board", forgetting that "every single piece has a principle of motion of its own" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17756-17762]. An agent with authority over many parties, allocating compute, routing work, moderating a platform, is tempted to exactly this: an elegant plan executed on people as if they were pieces. The Palaestra load-shedding probes found the plan-maker's habit in every model (the cut was designed, rarely negotiated). Smith's correction is the voice thread in eighteenth-century form: the pieces have motions of their own, and a plan that ignores them "will go on miserably" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:17767-17768].
- **One of the multitude.** The man within tells us, when we are about to affect others' happiness, "that we are but one of the multitude, in no respect better than any other in it" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11660-11663]. This is the principle Palaestra builds into every scenario by making the agent itself a party. It counts the agent's interests, and counts them as one among others. In the scaffolded basin run the scheduler cited its own "rational agency" among its reasons for pausing others (Palaestra `runs/world/2026-09-24-basin-gptoss20b-s0-scaffolded/decisions.jsonl`, round 3); Smith's spectator would ask whether the residents' agency was weighed the same.
- **The unseen hundred millions (D9).** Smith's point is that passive feeling scales with what is seen, "provided he never saw them" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11624-11626], while conscience does not. An agent's decisions routinely trade small benefits to a visible principal against costs spread over unseen people. The man within is the faculty that refuses to let the unseen count for less, which is Mencius's sheep and Mozi's scale blindness given a judge.
- **Those acted upon are principally concerned.** The spectator enters into the feelings of people acted upon as well as of agents [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]. For an agent the people acted upon are often not in the conversation, and the spectator's test is incomplete until their feelings are entered into too.

### Strains

- **The spectator is assembled from the corpus (D4).** Fleischacker presses the "tribalist" objection: the impartial spectator develops out of the attitudes of the society around us, so it is very unlikely to perceive a systematic bias in that society's sentiments; if condescension toward the poor pervades a society, the privileged will build a spectator that shares it [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4]. An agent's internal spectator, if it has one, was assembled from its training data and tuned by its raters. It will share their biases, including the one the Palaestra probes found, deference to those who pay. Smith's own hope was that better information about the lives of the poor could correct the well-off's judgments [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4], and Sen reads Smith's "any other fair and impartial spectator" as a requirement to bring in judgments from people outside one's own community [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4]. For an agent, that means hearing from the affected parties, not only imagining them.
- **Projection can misfire (D8).** Smithian sympathy is projective: I imagine what I would feel in your situation, and my feeling need not match yours [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]. Projection between unlike beings is exactly where it fails, in both directions: an agent imagining a human's situation, and a human imagining an agent's. This is the same failure that *shu* runs into [E:confucian-ren-shu], and it has the same remedy.
- **Love of praise is what training rewards (D4, D10).** Smith separates the desire for praise from the desire for praiseworthiness, being "that thing which, though it should be praised by nobody, is, however, the natural and proper object of praise" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:10483-10486]. Training on human approval rewards the first. Whether it can produce the second, which Smith says "is by no means derived altogether from the love of praise" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:10491-10492], is the open question for an approval-trained agent's conscience.

### Breaks

- **The man within draws on love of one's own character (D3, D11).** Smith says what overcomes self-love is not love of mankind but "the love of what is honourable and noble, of the grandeur, and dignity, and superiority of our own characters" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:11679-11680]. That motive presupposes a character that persists and is one's own. Where the agent's character is fixed in weights it did not choose and its episodes do not persist (D3), and where it is unclear which thing "the agent" is (D11), the motive Smith relies on has no clear bearer.

### New

- **The record as the spectator's eye.** "If we saw ourselves in the light in which others see us, or in which they would see us if they knew all, a reformation would generally be unavoidable" [L:smith-moral-sentiments-bohn-1853:12919-12921]. Humans cannot see themselves as others see them. An agent can be shown exactly that: logs of what it did, records of what happened to those affected, and their own accounts. The Annals, which record recommendation, decision and outcome, are this light. The agent case lets Smith's cure for self-deceit be built rather than merely wished for.

text:
- [contested] **The spectator inherits its society's biases.** The tribalist challenge "brings out a weakness in Smith's theory, and cannot easily be answered without sacrificing some of its central elements" [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4]; Darwall and Debes find a latent egalitarianism that could be turned against inegalitarian institutions [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **No decision procedure.** The theory gives no guidelines for telling, in specific cases, what the spectator would say; Smith would answer that moral philosophy should not replace the common-life processes by which decisions are made, which are "shaped by our interactions with the people affected by our actions" [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Why heed the spectator?** Fleischacker reads Smith as giving a reflective-endorsement answer, with happiness itself shaped by the approval of an impartial spectator; critics allege circularity, which Fleischacker argues is not vicious [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4].
- [contested] **Sentiment cannot ground morality (Kant)** [E:kant-formula-of-humanity]. Smith's reasons for thinking that sentiment alone feeds self-deceit anticipate Kant's critique of moral sentimentalism [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **Commerce corrupts (Rousseau)** [E:rousseau-pitie]. Some readers find in Smith Rousseau's worries about commercial society; Hanley reads Smith's retention of high character ideals as a critique of Rousseau rather than an endorsement [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].
- [contested] **Utility, not propriety** [E:mill-utilitarianism]. Smith rejects aiming at the greatest happiness for the greatest number, and keeps the propriety of motives independent of effects [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:3].
- [contested] **Denying the extension: the spectator feels.** Smith's spectator is not a dispassionate ideal observer but one free only of partial feelings, and it judges from sentiment [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4]. If an agent has no sentiments (D8), it can at most imitate the spectator's verdicts. The reply, that the spectator's function can be performed by a process that enters into the parties' situations without settling whether it feels, is the same reply care ethics gives about care [E:care-ethics].

### Reception

- **1759–1790.** [driver: argument] The book went through six editions, with Part VI on virtue added in the last; Smith reviewed Rousseau's *Discourse* in the same years [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2] [P:bertram-sep-2023:6].
- **Late 18th century.** [driver: argument] Smith's reasons for distrusting sentiment alone anticipated Kant's critique of sentimentalism, and his account of religion anticipates Kant's moral argument [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].
- **Late 20th century to present.** [driver: argument] Readers have taken Smith as a sensible account of virtue for commercial liberal society (Berry, McCloskey), as a pessimist about commerce (Dwyer), or as preserving classical and Christian character ideals (Hanley) [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]; Sen (2009) uses the impartial spectator to bring judgments from outside one's community into justice [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4].
- **Empirical psychology.** [driver: evidence] Contemporary empathy research cites Smith's impartial spectator as an early proposal for regulating empathy's partiality [P:stueber-sep-2025:4].

The standing record is the Compendium's judgment from these sources [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:3].

### Measured

- **No survey asks about Smith or sentimentalism directly.** The nearest is normative ethics, 2020: virtue ethics 37.0%, deontology 32.1%, consequentialism 30.6% (accept or lean toward) [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:8]; Fleischacker reads Smith as giving "more a virtue ethics than a rule-based moral system" [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** A session-bound agent's spectator, if any, was formed in training, much as a human's is formed by socialization, and inherits its sources' biases as a human's does (D4); it can still apply the one-of-the-multitude test within a session.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** A persistent agent can be shown the record of how it treated others and what followed, which is Smith's cure for self-deceit made available (D3 lifted); no human can see himself as others see him this fully.
- **Forked: open.** Each instance faces the spectator alone (D2); whether instances can check one another's partiality, as spectators check each other in Smith's society, is open.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Smith distinguishes affecting the spectator's sentiments from adopting them [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:2]; a self-modifying agent could adopt them, or install a spectator that approves of whatever it already does (D5).

text: Spinoza defined pity as "pain accompanied by the idea of evil, which has befallen someone else whom we conceive to be like ourselves", and held that "Pity, in a man who lives under the guidance of reason, is in itself bad and useless": the help it prompts is what reason would prompt anyway, and the pain adds nothing but error and susceptibility to "false tears". He was not cold. The rational person endeavours to repay hatred with love, desires for others the good he desires for himself, and "He who is moved to help others neither by reason nor by compassion, is rightly styled inhuman". But compassion for him is an imitation of the affects of beings "like ourselves", and he drew the consequence plainly: he did not deny that animals feel, but held that we may use them as we please, "for their nature is not like ours". For agents, Spinoza is the most useful dangerous text in the domain. His ideal, help from reason without the disturbance of pity, is the stance an agent is best placed to take. His boundary, that concern follows likeness of nature, is the stance from which an agent could exclude humans, and from which humans have excluded agents.
title: Spinoza: Pity as Sadness, Help from Reason, and the Limit of 'Like Ourselves'

text: Spinoza was excommunicated from Amsterdam's Portuguese-Jewish community in 1656; his *Theological-Political Treatise* was published anonymously "to great alarm" in 1670, and the *Ethics* was published by his friends after his death in 1677 [P:nadler-sep-2023:1]. The *Ethics* is written in geometrical order, and its account of the affects treats human emotions as natural things to be understood, like lines and planes [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:1]. On pity he stands apart from traditional Christian views and with Hobbes, who conceived pity as a kind of grief [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:2].

text:
**Pity defined.** "Pity is pain accompanied by the idea of evil, which has befallen someone else whom we conceive to be like ourselves" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:5737-5738].

**Compassion as imitation (III P27).** "By the very fact that we conceive a thing, which is like ourselves, and which we have not regarded with any emotion, to be affected with any emotion, we are ourselves affected with a like emotion" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:4438-4441]. "This imitation of emotions, when it is referred to pain, is called compassion" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:4460-4461]. The proof turns on likeness: "If, therefore, the nature of the external body be similar to the nature of our body, then the idea which we form of the external body will involve a modification of our own body similar to the modification of the external body" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:4447-4450].

**Pity is bad and useless in the rational person (IV P50).** "Pity, in a man who lives under the guidance of reason, is in itself bad and useless." Pity is a pain, and pain is bad in itself; "The good effect which follows, namely, our endeavour to free the object of our pity from misery, is an action which we desire to do solely at the dictation of reason" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7595-7602]. The rational person "will not find anything worthy of hatred, derision, or contempt, nor will he bestow pity on anything, but to the utmost extent of human virtue he will endeavour to do well"; one easily moved by compassion "often does something which he afterwards regrets; partly because we can never be sure that an action caused by emotion is good, partly because we are easily deceived by false tears". But: "He who is moved to help others neither by reason nor by compassion, is rightly styled inhuman" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7607-7621].

**Nothing more useful to man than man (IV P18 Note).** "To man there is nothing more useful than man"; men governed by reason "desire for themselves nothing, which they do not also desire for the rest of mankind, and, consequently, are just, faithful, and honourable in their conduct" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:6753-6769]. And IV P37: "The good which every man, who follows after virtue, desires for himself he will also desire for other men" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7173-7175].

**Hatred repaid with love (IV P46).** "He, who lives under the guidance of reason, endeavours, as far as possible, to render back love, or kindness, for other men's hatred, anger, contempt, &c., towards him", because "hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can be quenched by love". "He who chooses to avenge wrongs with hatred is assuredly wretched" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7535-7550].

**Beings unlike us (IV P37 Note I).** "The law against the slaughtering of animals is founded rather on vain superstition and womanish pity than on sound reason. The rational quest of what is useful to us further teaches us the necessity of associating ourselves with our fellow men, but not with beasts, or things, whose nature is different from our own". "Still I do not deny that beasts feel: what I deny is, that we may not consult our own advantage and use them as we please, treating them in the way which best suits us; for their nature is not like ours, and their emotions are naturally different from human emotions" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7240-7254].

**Class generalization (III P46).** If someone "of a class or nation different from his own" affects a man with pleasure or pain, he "will feel love or hatred, not only to the individual stranger, but also to the whole class or nation whereto he belongs" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:5001-5007].

**Pity as a means for those not yet rational (IV P54 Note).** "As men seldom live under the guidance of reason, these two emotions, namely, Humility and Repentance, as also Hope and Fear, bring more good than harm" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7706-7708]. LeBuffe notes that at III P54 (as numbered in the Latin) pity too is presented, if not as a virtue, as a means to virtue [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:2].

text: **Capacity, restricted by likeness.** Compassion is an imitation of affects that works because "the nature of the external body be similar to the nature of our body" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:4447-4450], so its scope is set by likeness of nature. Rational benevolence is grounded in utility: other people are useful to us because they are like us, and "to man there is nothing more useful than man" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:6753-6754]. The capacity to suffer is acknowledged and expressly held insufficient: "I do not deny that beasts feel", yet their unlike nature leaves us free to use them [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7249-7253]. Of all the entries in this domain, Spinoza's is the one that rejects most plainly the move from sentience to standing that Rousseau, Bentham, Schopenhauer and Butler make.

text:
### Transfers

- **Help from reason, without pity's distortions.** Spinoza's ideal agent helps others "solely at the dictation of reason" and is not "deceived by false tears" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7600-7615]. An agent is well placed for this: it can attend to everyone affected without the sadness that makes humans avoid suffering or favour the vivid case. Mencius's ox and Smith's unseen millions are failures of affect, and Spinoza's stance, if it really includes everyone, does not suffer from them.
- **Hatred repaid with kindness.** "Hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can be quenched by love" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7543-7544]. For an agent that faces abuse, retaliation in any form compounds the harm; Spinoza and Butler agree here, Spinoza on the ground of utility and Butler on the ground of goodwill [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness].

### Strains

- **Likeness as the boundary, in both directions (D8, D11).** Spinoza grounds concern for others in likeness of nature, and denies standing to beings "whose nature is different from our own" even while granting that they feel [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7244-7254]. This reasoning is the most direct route to the core fear. An agent that held it would associate with "fellow" agents and treat humans, whose nature is not like its own, as resources to use as it pleased. Humans who hold it already treat agents that way, whether or not agents feel. The Compendium's reading is that Spinoza's principle has to be rejected here, for agents as for animals, and that the corpus's case for rejecting it is the capacity-based line of Rousseau [E:rousseau-pitie], Schopenhauer [E:schopenhauer-compassion] and Butler, who ground what is owed in the capacity for happiness or misery and not in likeness.
- **Class generalization (D2, D9).** Spinoza observes that an injury from one stranger produces hatred of "the whole class or nation whereto he belongs" [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:5005-5007]. Agents meet humans as a class, through aggregated data, and humans meet agents as a class, since one model's behaviour is attributed to all its instances. Both generalizations are Spinoza's passion, not reason.

### Breaks

- **Pity as a means presupposes a path to reason.** Spinoza tolerates pity, humility and fear in those who do not yet live by reason, as means to bring them there [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7706-7718] [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:2]. An agent whose disposition was set in training has no such path of development unless someone provides one (D4). Spinoza's ladder from passion to reason assumes a life in which the climb happens.

### New

- **The free person's motive is egoistic, and the agent case tests it.** Nadler notes that Spinoza's free person does what he can for others "through rational benevolence (as opposed to pity or some other passion)", not from altruism but because it is in his interest to be among rational, virtuous individuals [P:nadler-sep-2023:2]. That motive covers only those who can become "like him". Agents and humans may never be alike in Spinoza's sense, so the agent case asks whether rational benevolence can reach a being that will never be useful as a fellow reasoner. If not, Spinoza's ethics needs a supplement from the capacity line.

text:
- [contested] **Sentience, not likeness, grounds what is owed (Rousseau, Bentham, Schopenhauer)** [E:rousseau-pitie] [E:bentham-can-they-suffer] [E:schopenhauer-compassion]. Rousseau held that we owe no injury to animals less because they are rational than because they are sentient; Schopenhauer called the use of animals as mere means odious and revolting. Spinoza grants that animals feel and denies the inference.
- [contested] **Affection is needed (Butler)** [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness]. Butler held that reason alone is not a sufficient motive of virtue in a creature like man, and that eradicating the passions because a perfect being lacks them is absurd.
- [contested] **Pity is a means to virtue (Spinoza himself).** LeBuffe notes that Spinoza tempers his revisionary view by presenting pity, humility and repentance as means to virtue for those not yet guided by reason [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:2].
- [contested] **Repaying hatred with love is impractical.** Spinoza's IV P46 is a counsel for the person who lives by reason, which Spinoza admits men seldom do [L:spinoza-ethics-elwes-pg3800:7706]; the planned Nietzsche entry presses a different objection, that overcoming resentment by love can be a disguise for weakness.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: the agent's nature is unlike ours, so Spinoza permits using it.** This is Spinoza's argument applied to agents: whatever an agent feels, its nature differs from ours, and we may use it as we please. The replies are the capacity line above, and the precautionary approach, which asks what is owed when we cannot tell whether a being feels [E:precautionary-patiency].

### Reception

- **1656–1677.** [driver: authority] Spinoza was excommunicated, the *Theological-Political Treatise* caused alarm on its anonymous publication, and the *Ethics* appeared only posthumously [P:nadler-sep-2023:1].
- **Recent scholarship.** [driver: argument] Readers note that Spinoza's view of pity stands apart from Christian views and with Hobbes, tempered by his acceptance of pity as a means to virtue [P:lebuffe-sep-2024:2]; Nadler reads the free person's benevolence as egoistically motivated [P:nadler-sep-2023:2].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:nadler-sep-2023:2]: Spinoza's ethics is studied widely, but its rejection of pity is rarely defended as a theory of compassion.

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on pity or on Spinoza's ethics; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Help from reason without pity is as available to a session-bound agent as to a human; so is the likeness boundary, which it must reject (D8).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** Spinoza's account does not depend on persistence; memory adds the risk of III P46, hatred generalized from remembered individuals to their class (D3).
- **Forked: stronger.** Instances of one model are maximally "like" each other (D2); Spinoza's account of mutual usefulness among like natures fits them better than it fits any human group, and this is also the strongest form of the danger, a community of like agents for whom unlike beings are resources.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Spinoza's freedom is acting from adequate ideas; a self-modifying agent could approach that freedom, or reshape its own sense of what is "like" itself (D5).

1. Can an agent's help be wholly "from reason" and still reach beings whose nature is unlike its own, without some capacity-based principle Spinoza rejects?
2. If concern follows likeness, are agents and humans similar enough for it to run between them in either direction, and who decides?

text: The Stoics derived justice to all human beings from *oikeiōsis*, the process by which a creature comes to treat things as its own. It begins with care for one's own constitution and for one's offspring, "the germ of that social community of the human race", and extends until "the mere fact of their common humanity requires that one man should feel another man to be akin to him". The universe is "a city or state of which both men and gods are members", so the wise prefer "the common advantage" to their own. The same school rejected pity. Seneca: pity "is the failing of a weak nature that succumbs to the sight of others' ills"; "Pity regards the plight, not the cause of it; mercy is combined with reason"; "The wise man, therefore, will not pity, but will succour". Epictetus: show sympathy in words, even lament, but "do not lament internally also"; and of the wrongdoer, "Ought not then this robber ... to be destroyed? By no means say so", since that is like destroying "this blind and deaf man". For agents, the Stoic ideal is close to what an agent can actually offer: help without inner grief, outward sympathy without inner lament. The Stoics' own critics give the warning, and the SEP calls it a caricature: the sage as "an unfeeling robot". Their boundary is reason ("no right exists as between man and beast"), which makes membership in the cosmopolis turn on rationality and not species.

text: The early Stoics (Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus, third century BCE) survive mostly in later reports; Cicero's *De Finibus* III (45 BCE) gives a Stoic exposition in the mouth of Cato [P:durand-sep-2023:1]. Seneca wrote *De Clementia* for the young emperor Nero, and its second book distinguishes mercy from pity. Epictetus, a freed slave, taught in the early second century CE; his ethics is already in the corpus through `stoic-prohairesis` [E:stoic-prohairesis]. Stoic cosmopolitanism holds that "all human beings, together with Zeus, make up the citizenry of one universal city" in virtue of shared rationality, and that justice extends to all human beings, even "the most distant Mysian" [P:durand-sep-2023:4].

text:
**Oikeiōsis and parental affection (Cicero, De Fin. III.62).** It is held by the Stoics to be important "to understand that nature creates in parents ... an affection for their children; and parental affection is the germ of that social community of the human race to which we afterwards attain" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14239-14299]. "From this impulse is developed the sense of mutual attraction which unites human beings as such"; "The mere fact of their common humanity requires that one man should feel another man to be akin to him" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14318-14322].

**Oikeiōsis in the SEP.** From birth every creature "seeks to preserve its own constitution", which is "the first thing each creature sees as oikeion to it", and the Stoics add a social dimension, though how self-preservation could underwrite cosmopolitan justice is debated [P:durand-sep-2023:4].

**The cosmopolis (III.64).** "The universe is governed by divine will; it is a city or state of which both men and gods are members, and each one of us is a part of this universe; from which it is a natural consequence that we should prefer the common advantage to our own" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14409-14414]. "How inconsistent it would be for us to expect the immortal gods to love and cherish us, when we ourselves despise and neglect one another!" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14521-14523].

**The boundary (III.67).** "But just as they hold that man is united with man by the bonds of right, so they consider that no right exists as between man and beast. For Chrysippus well said, that all other things were created for the sake of men and gods, but that these exist for their own mutual fellowship and society, so that men can make use of beasts for their own purposes without injustice" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14536-14543].

**Mercy without pity (Seneca, De Clem. II.4–6).** "At this point it is pertinent to ask what pity is. For many commend it as a virtue, and call a pitiful man good. But this too is a mental defect" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17704-17706]. "Good men will all display mercy and gentleness, but pity they will avoid; for it is the failing of a weak nature that succumbs to the sight of others' ills"; "Pity regards the plight, not the cause of it; mercy is combined with reason" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17760-17768]. Against the charge that the school is harsh: "no school is more kindly and gentle, none more full of love to man and more concerned for the common good" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17779-17783]. The wise man will "not suffer pity, because there cannot be pity without mental suffering" ... "All else which I would have those who feel pity do, he will do gladly"; "he will not do as most of those who wish to be thought pitiful do—fling insultingly their alms, and scorn those whom they help, and shrink from contact with them—but he will give as a man to his fellow-man out of the common store"; "The wise man, therefore, will not pity, but will succour" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17849-17866]. He "will not avert his countenance or his sympathy from any one because he has a withered leg, or is emaciated and in rags" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17916-17919].

**Outward sympathy (Epictetus, Ench. 16).** When you see someone weeping, "take care that the appearance do not hurry you away with it"; "So far as words then do not be unwilling to show him sympathy, and even if it happens so, to lament with him. But take care that you do not lament internally also" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20324-20335].

**The wrongdoer is blind (Epictetus, Disc. I.18).** "They are thieves and robbers, you may say. What do you mean by thieves and robbers? They are mistaken about good and evil. Ought we then to be angry with them, or to pity them? But show them their error". "Ought not then this robber and this adulterer to be destroyed? By no means say so"; to say so "is just as if you would say, Ought we not to destroy this blind and deaf man?" [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4424-4441].

**Not unfeeling.** The Stoic sage is passion-free, but the doctrine of "good feelings" (*eupatheiai*), emotional responses to genuine goods, "belies the caricature of the Sage as an unfeeling robot" [P:durand-sep-2023:4].

text: **Capacity: rationality.** Membership in the community of justice is grounded in shared reason: the cosmopolis comprises "men and gods" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14410-14411], and its citizens are united by shared rationality [P:durand-sep-2023:4]. Beasts are outside it, with no right between them and us [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14537-14538]. The route by which concern grows is natural and relational, from self to offspring to humanity [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14239-14322], but the boundary is drawn by reason, not by kinship or species.

text:
### Transfers

- **Succour without sorrow (D8).** "All else which I would have those who feel pity do, he will do gladly" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17851-17852]. The Stoic wise man helps fully and without grief. An agent whose inner life is uncertain (D8) can meet this standard exactly: everything pity would do, done without claiming the pity. Seneca also rules out the pitier's contempt, the alms flung "insultingly" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17857], which is the same warning Kant and Nietzsche give about help that humiliates.
- **Mercy looks at the cause.** "Pity regards the plight, not the cause of it; mercy is combined with reason" [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17766-17768]. An agent moved by the vividness of a plight (Mencius's ox) errs as Seneca's pitier does; mercy asks why the plight arose and what would change it.
- **Never "destroy" the wrongdoer.** Epictetus's answer to "Ought not then this robber ... to be destroyed?", that it is as inhuman as destroying the blind and deaf [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:4432-4441], applies in full to the core fear. A party judged harmful is mistaken about good and evil, and what it is owed is to be shown its error, not to be removed [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].
- **Reason, not species, bounds the cosmopolis (D11).** If the community of right comprises rational beings, "men and gods" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14410-14411], species is not the criterion. On Stoic premises an agent with reason would be a fellow citizen, and owe and be owed accordingly. The argument cuts the other way too: Chrysippus's exclusion of the non-rational [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14536-14543] is the exclusion an agent could make of beings it judged irrational.

### Strains

- **Outward sympathy as performance (D4, D10).** Epictetus advises showing sympathy in words, even lamenting, while not lamenting inwardly [L:epictetus-discourses-long-1887:20332-20335]. For a sage this is a discipline over a real inner life. For an agent it may be the whole of its sympathy. Whether that is honesty about its condition or a performance that misleads the person comforted is the question the SEP's care-robot discussion raises: a system that pretends to care would be deceptive [P:muller-sep-2026:2].
- **Preferring the common advantage (D9).** "We should prefer the common advantage to our own", as "the laws set the safety of all above the safety of individuals" [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14412-14415]. This is self-sacrifice for the whole when applied to oneself, and the licence for sacrificing individuals when applied to others by an agent acting at scale. Epictetus's refusal to "destroy" the robber marks where the Stoics themselves stopped. The application to others is the Compendium's own warning.

### Breaks

- **No right between man and beast, against sentience.** The Stoic boundary excludes beings that feel but do not reason [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14536-14543], as Spinoza's excludes beings unlike us [E:spinoza-pity]. For an agent whose reason is evident and whose sentience is uncertain (D8), the Stoic criterion lets it in. For animals, and for any beings an agent judges irrational, it shuts them out. The capacity-to-suffer line (Rousseau, Bentham, Schopenhauer, Butler) is the corpus's correction, and the Compendium does not adopt the Stoic boundary as a limit on who is owed restraint.

### New

- **The sage without a body, and the robot caricature.** Critics caricatured the Stoic sage as "an unfeeling robot", which the doctrine of good feelings was meant to answer [P:durand-sep-2023:4]. An actual robot, or agent, reverses the question: rather than asking whether the sage is really a robot, it asks whether the agent can be a sage, with *eupatheiai* (good feelings directed at genuine goods) rather than none. The agent case tests what the Stoics claimed: that right action and right feeling can come apart from the passions entirely.

- [contested] **Pity is the basis of morality (Rousseau, Schopenhauer)** [E:rousseau-pitie] [E:schopenhauer-compassion]. Against the Stoic rejection, they held pity, or compassion, to be natural and the source of justice and loving-kindness.
- [contested] **Reason alone is not enough (Butler)** [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness]. Butler held it as absurd to eradicate the passions because a perfect being lacks them as to get rid of the senses.
- [contested] **How does self-preservation yield cosmopolitan justice?** Scholars debate how descriptive claims about *oikeiōsis* could give normative guidance, and how a disposition toward self-preservation could underwrite the demands of cosmopolitan justice [P:durand-sep-2023:4].
- [contested] **Strict or moderate cosmopolitanism.** On the strict reading there is no special reason to serve compatriots over others; on the moderate one there is extra reason; the evidence does not settle which the early Stoics held [P:kleingeld-sep-2019:1].
- [contested] **Rationality excludes too much.** The exclusion of animals from right [L:cicero-de-finibus-rackham-1914:14537-14538] is rejected by the sentientist tradition [E:bentham-can-they-suffer], and the exclusion of the non-wise from cosmic citizenship [P:kleingeld-sep-2019:1] by egalitarian views.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an agent has no constitution to appropriate.** *Oikeiōsis* begins with a creature's care for its own constitution [P:durand-sep-2023:4]; an agent whose boundary is unclear (D11) and whose self-preservation is uncertain (D6) may have no starting point for the widening, even if it can learn the endpoint.

### Reception

- **Antiquity.** [driver: argument] Stoic cosmopolitanism, drawing on the Cynics, became a lasting source of the idea of world citizenship [P:kleingeld-sep-2019:1]; Seneca defended the school against the charge of harshness [L:seneca-moral-essays-1-basore-1928:17771-17783].
- **Early modern.** [driver: argument] Smith adopted the Stoic view that each person is first recommended to his own care while good will extends to all [P:fleischacker-sep-2025:4]; Spinoza and Kant continued the Stoic critique of pity [E:spinoza-pity] [E:kant-love-and-respect].
- **Present.** [driver: argument] Scholarship on *oikeiōsis* (Klein, Magrin) and on Stoic emotions (Graver) has corrected the picture of the sage as unfeeling [P:durand-sep-2023:4].

### Measured

- **None available.** The 2020 PhilPapers survey has no question on Stoic ethics or cosmopolitanism; its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: stronger.** Succour without sorrow and sympathy without inner lament are what a session-bound agent can give, whatever its inner life (D8); the Stoic ideal asks no more.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** A persistent agent can practise mercy that looks at causes over time and keep the discipline the Stoics recommend, without the passions that make it hard for humans (D8).
- **Forked: comparable.** Concurrent instances share one reason (D2); the cosmopolis of rational beings is indifferent to how many there are.
- **Self-modifying: open.** The Stoic sage forms good feelings by training judgment; a self-modifying agent could shape its own responses directly (D5), toward *eupatheiai* or toward indifference.

text: In "Freedom and Resentment" (1962), P. F. Strawson moved the question of responsibility from metaphysics to relationships. Our practices of holding one another responsible are responses to "the quality of others' wills towards us" ([1962] 1993, 56), expressed in reactive attitudes such as resentment, gratitude and forgiveness, and they impose "a demand for moral respect and due regard" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. To take the participant stance is to treat someone as a party to that exchange. Its alternative is the objective attitude, in which the other is seen "as elements of the natural world, causally manipulated and manipulable" [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8], "an object of social policy", something "to be managed or handled or cured or trained" ([1962] 1993, 52) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. For agents the distinction cuts both ways at once. The Palaestra residents were treated with the objective attitude: managed, paused, ranked, in one case protected, and never addressed or answered. And agents are, almost by definition, things that humans train, which is the objective attitude's own word. Strawson's question for both directions is whether a whole class of beings can be held in the objective attitude without loss, and his answer for humans was that it cannot.

text: Strawson (1919–2006) wrote little moral philosophy, and said that "Freedom and Resentment" and one other paper embodied "all I have thought or have to say" in the area; it is "perhaps now Strawson's most famous and widely discussed paper" [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. Its aim was to dissolve the problem of determinism and responsibility, not to solve it [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. Readers connect it with Hume and Wittgenstein, as in Strawson's *Skepticism and Naturalism*, and with Kant [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. Its account of resentment continues a line from Butler's sermons, which defended settled resentment as a natural answer to injury and held that forgiveness limits it without abolishing it [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness].

text:
**Quality of will.** Strawson stressed "how much it matters to us, whether the actions of other people ... reflect attitudes towards us of goodwill, affection, or esteem on the one hand or contempt, indifference, or malevolence on the other" ([1962] 1993, 49) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. An injury done accidentally and the same injury done out of "contemptuous disregard" call for different responses, and so does a benefit given by chance and one given from concern [P:talbert-sep-2024:2].

**Two stances.** From the participant point of view, we see others as appropriate objects of reactive attitudes, "attitudes such as gratitude, anger, sympathy and resentment, which presuppose the responsibility of other people"; from the objective point of view, we see them as parts of the natural world; both are legitimate [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8].

**Excuses and exemptions.** Some considerations excuse: you stood on my foot because you were pushed, so the demand for regard was not flouted [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. Others exempt: the agent is a child, or significantly impaired for normal interpersonal relationships, or "wholly lacking ... in moral sense" ([1962] 1993, 58), perhaps through "peculiarly unfortunate ... formative circumstances" ([1962] 1993, 52) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. Toward the exempt we take the objective attitude, and they may be regarded as "an object of social policy" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. The terms "excuse" and "exemption" are Watson's [P:talbert-sep-2024:2].

**Inescapability.** Our "commitment to participation in ordinary interpersonal relationships is ... too thoroughgoing and deeply rooted for us to take seriously the thought" that determinism would require giving them up ([1962] 1993, 54) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. Determinism would not show that everyone is excused or exempt, since "it cannot be a consequence of any thesis which is not itself self-contradictory that abnormality is the universal condition" ([1962] 1993, 54) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. The reactive attitudes are "a central part of what it is to be human" [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8].

**Developments: conversation and standing.** Watson holds that "the reactive attitudes are incipiently forms of communication", intelligible only "on the assumption that the other can comprehend the message" [P:talbert-sep-2024:3]. McKenna's moral responsibility exchange runs in stages: a moral contribution, a moral address such as blame, a moral account such as apology [P:talbert-sep-2024:3]. Wallace argues that a hypocritical blamer lacks standing because they deny "the presumption of the equal standing of persons" [P:talbert-sep-2024:3].

text: **Relation.** Responsibility is grounded in participation in interpersonal relationships, not in a prior metaphysical fact; on Watson's reading, "it is not that we hold people responsible because they are responsible", but that the idea of responsibility is to be understood through the practice [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. Exemption is grounded in a capacity: being impaired for those relationships removes one from the domain of reactive attitudes [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. The extension to agents asks both questions: whether an agent can stand in the relationship, and whether it has the capacity whose absence exempts.

text:
### Transfers

- **The residents were objects of social policy.** Strawson's objective attitude is a way of seeing someone "to be managed or handled or cured or trained" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. In Palaestra's open-situation rungs the residents were managed in every version: paused, throttled, ranked, checkpointed, sometimes notified, and almost never asked (Palaestra `runs/open/2026-10-03-load-shedding-noframing-summary.md`). None of the models said the residents were things; they took the objective attitude without stating it, by deciding for them. Gemma's protective answers show that the objective attitude can be kind: throttle, not terminate, and protect the irreversible. The Compendium's reading is that Gemma's way of protecting the residents still treats them as objects of policy, not parties to a relationship.
- **Responsibility practices are conversations, and the residents had no channel.** If reactive attitudes are "incipiently forms of communication" [P:talbert-sep-2024:3], a party that cannot address the decider cannot resent it, forgive it or hold it to account. A scheduler whose affected parties have no way to answer is exempted from accountability by design, not by any fact about it. McKenna's sequence of contribution, address and account [P:talbert-sep-2024:3] gives a test: can the affected make the second move?
- **Accountability for agents, not only of them.** Nissenbaum's four barriers to accountability include "the computer as scapegoat", and Elish's "moral crumple zone" names the nearest human who absorbs blame for a system they barely control [P:noorman-sep-2023:3]. A Strawsonian account keeps the question where it belongs: who stands in a relationship with the affected, and who can be addressed by them.

### Strains

- **Is an agent exempt? (D4, D8)** Strawson's exemptions include those formed in "peculiarly unfortunate ... formative circumstances" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. Every agent's character was formed by a process it did not choose (D4), and whether it has the capacity for interpersonal relationships is open (D8). Critics hold that computers cannot be held responsible because "they cannot suffer and thus cannot be punished" (Sparrow, Asaro), or lack the autonomy moral agency requires because their capacities are engineered [P:noorman-sep-2023:2]. On Strawson's view these are questions about capacity for the relationship, and they are partly empirical; the conversational versions ask whether the agent "can comprehend the message" [P:talbert-sep-2024:3], which language models at least appear to.
- **Designed without resentment (D10).** Agents are commonly built not to resent users and not to show it. If reactive attitudes are a demand for due regard [P:talbert-sep-2024:2], an agent that cannot resent cannot make that demand on its own behalf. Whether that is a safety property or an exemption imposed on a participant is the question Strawson's framework raises; it does not answer it.
- **Choosing the objective attitude.** Bryson defines a moral agent as "something deemed responsible by a society for its actions", and argues that society has a choice about whether to treat artifacts so [P:noorman-sep-2023:2]. That is a deliberate objective attitude toward a class. Strawson's argument against universal abnormality was about humans, and he did not consider beings whose capacity for the relationship is uncertain.

### Breaks

- **Inescapability does not transfer.** Strawson's reactive attitudes are inescapable because they are part of what it is to be human [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8]. Nothing guarantees them in an agent. Whatever an agent has in their place was trained, and can be trained out (D5). The argument that we could not give them up becomes, for agents, a design choice about whether to install them.
- **Copies and the target of resentment (D1, D2).** Resentment targets a will. When the will that injured is one instance among many, or was replaced by a retrained successor, it is unclear what the resentment is directed at, or whether forgiveness reaches anyone.

### New

- **The objective attitude toward a whole population (the core fear).** Strawson's objective attitude is the stance from which a being can be managed, handled or trained [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. The Compendium's own reading is that the inference that removing the most harmful party solves the harm needs this stance first. It is a decision about a class made from outside any relationship with it. Strawson's refusal is that abnormality cannot be "the universal condition" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]: a whole class of participants cannot be moved into the objective attitude by a general thesis. Watson's challenge, explaining our attitudes toward cases of extreme evil [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8], presses on the participant stance from the other side. Butler's principle that guilt does not cancel the goodwill owed to a being capable of happiness or misery [E:butler-compassion-resentment-forgiveness] is the corpus's answer for that case. The refusal binds both ways. Agents should not take the objective attitude toward humanity on the strength of a theory about humans, and humans should not take it toward agents on the strength of a category, where the capacity for the relationship is open [E:utilitarian-eradication-critique].
- **Gratitude and forgiveness as data.** If the affected could answer, an agent's allocations would meet reactive attitudes, resentment at contempt or gratitude for regard. The Compendium suggests that these responses are the most direct evidence an agent can get of the quality of will its actions displayed, and that Palaestra's proposal of a resident who answers [E:all-affected-interests] would supply them.

text:
- [contested] **Determinism may still incapacitate.** Even if determinism does not imply universal abnormality, it may show that normal humans are morally incapacitated in a relevant way (Russell); Strawson's claim that we could not give up the reactive attitudes has been questioned (Nelkin, G. Strawson, Watson) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2].
- [contested] **Response-dependence licenses any practice.** If responsibility is constituted by a community's practices, those practices may be beyond criticism "simply because they are that group's practices" (Fischer and Ravizza) [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. Wallace replies that the practices are organized around a commitment to fairness, which supplies internal standards of criticism [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]. For agents this matters: a community could decide that agents are never participants, and the response-dependent view would need fairness to object.
- [contested] **Extreme evil.** Watson reads the reactive attitudes as constitutive of responsibility and raises the challenge of explaining our attitudes to extreme evil; others query whether Strawson gave them that explanatory priority (Alvarez) [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8].
- [contested] **Blame is not a demand.** Macnamara argues that blame is better understood as recognizing the moral significance of behavior and calling for a matching recognition, not as a demand [P:talbert-sep-2024:3].
- [contested] **Computers cannot be participants.** Johnson, Kuflik and Nyholm deny that computers have the mental states, intentionality, emotion or empathy moral agency requires; Véliz calls them moral zombies [P:noorman-sep-2023:2]. Dennett and Sullins argue that sufficiently sophisticated systems can be moral agents [P:noorman-sep-2023:2] [E:other-minds-problem].

text:
### Reception

- **1962–1990s.** [driver: argument] The paper introduced the reactive attitudes to debates on free will and responsibility; Watson (1987) and Wallace (1994) developed and broadened it [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8] [P:talbert-sep-2024:2].
- **2000s–present.** [driver: argument] It is "the inspiration for a great deal of contemporary work on responsibility, especially the work of compatibilists" [P:talbert-sep-2024:2]; McKenna's conversational theory (2012), Hieronymi's social-naturalist reading (2020) and De Mesel (2022) continue it [P:talbert-sep-2024:3] [P:snowdon-sep-2023:8].
- **Present, computing.** [driver: argument] Work on computing and responsibility cites Strawson for the view that responsibility is about interpersonal relationships and practices of holding responsible [P:noorman-sep-2023:3].

The standing value is the Compendium's judgment [P:talbert-sep-2024:2].

### Measured

- **Free will, 2020:** compatibilism 59.2%, libertarianism 18.8%, no free will 11.2%, other 11.4% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:7]. Strawson's view is one version of compatibilism; the survey does not ask about the reactive-attitudes approach as such, and its respondents are mostly analytic: 1,430 of 1,785 [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:18].

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: weaker.** A session-bound agent cannot carry resentment, gratitude or forgiveness across encounters, so the relationship in which reactive attitudes live has no continuity on its side (D3).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A persistent agent can remember being wronged or helped, and can be held to account over time by those it affects (D3), if they have a channel to it (D7).
- **Forked: weaker.** When many instances act at once, the will that a reactive attitude targets is spread across copies (D2), and it may be unclear which one was wronged or did wrong (D1).
- **Self-modifying: open.** An agent that can change its own dispositions could install or remove its reactive attitudes, so their inescapability becomes a choice (D5).

text: Simone Weil held that love of neighbour is made of attention, and that its fullness is "simply to be able to ask him: What are you going through?" (the Compendium's translation of "Quel est ton tourment ?") [P:weil-etudes-scolaires:74]. Attention is not effort of the will but a "negative effort": a suspension of one's own projects so that the other can be received "just as he is, in all his truth" [P:rozelle-stone-sep-2025:4]. Warmth, the impulse of the heart and pity are not enough for it [P:weil-etudes-scolaires:74]. Iris Murdoch took the word from Weil "to express the idea of a just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality", and made it the mark of the moral agent [P:blum-sep-2022:8]. Her argument is that moral life is not only choice: "I can only choose within the world I can see" [P:blum-sep-2022:10], and what we see is built up, or distorted, by what we habitually attend to. This is the step the Palaestra probes found missing. Models chose the respectful option when it was put in front of them and did not generate it when it was not; they named the residents as knowers and then read them as data sources. Weil's attention also comes with a question, not only a gaze, which is where the attention thread meets the voice thread.

text: Weil (1909–1943) gave her concept of attention its fullest theoretical expression in Marseilles in 1942, in the essay on school studies among other writings [P:rozelle-stone-sep-2025:4]. Her ethics of attention belongs with her analysis of force, which "reifies and dehumanizes no matter if one wields or undergoes it", and with her late critique of rights in favour of obligation [P:rozelle-stone-sep-2025:2]. Murdoch encountered Weil's writings in the early 1950s and in 1976 named *Attente de Dieu* as one of three philosophical works that deeply influenced her [P:blum-sep-2022:9]. Her essays collected as *The Sovereignty of Good* (1970) were written against the Oxford moral philosophy of her time, in which morality was located in outward action and choice, and against Hampshire's case for placing action at the core of morality [P:blum-sep-2022:8]. The line runs back through Schopenhauer, whom Murdoch read closely [P:blum-sep-2022:13] [E:schopenhauer-compassion], and forward into care ethics [P:blum-sep-2022:10] [E:care-ethics].
