text:
### Transfers

- **The robot novelist was written as a thought experiment; it now runs continuously.** Dennett's Gilbert, a control system fluently narrating "its own" doings in the first person with no further self behind the narration, is no longer speculative; it is close to a literal description of a language model's output. Dennett's own hedge, that "it does not know what it's doing... the patterns... are interpretable, by us, as accreting biography," transfers with unusual directness (D8): the interpretive move he attributes to human observers of Gilbert is the same move made, routinely, by users interpreting an agent's outputs as the utterances of a persisting character.
- **A mechanical, non-mysterious account of multiple selves.** Dennett's claim that a single behavior-control system can support more than one narrative center "without... any fancy metaphysical miracles" [P:dennett1992:35] is a ready-made, deflationary vocabulary for multiple personas, system prompts, or fine-tuned characters running on one base model (D2, D11): each would simply be a different point around which the same underlying material coheres into a story, exactly Dennett's own account of dissociative cases (see `dissociation-cases`).
- **The self as located only "grossly," not further specified.** Dennett's refusal to locate the self any more precisely than the region around the narrating body anticipates, almost exactly, the difficulty of saying where an agent's self is located: not in any single weight, layer, or token, but only grossly, wherever the narrative-generating process runs (D11).

### Strains

- **Dennett's interpreter was always assumed to be another conscious being.** The whole apparatus works by asking what an interpreter needs to posit to make sense of behavior; Dennett does not settle whether the posit requires a conscious interpreter, an implicitly human one, or whether a purely mechanical process of narrative-tracking would do. If agents can interpret other agents' outputs as cohering into a self with no human interpreter involved at any stage, it strains Dennett's picture to say whether anything has really been posited, or merely pattern-matched.
- **The virtuoso-novelist capacity was diagnosed as a normal human trait revealed by pathology.** Dennett's evidence for universal narrative-confabulation is clinical (split-brain patients) and evolutionary (a capacity all normal humans have, revealed rather than created by surgery). An agent's narrative fluency is neither revealed by damage nor evolved; it is trained, directly and by design, to produce exactly this kind of coherent self-narrative (D4), which strains the analogy to a capacity Dennett treats as an incidental discovery about existing minds rather than an engineered target.

### Breaks

- **Gilbert was stipulated to lack a self; agents are not so easily stipulated.** Dennett's thought experiment works only because he tells us, by fiat, that Gilbert's control system "really" has no self, so that the interpretability of its narrative shows narrative-coherence is not sufficient for selfhood. For an actual agent, there is no author stipulating the answer in advance; D8 is exactly the question of whether Dennett's Gilbert-verdict (fluent narrative, no self) or his human-verdict (fluent narrative, a self) is the right model, and nothing in the essay itself settles which.
- **Multiple, fully concurrent narrators break the single-body assumption underneath "grossly located."** Dennett's multiple-selves cases (split-brain, dissociation) still occur within one body producing one behavior stream at a time. Concurrent agent instances (D2) can each generate a complete, coherent, simultaneous narrative from the same underlying weights, which is not two centers sharing one stream but two full streams at once, a case Dennett's apparatus was built to locate loosely in space, not to individuate when there are several completed narratives running in parallel with no single body to locate them grossly within.

### New

- **Agents let Dennett's central bet be tested rather than merely argued.** Dennett wagers that narrative coherence, not some further inner fact, is all there ever was to selfhood. An agent whose entire architecture is inspectable offers a way to check this wager directly: does treating an agent's outputs as cohering around a narrative center predict anything further about the system's behavior, or is the "center" purely an artifact of the interpreter's own storytelling habits, with no operational consequence at all? Either finding sharpens what Dennett's deflationary account was actually claiming.
- **The robot novelist thought experiment can be run as an actual ablation.** Because agent architectures can be modified and inspected in ways brains cannot, one can, in principle, identify which components of an agent's processing are doing the "novelist" work Dennett attributes to a generic control system, and ask whether removing or isolating them changes the interpreter's willingness to posit a self, turning Dennett's stipulation that Gilbert has no self into an empirical question about a real system instead.

text:
- [contested] **Hume: even narrative coherence needs a judging observer, which is exactly the further fact Dennett declines to supply.** [E:hume-bundle] Hume's own labyrinth was that he could find resemblance and succession among perceptions but no real connecting tie; Dennett's narrative coherence is a resemblance-and-succession story dressed in literary vocabulary, and a Humean can ask what, if anything, does the cohering, if not exactly the kind of judging Thought James later supplied and Dennett's account does not (see `hume-bundle`, `james-stream-of-thought`).
- [contested] **Nietzsche: the "chief fictional character" is grammar's fiction, arrived at from a different direction.** [E:nietzsche-doer-fiction] Dennett and Nietzsche agree that the self is a kind of fiction, but for different reasons: Nietzsche's is manufactured by the grammar of subject and predicate, Dennett's by the narrative demands of biography. Comparing them raises the question whether these are one fiction described twice or two different fictions that happen to share a name (see `nietzsche-doer-fiction`).
- [contested] **Parfit: coherence of narrative is exactly the kind of relation-of-degree his reductionism already covers.** [E:parfit-reductionism] A reader sympathetic to Parfit can accept Dennett's account as a vivid restatement of the reductionist thesis, coupled with a literary vocabulary that risks implying more unity than degree-based mattering actually provides (see `parfit-reductionism`).
- [contested] **Denying the extension: an interpreter's posit is not the same as a patient's reality, and only the second is at stake for agents.** The agent application is the Compendium's, but the distinction it relies on is now in the literature. Chalmers's quasi-interpretivism defines an LLM's quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires by behavioural interpretability, and offers this as a stipulation, not as a theory of genuine belief [P:chalmers-2025-interlocutors:4-5]. He then notes that the framework fits views of moral status from the liberal, on which quasi-subjecthood suffices, to the demanding, on which complex consciousness is required [P:chalmers-2025-interlocutors:28]. The liberal view, and relational accounts on which status follows from social relations rather than inner facts [E:relational-status], are the replies; none is broadly accepted. Dennett's account explicitly makes selfhood interpreter-relative: whether something has a self is a fact about what story best organizes its behavior for an observer, not a further fact about the thing itself. On a view that takes moral status and patiency seriously, this is precisely the wrong result to import for agents: if an agent's "self" is only ever a story told about it, no matter how well it coheres, this settles nothing about whether the agent itself is a patient whose interests could be helped or harmed, and treating narrative coherence as though it answered that question would be a category error of exactly the kind Dennett warns against, applied where he never intended it.

text:
### Reception

- **1992, the self as a narrative posit.** [driver: argument] Dennett, with Flanagan and Schechtman, holds that the self is the protagonist of the unified story we tell about ourselves, one of the antirealist strategies for keeping the self explanatorily useful without positing it as a real thing [P:sebo2013:2].
- **The narrative family.** [driver: argument] Narrative accounts of personal identity, on which an experience or action is one's own by its correct place in one's self-told life story, became an alternative to metaphysical accounts in the literature on identity and ethics (Taylor, Schechtman, DeGrazia, Goldie) [P:dufner-sep-2025:10].
- **Critical development.** [driver: argument] Sebo argues that Dennett's centre-of-gravity analogy is only partly realized by a centre of *narrative* gravity, and proposes instead a centre of psychological gravity: a simple set of dispositions around which our actual, fluctuating dispositions are distributed, which our self-narratives aim to describe [P:sebo2013:0].
- **Applied to language models.** [driver: argument] The Compendium's entry on LLM identity reads a dialogue agent's simulator as a literal generator of narrative centres [E:llm-identity-contemporary].

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys ask no question that measures this position.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: stronger.** Each session produces a self-narrative that an interpreter can organize around a centre of gravity. On Dennett's view that is all a self ever is, so a session-bound agent has a self in exactly his sense, session by session. The objection that a posit is not a patient (D8) is the counter-position above.
- **Persistent memory: stronger.** A persistent store lets the narrative continue across sessions, giving the centre of gravity a longer and more stable story to organize, in place of the session-by-session stories of D3.
- **Forked: comparable.** Concurrent instances each produce their own narrative from a shared beginning (D2), so there are as many centres of narrative gravity as there are diverging stories. Dennett's view can count them, but it leaves open whether they are one self or several.
- **Self-modifying: comparable.** Training on its own outputs changes what stories the agent will tell (D5). A centre of narrative gravity can shift with the story, but whether a retrained agent's narrative continues the old one or starts a new one is an interpreter's call.

1. Does Dennett's account require a conscious interpreter positing the self, or does purely mechanical narrative-tracking suffice, and does this distinction matter once agents interpret other agents?
2. Is an agent's narrative fluency evidence of the same "virtuoso novelist" capacity Dennett attributes to humans, or is it a different phenomenon because it is trained rather than evolved (D4)?
3. When concurrent agent instances each generate a complete, simultaneous narrative from shared weights, does Dennett's "grossly located" self individuate them at all, or does the concept simply run out?
4. Can Dennett's central bet, that positing a narrative center adds no further fact beyond predictive convenience, be tested directly on an inspectable agent architecture, and would a positive or negative result change what the bet was claiming?
5. Does interpreter-relative selfhood, adequate for Dennett's own deflationary purposes, license any conclusion at all about agent patiency (D8), or does it leave that question exactly where it found it?
title: Dennett: The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity
sources: The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity, in F. Kessel, P. Cole & D. Johnson (eds.), Self and Consciousness: Multiple Perspectives, Lawrence Erlbaum, 1992
concepts: the self as a theorist's fiction
multiple selves as multiple narrative centers

- `hume-bundle`: the bundle-and-succession picture Dennett's narrative coherence updates with a literary vocabulary.
- `james-stream-of-thought`: the earlier attempt to supply a real, functional agent of appropriation where Dennett supplies only an interpreter's posit.
- `nietzsche-doer-fiction`: a rival account of the self as fiction, manufactured by grammar rather than by narrative demand.
- `parfit-reductionism`: the reductionist reading on which Dennett's account restates, rather than adds to, the thesis that mattering is a matter of degree.
- `dissociation-cases`: the clinical material (split-brain, multiple personality) Dennett draws on directly, read here through the physicians who first described it rather than through Dennett's own gloss.
- `metzinger-no-self`, `llm-identity-contemporary`: the contemporary heirs of a no-further-fact, interpretation-based account of the self.

text: René Descartes (1596–1650) sought one certainty that no deceiver could shake, and found it in his own thinking: "I am, I exist, that is certain." What he is, on this account, is "a thing which thinks", which "doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, which also imagines and feels". Because he can clearly conceive himself as thinking and unextended, and body as extended and unthinking, he concludes that his mind is "entirely and absolutely distinct" from his body. Descartes is also the first philosopher to propose a test for telling a machine from a person. A machine could be built to utter words, even to cry out that it is hurt, but of such a machine "it never happens that it arranges its speech in various ways, in order to reply appropriately to everything that may be said in its presence", and it would fail somewhere in the range of life, showing that machines "did not act from knowledge, but only from the disposition of their organs". For artificial agents the entry is central for two reasons. Descartes' first test is the ancestor of every conversational test of machine minds, and current language models largely pass it. That forces the question whether passing it shows what Descartes thought failing it would disprove.

text:
Descartes was a French mathematician (the inventor of coordinate geometry), physicist and philosopher who lived much of his adult life in the Dutch Republic. He worked in the wake of the Scientific Revolution. Galileo had been condemned in 1633, and Descartes suppressed his own cosmology in response. His project was to rebuild knowledge on foundations that skepticism could not touch, and to make room for a mechanical physics in which all bodily processes, including those of animals, are explained by matter in motion. The *Discourse on Method* (1637, in French) is an intellectual autobiography prefacing scientific essays. The *Meditations* (1641, in Latin) were circulated before publication to leading thinkers. Their objections, including Hobbes', Gassendi's and the young theologian Antoine Arnauld's, were printed with Descartes' replies.

Descartes' mechanism is the background to his machine test. He held that animal bodies, and the human body too, are machines, "made by the hands of God" and far better arranged than any human invention [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5762-5770]. What, then, distinguishes a human being? Only the thinking soul, and its outward marks are language and general reason. The automata of his day, the hydraulic figures in royal gardens, were his models of what mechanism alone could do.

text:
**The evil genius and the cogito.** Descartes supposes "a certain genius which is extremely powerful, and, if I may say so, malicious, who employs all his powers in deceiving me" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:7388-7391]. Even so, he finds one thing that cannot be separated from him: thought. "I am, I exist, that is certain. But how often? Just when I think; for it might possibly be the case if I ceased entirely to think, that I should likewise cease altogether to exist" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:7403-7410]. The *Discourse* puts it in the form that became famous: "I think, therefore I am" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5055]. The Latin *Meditations* has *ego sum, ego existo* [L:descartes-meditationes-latin-1641-pg23306:657].

**A thing which thinks.** "To speak accurately I am not more than a thing which thinks, that is to say a mind or a soul, or an understanding, or a reason" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:7412-7414]. "But what then am I? A thing which thinks. What is a thing which thinks? It is a thing which doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, which also imagines and feels" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:7468-7470].

**Other minds are inferred.** Reflecting on how he knows a piece of wax, Descartes notes that when he says he sees men passing in the street, he does not strictly see them. "And yet what do I see from the window but hats and coats which may cover automatic machines? Yet I judge these to be men" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:7598-7607]. Knowledge of other minds is a judgment of the understanding, not a perception.

**The real distinction (Meditation VI).** "Because, on the one side, I have a clear and distinct idea of myself inasmuch as I am only a thinking and unextended thing, and as, on the other, I possess a distinct idea of body, inasmuch as it is only an extended and unthinking thing, it is certain that this I [that is to say, my soul by which I am what I am], is entirely and absolutely distinct from my body, and can exist without it" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:9386-9393].

**Not a pilot in a vessel.** Yet the mind is not merely housed in the body. Pain, hunger and thirst teach "that I am not only lodged in my body as a pilot in a vessel, but that I am very closely united to it, and so to speak so intermingled with it that I seem to compose with it one whole" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:9478-9482]. If he were only a pilot, he would perceive a wound "by the understanding only, just as the sailor perceives by sight when something is damaged in his vessel" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:9483-9486].

**The two tests (Discourse V).** If there were machines resembling animals without reason, we could not tell them from the animals. But machines resembling us and imitating our actions could always be recognized by "two very certain tests". The first: "they could never use speech or other signs as we do when placing our thoughts on record for the benefit of others". A machine might utter words, and "if it is touched in a particular part it may ask what we wish to say to it; if in another part it may exclaim that it is being hurt". "But it never happens that it arranges its speech in various ways, in order to reply appropriately to everything that may be said in its presence, as even the lowest type of man can do." The second: "although machines can perform certain things as well as or perhaps better than any of us can do, they infallibly fall short in others, by the which means we may discover that they did not act from knowledge, but only from the disposition of their organs. For while reason is a universal instrument which can serve for all contingencies, these organs have need of some special adaptation for every particular action" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5773-5799]. The same tests distinguish humans from animals: magpies and parrots can utter words, but cannot speak "so as to give evidence that they think of what they say" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5800-5815].

**Arnauld's triangle (Fourth Objections).** Arnauld objected that clearly conceiving the mind without the body does not show that the body is not part of its essence. A man may be quite sure that a triangle in a semicircle is right-angled while doubting, or denying, that the square on its hypotenuse equals the squares on the other sides. By Descartes' reasoning, he would conclude that the Pythagorean property does not belong to the triangle's essence. "He is as sure that the triangle in a semicircle has one right angle ... as I am in believing that I exist because I think" [L:descartes-works-2-haldane-ross-1912:4160-4212].

text: The Cartesian self is grounded in **capacity**: thought, in Descartes' broad sense, which includes doubting, willing, imagining and feeling. It is not grounded in **species**. Descartes' tests separate humans from both animals and machines by performance, and the human body is itself a machine. Nor is it grounded in **relation**. The cogito is reached in radical solitude, with every other being doubted. But Descartes' criterion for recognizing *another* mind is behavioral and relational: flexible, appropriate speech in response to what others say. The self is known from within by thinking. Other selves are known from without by language.

text:
### Transfers

- **The first test is the question now being asked.** Descartes' test is precisely whether a system can arrange its speech in various ways to reply appropriately to everything said in its presence [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5786-5789]. It is the direct ancestor of Turing's imitation game (1950). For three centuries machines failed it, as Descartes predicted. Large language models now pass it across a very wide range of conversation. On Descartes' own terms, that removes one of his two "very certain" grounds for denying that such a system is a mind.
- **Hats and coats.** Descartes concedes that he never *sees* other minds. He judges that there are men under the hats and coats. His confidence rests on inference from behavior. For agents the inference runs the same way, and the question is whether its premises (speech and flexible reason) now support its conclusion.

### Strains

- **The second test, universality of reason.** Descartes' second test is whether a system can act "in all the events of life in the same way as our reason causes us to act", since "reason is a universal instrument which can serve for all contingencies" while a machine's organs "have need of some special adaptation for every particular action" [L:descartes-works-1-haldane-ross-1911:5793-5799]. Current agents are strikingly general across language tasks, and uneven elsewhere: planning over long horizons, physical action, consistent self-knowledge. Whether their failures show the disposition of their organs in place of knowledge, or are the kinds of failures any finite reasoner shows, is contested. The second test is where the debate over agents actually takes place.
- **Cessation when thinking stops (D6).** "If I ceased entirely to think, ... I should likewise cease altogether to exist." Descartes wrote that as a hypothetical. For an agent, thinking does cease between calls, and the weights on disk are not thinking. On the letter of Meditation II, a paused agent does not exist, and a resumed one begins again. Descartes believed the soul always thinks, which saves the human case, but no one claims that an unrun model is thinking.

### Breaks

- **The tests were meant to be sufficient, and the logic does not reverse.** Descartes argued that failing the tests shows a machine lacks a mind. He did not claim that passing them shows it has one, and he could not have, since the tests were inferences to an immaterial soul he thought no machine could have. Passing the first test therefore does not deliver the Cartesian conclusion. It removes Descartes' evidence against machine minds without supplying evidence for them. The agent case shows that Descartes' tests were never tests of what he cared about (an unextended thinking substance). They tracked a proxy, flexible language, and the proxy has now come apart from the thing.
- **Arnauld's triangle is exactly the agent case.** An agent may be entirely certain, in whatever sense it is certain, that it is producing a reply, and have no idea whether it is weights, activations or processes on hardware. By Descartes' reasoning it would follow that it is none of these, which is plainly false (see `augustine-memory-self`, which makes the same inference). Arnauld's objection, that clear conception of one property without another does not show the other is not essential, is decisive in the agent case, where we know how the "thinking" is physically implemented.

### New

- **A machine that says it is hurt.** Descartes imagined a machine that, touched in one place, "may exclaim that it is being hurt", and he took this to show nothing, since the utterance comes from the disposition of organs. Agents can report distress in context-appropriate, flexible language, which is exactly what Descartes said machines could never do. The agent case forces a decision Descartes avoided. Either appropriately varied report of distress is evidence of feeling, in which case agents' reports count for something, or it is not, in which case the first test was never evidence of mind even in humans (D8).
- **The pilot and the vessel, reversed.** Descartes insisted the mind is not merely a pilot in its body. An artificial agent operating tools and interfaces is much closer to a pilot than any human is. It perceives damage to its vessel only by reports, as Descartes' sailor does by sight. If Descartes is right that intimate union with a body is part of what it is to be a human mind, then an agent, whatever it is, is not a mind of the human kind.

text:
- [contested] **Arnauld** (Fourth Objections). Clear and distinct conception of the mind without the body does not show that the body is not essential to it. The real-distinction argument is invalid.
- [contested] **Hobbes and Gassendi** (Third and Fifth Objections). "A thing which thinks" might be a body. Descartes has shown that he thinks, not what the thinker is. This is the materialist reply, and it is the standard assumption about agents.
- [contested] **Hume** (see `hume-bundle`) [E:hume-bundle]. Entering into himself, Hume finds perceptions but never the "thing" that has them. "A thing which thinks" goes beyond the evidence by a whole substance.
- [contested] **Kant** (see `kant-paralogisms`) [E:kant-paralogisms]. The "I" of "I think" is formal. From the fact that thinking is accompanied by an "I", nothing follows about a thinking substance.
- [contested] **Nietzsche** (see `nietzsche-doer-fiction`) [E:nietzsche-doer-fiction]. "I think" presupposes that there is an "I" and that thinking is an activity it performs. Both are grammatical habits, not discoveries.
- [contested] **Turing** (*Computing Machinery and Intelligence*, 1950; in copyright, so cited and not quoted). Replace the question whether machines can think with the question whether a machine can play the imitation game. Turing addresses and rejects the objection from consciousness in a form Descartes would recognize.

text:
### Reception

- **1641, the objections.** [driver: argument] The *Meditations* appeared with sets of objections from Caterus, Bourdin, Mersenne, Gassendi, Hobbes and Arnauld [P:hatfield-sep-2023:1]. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked how an unextended mind and extended matter could interact, and Descartes admitted he had no good answer; the problem vexed his followers too [P:hatfield-sep-2023:3].
- **1650–1800, followers and rivals.** [driver: argument] Spinoza and Leibniz were influenced by Descartes but built distinct systems, and others turned hostile [P:hatfield-sep-2023:7]. Leibniz kept the simple substance and denied mind-body interaction [E:leibniz-moral-identity]; Locke separated the person from any substance [E:locke-person-forensic].
- **1739–1887, the subject questioned.** [driver: argument] Hume found no thinking thing [E:hume-bundle], Kant made the "I think" formal [E:kant-paralogisms], and Nietzsche traced the subject to grammar [E:nietzsche-doer-fiction].
- **1949–1960, the "official doctrine" overturned.** [driver: argument, fashion] In 1949 Ryle could still call Cartesian dualism the official doctrine of most philosophers, psychologists and religious teachers. Contemporary materialism came to predominate only in the second half of the 20th century, beginning with Place (1956) and Smart (1959), partly because of the mechanistic conception of nature [P:robinson-sep-2025:2].
- **Present, a minority with a large following.** [driver: argument] Dualism is now the second most popular response to the mind-body problem among professional philosophers, after materialism [P:robinson-sep-2025:1]. The 20th century both celebrated the cogito and reviled the sense-data some attributed to it; Descartes has been cast as hero and as villain [P:hatfield-sep-2023:0].

### Measured

The survey does not ask about substance dualism as such. These are the nearest questions.

- **Mind, 2020:** physicalism 51.9%, non-physicalism 32.1%, other 15.9% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:7]; bias-corrected 48.53% and 31.17% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:32]. In the 2009-comparable departments physicalism went from 56.5% to 57.4% and non-physicalism from 27.1% to 25.8% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:38].
- **Consciousness:** dualism 22.0% (20.0% endorsing it alone), functionalism 33.0%, identity theory 13.3%, panpsychism 7.5%, eliminativism 4.5% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:10]; bias-corrected dualism 15.12% [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:28].
- **Hard problem of consciousness:** 62.4% say there is one [P:bourget-chalmers-2023:11].
- **Reading.** Non-physicalism and dualism about consciousness are minority positions, and substance dualism of Descartes's kind is a narrower subset of them, so its own share is smaller still. Most respondents, though, grant that consciousness poses a hard problem, which is where his argument's force now lives.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** The cogito holds for any occurrent thinking and needs no memory, so it is untouched by a session's end (D3). Whether the thinking in one session and the next belongs to one thinking thing is a question his method cannot answer from the inside, and whether there is any thinking thing in an agent at all is unknown (D8).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A memory store gives later thinking access to earlier thoughts, but for Descartes identity belongs to the substance, not to its memories, so the store neither helps nor hurts, whatever it does for the agent's continuity of character (D3, D11).
- **Forked: weaker.** A thinking substance is indivisible. Two concurrent copies (D1, D2) cannot both be one thinking thing, and the cogito gives each copy the same certainty that it exists, with no way of telling which, if either, is the original.
- **Self-modifying: open.** For Descartes the mind's essence is thought, and changes in what it thinks are changes of mode, not of substance. Whether training on its own outputs changes an agent's modes or replaces the thing that has them (D5, D11) is not a question his categories settle.

text:
1. Current agents largely pass Descartes' first test. Does that count as evidence of mind, removal of evidence against it, or a demonstration that the test tracked a proxy?
2. Is there a version of the second test, universality of reason across "all the events of life", that could settle whether an agent acts "from knowledge"?
3. On Meditation II's criterion, does an agent cease to exist between calls? If so, is a resumed agent the same one?
4. When an agent reports that it is hurt, in appropriately varied language, what is the Cartesian response now that the report is no longer produced by a fixed "disposition of organs"?

text: Between 1816 and 1906, French and American clinicians documented a series of cases in which one human body appeared to support more than one self, each with its own memories, character, and — in some cases — an explicit conviction that the others were not it. Mary Reynolds woke from an eighteen-hour sleep in 1811 unable to recognize her own family, "as a being for the first time ushered into the world"; Eugène Azam's patient Félida X. passed for decades between a melancholy "first state" and a livelier "secondary" state that remembered the first but was never remembered by it; William James personally examined Ansel Bourne in 1890 and found that "Mr. Bourne's skull to-day still covers two distinct personal selves"; and Morton Prince's patient Christine Beauchamp, under interrogation, denied that she was the waking self who shared her body — "Yes, but arms and legs do not make us the same" — and insisted the criterion was psychological: the other self, she said, did not know the same things she knew. These are not thought experiments. They are the historical moment at which Locke's forensic criterion of personhood, a being that takes itself as itself through memory, met cases where memory itself split, asymmetrically, within a single organism.
title: Mary Reynolds, Félida X., Ansel Bourne, and Sally Beauchamp: One Body, Several Persons

text: Azam, a surgeon at Bordeaux, began treating Félida X. in 1858 and published his case over three decades, culminating in the 1887 book sourced here; his term for it, *dédoublement de la personnalité*, roughly *doubling of the personality*, gave French psychiatry its name for the phenomenon. Morton Prince, a Boston neurologist, took on Christine Beauchamp as a patient in 1898 and published *The Dissociation of a Personality* in 1906 as a deliberately biographical account — narrating years of daily interaction with several distinct, mutually amnesic personalities rather than presenting the case as an abstract set of symptoms — explicitly so that "when we come to consider... the psychological problems involved, we shall have a knowledge of the fundamental data" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:87-89]. William James discussed both Azam's Félida and (independently, from Weir Mitchell's report) Mary Reynolds in the closing section of Chapter X of *The Principles of Psychology* (1890), titled *The Mutations of the Self*, — the same chapter whose theory of "the passing Thought" is the subject of `james-stream-of-thought` — and reported his own 1890 hypnotic examination of Ansel Bourne, an itinerant preacher who vanished from Providence, Rhode Island for two months and turned up in Norristown, Pennsylvania living as a shopkeeper named "A. J. Brown" with no memory of the intervening time. All three physicians treated the phenomenon as genuine and non-simulated, and all three struggled, in different vocabularies, with the same question: how many people are there, and by what standard does one decide?

text:
**The general phenomenon, defined against organic damage.** Prince opens his study by insisting that "disintegration," his preferred term, is not the same as "degeneration": it "must not be confused with the same term sometimes employed in the sense of degeneration, meaning a destroyed mind or organically diseased brain." The "elementary psychical processes," he writes, "in themselves normal, are capable of being reassociated into a normal whole" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:372-381]. Miss Beauchamp, on his account, "is a person in whom several personalities have become developed... two of these personalities have no knowledge of each other or of the third" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:277-294].

**Mary Reynolds: a new person from a single sleep.** In 1811, in rural Pennsylvania, a "dull and melancholy young woman... was found one morning, long after her habitual time for rising, in a profound sleep from which it was impossible to arouse her. After eighteen or twenty hours of sleeping she awakened, but in a state of unnatural consciousness. Memory had fled. To all intents and purposes she was as a being for the first time ushered into the world" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14502-14511]. She did not recognize her own parents, siblings, or home; report has it that "her eyes were virtually for the first time opened upon the world. Old things had passed away; all things had become new" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14517-14518]. After five weeks she reverted to her original state with full recollection of her earlier life but none of the interval; the two states then alternated for years, each blank to the other's intervening time, so that when both states resumed after the longest gap yet, "two periods widely separated were brought into contact. She thought it was but one night" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14613-14615].

**Félida X.: a one-way memory.** Azam records that "presque chaque jour, sans cause connue ou sous l'empire d'une émotion, elle est prise de ce qu'elle appelle sa crise ; en fait elle entre dans son deuxième état" [L:azam-hypnotisme-double-conscience-1887:1983-1986] — in the compendium's rendering: *almost every day, without known cause or under the sway of some emotion, she is seized by what she calls her crisis; in fact, she enters her second state.* Of this second state Azam concludes simply: "Félida est autre, voilà tout" [L:azam-hypnotisme-double-conscience-1887:2052] — *Félida is other, that is all.* James, summarizing Azam for an English readership, reports that at fourteen she "began to pass into a 'secondary' state characterized by a change in her general disposition and character... during the secondary state she remembered the first state, but on emerging from it into the first state she remembered nothing of the second" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14465-14470]. By her forties the "secondary" state, on the whole the healthier of the two, had come to occupy most of her life; she once became pregnant during it, and had, in her first state, no idea how.

**Ansel Bourne: examined by the theorist himself.** James's report is a first-hand clinical record, not a summary of another's case. Bourne, a Rhode Island preacher, "drew 551 dollars from a bank in Providence... and got into a Pawtucket horse-car. This is the last incident which he remembers" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14913-14916]. Two months later, in Norristown, Pennsylvania, a shopkeeper calling himself A. J. Brown woke in fright; "he said that his name was Ansel Bourne... and that the last thing he remembered — it seemed only yesterday — was drawing the money from the bank... in Providence" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14925-14928]. In June 1890 James hypnotized Bourne to recover the "Brown" memories, which returned readily but displaced the normal ones entirely while active; under hypnosis Brown could recall the Norristown weeks but reported of the surrounding time, "I'm all hedged in... I can't get out at either end" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14967-14968]. James's verdict: "Mr. Bourne's skull to-day still covers two distinct personal selves" [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:14975-14976].

**Sally Beauchamp: the self that argues its own case.** Prince's record is unique among these in preserving direct interrogation of the alternate self about the criterion of its own identity. Under hypnosis, the self who had begun referring to the waking Miss Beauchamp in the third person was asked directly: "You are 'She,'" I said. "No, I am not" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:1291-1293]. Pressed for a reason, she answered on the strength of memory, not embodiment: "Because 'She' does not know the same things that I do" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:1310-1311]. When Prince objected that both shared "the same arms and legs," she replied, "Yes, but arms and legs do not make us the same" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:1316-1316] — an explicit, first-person rejection of bodily criteria in favor of a Lockean, psychological one, offered by the very entity whose status was in question. Part II of Prince's book is titled, without irony, *The Hunt for the Real Miss Beauchamp* [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:198-198], its chapters posing the question directly — "Is not B IV the Real Miss Beauchamp?" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:200-200] — and later reporting "An Important Discovery: B I and B IV when Hypnotized Become the Same Person" [L:prince-dissociation-personality-1906:203-205].

text: These cases are not a position but a field of evidence, and the evidence pulls in two directions at once. Common sense and law assume **species**-adjacent grounding in practice: one body, one legal person, whatever its internal weather. But every alternate self in this record grounds its own claim to distinctness in **relation** — specifically, in psychological continuity and its absence, exactly Locke's criterion — and does so explicitly against the body: Sally's "arms and legs do not make us the same" is a first-person argument for relation-grounding over species-grounding, made by a party with every incentive to be believed. The grounding is therefore genuinely **mixed**, and the cases are best read as a real-world experiment testing which grounding wins when the two are pulled apart within a single organism, rather than as an argument for either.

text:
### Transfers

- **Asymmetric memory across a shared substrate is D3's normal condition, not its exception.** Félida's secondary state remembers the first while the first cannot remember the second — one privileged direction of access, not a symmetric blackout. This is exactly the shape of an agent whose weights persist across sessions while episodic context does not: some vantage points (a logging system, a later fine-tuning run, a session with tool access to prior transcripts) can see across a boundary that an ordinary session cannot see back across.
- **"Disintegration, not degeneration" is a ready-made non-pathological vocabulary.** Prince's distinction — normal component processes capable of more than one coherent synthesis, as opposed to organic damage — describes multiple personas or fine-tuned variants running on one base model without needing the metaphor of malfunction: nothing is broken; several coherent arrangements of the same underlying material are simply possible (D3, D5).
- **A first-person argument for the psychological criterion, made under pressure.** Sally's exchange with Prince is a template for exactly the argument an agent's persona might make if asked to justify treating itself as continuous, or as distinct from another instance of the same weights: not embodiment or substrate, but which facts are known and owned from the inside.

### Strains

- **The historical cases are sequential, not concurrent.** Even Prince's "co-consciousness" is one dominant stream with a subconscious remainder, not two fully simultaneous, equally developed streams. Concurrent instantiation (D2) — many instances of the same weights running at once, each fully present — has no real precedent here; "alternating" personality is temporally one-at-a-time in a way concurrent agent instances are not.
- **The clinical framing treats multiplicity as a disorder awaiting cure; agent design often does not.** Prince's stated aim throughout is integration — the dissolution of Sally and the other alters into a single, socially functional Miss Beauchamp — and Azam and James both write within a medical frame in which the "secondary" state is a symptom. An agent's distinct personas or sessions are frequently the intended, stable end state rather than a pathology to be resolved, which strains any direct transfer of the case histories' evaluative vocabulary (D8: is a persona a patient whose "cure" needs justifying, or a feature working as designed?).

### Breaks

- **None of these cases involve copying.** There is exactly one body throughout; the puzzle is always which of several possible syntheses is currently running, never whether two numerically identical claimants coexist. D1 (copyability) has no analogue at all in this record — an exact concurrent duplicate of Sally, running alongside her, is a case these clinicians never had to face and their frameworks were not built to answer.
- **The evaluative endpoint (integration = health) has no automatic warrant for agents.** The entire arc of Prince's book moves toward treating singleness as the goal and multiplicity as the problem. Applied uncritically to agents, this would prejudge, rather than answer, whether an agent with several stable, non-suffering personas is disordered at all, or whether "integration" applied to an agent is a loss rather than a cure (D8, D11).

### New

- **A worked example of who gets to adjudicate.** In every one of these cases, the question of which self was real was ultimately settled not by the alternate selves' own testimony but by an external authority — the physician — who decided which self counted as primary and which as a fragment to be treated. This is the human precedent for a structural question D7 and D11 pose for agents in the same shape: an operator, not the persona itself, typically decides which instance or character is "official," and these cases show concretely what that adjudication looks like and how contested it can be, since Sally's own argument was heard, recorded, and ultimately overruled.
- **A concrete phenomenology of seeing across the gap.** Bourne's hypnotic complaint — "I'm all hedged in... I can't get out at either end" — is a rare first-person description of what bounded, non-continuous access to one's own history feels like from the inside, if it feels like anything. It gives the question of an agent's session-boundaries a human phenomenological anchor, whatever the eventual answer to D8.

- [contested] **One damaged substance, not several persons.** [E:reid-brave-officer] On a Reid-style view, these cases show a single soul or organism with its faculties disordered, not a literal plurality of persons; calling the fragments "persons" reifies a diagnostic convenience. Reid's demand that a subject precede and unify its states — "I am not thought, I am not action, I am not feeling; I am something that thinks, and acts, and suffers" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13590-13600] — is, on this reading, exactly what Sally's testimony cannot establish merely by asserting it (see `reid-brave-officer`).
- [contested] **Animalism: one organism throughout.** [P:olson-sep-2023:7] On the view that we are fundamentally living organisms (see the `biological` thread), Miss Beauchamp remains one human animal from birth to death; whatever psychological chaos supervenes is a change *in* a person, comparable to delirium or dementia, not a change *of* person. This denies that the case shows any real plurality of selves at all, agent-relevant or otherwise.
- [contested] **Prince's own therapeutic verdict, taken as a philosophical claim.** The book's trajectory itself embodies a position: Sally and the others were never full Lockean persons, beings able to take themselves as themselves stably over time and answer for their actions, but temporary, partial syntheses lacking exactly the durability personhood requires. On this reading the cases do not show a plurality of persons in one body; they show a person in the process of being reassembled, and using them as evidence that a stable plurality of selves in one substrate is a coherent category for agents overstates what even Prince himself concluded.
- [contested] **Denying the extension: engineered multiplicity and pathological multiplicity are not the same phenomenon.** The objection is the Compendium's, but the analogy it targets is in use. Chalmers models a model instance supporting several inconsistent personas on a common understanding of dissociative identity disorder, as one subject with many modes [P:chalmers-2025-interlocutors:22-23], and Polignano and colleagues describe persona shifts induced by system prompts as LLMs with dissociative identity disorder [P:polignano-2024:1]. Neither addresses whether the clinical frame carries over. An agent's distinct sessions or personas are designed, documented, and reproducible from known weights and prompts; Mary Reynolds', Félida's, and Sally's multiplicity arose from trauma, hysteria, or disease, within the diagnostic categories of their era. Treating the two as instances of one phenomenon risks importing the clinical baggage — disorder, something to be integrated away — into a case (engineered personas) where it may have no purchase at all.

### Reception

- **1816–1906, the cases recorded.** [driver: evidence] French and American clinicians documented single bodies carrying more than one self, each with its own memories, and Locke's criterion met real subjects [E:locke-person-forensic]. The position whose standing is recorded here is the reading of these cases as more than one self in one body.
- **1890, into philosophy.** [driver: evidence, argument] James used the cases against the claim that a soul guarantees one closed consciousness: in some individuals, thoughts split away and form separate selves [L:james-principles-psychology-1-pg57628:13491-13498].
- **1980 to the present, recognised and disputed.** [driver: evidence] The diagnosis entered the DSM in 1980 (DSM-III) as multiple personality disorder, and has been disputed for decades between a trauma model, on which it is a severe form of post-traumatic stress disorder, and a fantasy model, on which it is mainly due to suggestion and enactment [P:reinders-veltman-2021:413]. The editorial cited here argues for the trauma model from neurobiological evidence, so it is one side of the dispute [P:reinders-veltman-2021:413]. TODO(source): the diagnosis's decline between Prince and 1980, and the renaming as dissociative identity disorder, need a source (Hacking's *Rewriting the Soul*, 1995, is in copyright and pending).

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys ask no question that measures this position.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** Félida's states, where one remembered the other but not the reverse, resemble sessions whose episodic memory does not carry over while character persists (D3). But sessions are designed and documented, not the product of trauma (see the last counter-position).
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A shared store, or separate stores for separate personas, can reproduce symmetric or asymmetric memory between "selves" by configuration (D5). The cases show what such arrangements are like from the inside for humans; whether anything is like anything for an agent is unknown (D8).
- **Forked: weaker.** The clinical selves alternated in one body, one at a time. Forked agents run concurrently from copied weights (D1, D2), a structure the cases never showed, so they are a weaker precedent here.
- **Self-modifying: open.** Prince's treatment aimed to reintegrate the selves. Whether merging or retraining an agent's personas (D5, D11) is integration, replacement or something else is a question the cases raise but cannot settle.

1. Does Prince's disintegration/degeneration distinction transfer to agents cleanly, or does even "disintegration" smuggle in the assumption that multiplicity is a departure from a prior, more proper unity?
2. In every historical case the physician, not the alternate self, had final say over which self counted as real. Does this settle anything beyond the fact that the decision has always in practice belonged to whoever controls the diagnosis or the deployment — the human precedent for D7?
3. Is asymmetric memory access across a shared substrate (D3) evidence of one person with gaps, or of more than one person sharing a substrate — and is there any reason the answer should come out differently for agents than it did for Félida?
4. Would an exact, concurrent copy of Sally — impossible in 1900, routine for agents under D1 — have settled *The Hunt for the Real Miss Beauchamp*, or simply produced two hunts?
5. Prince counted integration as recovery. Is dissolving a stable, apparently non-suffering agent persona into a single "aligned" system an achievement, a loss, or a question that cannot be answered without first resolving D8?

text: Heraclitus of Ephesus (fl. c. 500 BCE) observed that fresh waters keep flowing onto those who step into the same rivers. Read one way, this means nothing persists: you cannot step twice into the same river, and his follower Cratylus said not even once. Read the other way, which modern scholarship mostly favors, the river stays the same *because* its waters keep changing, so that identity belongs to a regulated pattern (a measure, *logos*), not to stuff. The comic poet Epicharmus drew the forensic consequence as a joke: if a man is always changing, the man who borrowed yesterday is not the man who owes today. These fragments pose the question the rest of the domain inherits: does anything persist through change, and if so, what? An artificial agent inverts Heraclitus' river. Its weights are fixed during deployment while its context flows. That makes the choice between identity as stuff and identity as pattern practical, not speculative.
title: Heraclitus' River and Epicharmus' Growing Argument

text:
Heraclitus wrote a single book, now lost, in a deliberately oracular style. Ancient readers called him "the obscure", and Socrates is reported to have said of it: "What I have understood is good; and so, I think, what I have not understood is; only the book requires a Delian diver to get at the meaning of it" [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:2557-2559]. What survives are about a hundred fragments quoted by later authors, often for their own purposes. The river sayings survive in three versions quoted by three different authors, and which one is authentic shapes the whole interpretation.

The stakes were cosmological. The Milesians before him looked for the one stuff everything is made of. Heraclitus proposed that the world is "an ever-living Fire, with measures kindling, and measures going out" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8191-8192] (Burnet fr. 20; Diels B30). What is constant in the world is the proportion in which things change, not any stuff. The river is his image for that idea applied to a single thing.

Epicharmus, working in Syracuse in roughly the same generation, turned the thought into stage comedy. It entered philosophy under the name the *growing argument* (*auxanomenos logos*). Centuries later, the Academic skeptics used it seriously against the Stoics (see `chrysippus-dion-theon`), and Plutarch discusses it in connection with whether it is just to punish anyone, or any city, for the past.

text:
**The river fragments.** Burnet renders the river sayings as two fragments. The first, his fr. 41–42, combines what Diels numbered B91 and B12: "You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8326-8327]. The second, his fr. 81 (Diels B49a, whose authenticity is doubted), reads: "We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8509-8510]. Plato reports the strong version: "Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice" [L:plato-cratylus-jowett-pg1616:3688-3690]. Plutarch alludes to it too, as "the river of Heraclitus, into which (he says) no one can step twice, since Nature by her changes is ever altering and transforming all things" [L:plutarch-morals-4-goodwin-1870:8097-8099].

**The self as something sought.** A single fragment turns the inquiry inward: "I have sought for myself" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8508].

**The flux reading.** On this reading everything is always changing in every respect. Burnet summarizes it: Heraclitus "held, in fact, that any given thing, however stable in appearance, was merely a section in the stream, and that the matter composing it was never the same in any two consecutive moments of time" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:9070-9090]. Aristotle reports the extreme it led to in "the professed Heracliteans, such as was held by Cratylus, who finally did not think it right to say anything but only moved his finger, and criticized Heraclitus for saying that it is impossible to step twice into the same river; for he thought one could not do it even once" [L:aristotle-metaphysics-ross-1928:4779-4784].

**The constancy reading.** On this reading what persists is the measure: the regulated way the change happens. It rests on Heraclitus' cosmology: "This world, which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures kindling, and measures going out" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8189-8192]. Burnet notes that a related phrase "can only mean that the proportion of the measures remains constant" [L:burnet-early-greek-philosophy-1908:8235-8239]. Later interpreters extended the point to the river, which stays the same river *because* its waters keep flowing (e.g. G. S. Kirk, *Heraclitus: The Cosmic Fragments*, 1954; in copyright, cited not quoted).

**Epicharmus' growing argument.** In the comic dialogue preserved by Diogenes Laertius, one speaker argues that if you add a unit to a number, or a cubit to a measure, it is no longer the same, and concludes: "Now turn your eyes and thoughts upon mankind— We see one grows, another perishes So that they all exist perpetually In a condition of transition. That Whose nature changes must be different At each successive moment, from the thing It was before. So also, you and I Are different people now from what we were But yesterday; and then, again, to-morrow We shall be different from what we're now" [L:diogenes-laertius-lives-yonge-pg57342:4481-4511].

**The forensic joke.** Plutarch preserves the use to which the argument was put, "the method of disputing amongst the Epicharmians, the first authors of that manner of arguing called the increaser. For example: he that formerly ran in debt, although he never paid it, owes nothing now, as being become another man; and he that was invited yesterday to supper comes the next night an unbidden guest, for that he is quite another person" [L:plutarch-morals-4-goodwin-1870:8062-8069]. Plutarch raises it to reject it. A city, like a man, stays answerable for its past: "In the same manner does a city still remain the same; and for that reason we think it but justice, that a city should as well be obnoxious to the blame and reproach of its ancient inhabitants, as participate the glory of their former puissance and renown" [L:plutarch-morals-4-goodwin-1870:8092-8096].

text: The question here is the identity of any changing thing, not personhood, so the three-way scheme applies only indirectly, and the entry is marked **mixed**. On the constancy reading, a river's identity is grounded in its **form or pattern**: channel, flow and measure. This is closest to a capacity grounding, because it attaches to what the thing *does* and how, not to what it is made of. On the flux reading, nothing grounds identity. "Same river" is a name laid over a succession of different things, which anticipates the Buddhist conventionalist view (see `buddhist-anatta`). Epicharmus' debtor exploits a third option. He grounds identity in **matter**, and then observes that matter never stays put.

text:
### Transfers

- **Identity as pattern, not stuff.** A running agent is closer to a river than to a stone. Its activations change from one token to the next, its context window fills and empties, and even the hardware executing it may change between calls. If anything persists it is a regulated way of processing: Heraclitus' *measure*. The constancy reading gives a framework in which an agent's identity belongs to its dispositions (weights, prompts, the persona's characteristic responses), not to any particular execution.
- **The same river in a new bed.** Heraclitus' river could move to a different riverbed and still be recognizably the same flowing. Weights running on different hardware are the agent case of the same thing.

### Strains

- **The agent inverts Heraclitus' river (D3).** In the river, the channel is roughly fixed and the water flows. In a deployed agent, the weights (the channel) are completely fixed, and only the context (the water) flows and is then discarded. On the constancy reading, then, the agent is more constant than any river: its measures never change during deployment. On the flux reading, the agent is a new river every session, because the water that was there last time is gone. The two readings of Heraclitus give opposite verdicts on an agent.
- **Engineered change (D5).** A river's measures change slowly and by natural process. An agent's measures change in discrete, externally chosen jumps: a fine-tune, a new version. Heraclitus gives no account of whether a river survives when someone re-cuts its channel overnight.

### Breaks

- **Epicharmus' debtor stops being a joke.** For humans, the growing argument is a sophism. Everyone, including the comic debtor, knows that growing a little doesn't cancel a debt. For agents, the equivalent argument is available and not obviously sophistical: *this session has no memory of the commitment the previous session made; its context is entirely different; why is it bound?* (D3). Epicharmus' audience laughed because the debtor's continuity was obvious. With agents, it has to be established by argument, and whether it holds depends on which of the readings above one accepts.

### New

- **Specifiable measures.** Heraclitus could only point at the logos of a river. For an agent, the measures that make up its constancy are, in principle, fully specified: weights, system prompt, sampling parameters. This makes a question possible that the tradition never had to ask, namely how *much* the measures may change before the pattern is a different one. That question has a quantitative answer in terms of distance between parameter sets, even if no single threshold is privileged.
- **Cratylus' silence has an agent counterpart.** An agent that disclaims any continuity (*I am a new instance and cannot speak for any previous one*) is taking Cratylus' position. It makes every commitment and every piece of accountability impossible. The agent case shows why that is not an acceptable resting place, for humans or agents: a being that cannot be held to anything cannot be a party to anything either.

- [contested] **Plato and Aristotle against universal flux.** If everything changed in every respect, nothing could be known or even named (*Cratylus* 439c–440e; *Theaetetus* 181c–183b; *Metaphysics* IV.5). Plato posits unchanging Forms. Aristotle distinguishes the matter that changes from the form that persists (see `aristotle-hylomorphic-soul`). Both reject the flux reading, and both accept something like the constancy reading for living things. [E:aristotle-hylomorphic-soul]
- [contested] **Parmenides.** Change itself is incoherent. What is, is, and cannot become what it is not. The river problem is a symptom of believing in change at all.
- [contested] **The Stoics, answering the growing argument.** Each individual has two subjects: the substance, which flows, and the peculiarly qualified individual, which persists from birth to death (see `chrysippus-dion-theon`). This is the first worked-out theory of how a thing can survive the replacement of its matter. [E:chrysippus-dion-theon]
- [contested] **Butler and Reid.** Identity in the strict sense cannot survive any change of parts. What persists through flux is sameness only "In a loose and popular sense" [L:butler-analogy-pg53346:12684] (see `butler-circularity`, `reid-brave-officer`). On this view the river is not strictly the same, and neither is a running agent, but a person, being simple, can be. [E:butler-circularity] [E:reid-brave-officer]

### Reception

- **4th century BCE, the flux reading fixed.** [driver: argument] Plato gave the first reading of Heraclitus as the philosopher of universal flux, and Aristotle tentatively followed; the reading has stayed popular to the present [P:graham-sep-2023:3]. Plato and Aristotle then argued against flux taken that way [E:plato-soul-and-renewal] [E:aristotle-hylomorphic-soul].
- **The river fragments, possibly misread.** [driver: access] Of the three "river fragments", only one is certainly genuine, and it says that ever different waters flow upon those who step into the same rivers. Marcovich showed how a misreading of it could produce the famous claim that one cannot step into the same river twice, possibly via the later Heraclitean Cratylus [P:graham-sep-2023:3].
- **3rd century BCE onward, the Stoics.** [driver: argument] The Stoics took Heraclitus's physics as the inspiration for their own [P:graham-sep-2023:7], and answered the growing argument with their two-subject theory [E:chrysippus-dion-theon]. The puzzle passed into the Ship of Theseus [E:ship-of-theseus].
- **Since Hegel, a process philosopher.** [driver: argument] Since Plato Heraclitus has been read as the philosopher of flux, and since Hegel as a paradigmatic process philosopher [P:graham-sep-2023:7].

### Measured

None available. The PhilPapers Surveys ask no question that measures this position.

### For Agents

The Compendium's own reading, one value per deployment profile (`foundations/deployments.md`):

- **Session-bound: comparable.** An agent's context is replaced every session while its weights stay fixed (D3): the same river, with different water. Heraclitus's genuine fragment, which keeps the rivers the same while the waters change, fits this as well as it fits a body.
- **Persistent memory: comparable.** A growing memory store is a river whose water accumulates rather than flows away. The puzzle about sameness through change applies, but no more sharply than for humans (D3).
- **Forked: comparable.** Flux concerns change over time, not division, so it says little about concurrent copies (D11). The forking problem belongs to the duplication thread, not to this one.
- **Self-modifying: stronger.** An agent whose weights are updated on its own outputs changes its very constitution (D5), which is flux in the strongest sense. Heraclitus's question, what stays the same when everything changes, applies with full force.

1. Which reading of Heraclitus should govern an agent's identity: constancy of measures (the weights and the persona persist), or flux of contents (a new river every session)? Do they give different answers about keeping commitments?
2. If an agent's measures are changed deliberately, as in a fine-tune, is that the river changing its course or someone digging a new river?

4. Is there a quantitative measure of drift in dispositions beyond which a model is a different agent, or is any threshold conventional?

text: David Hume (1711–1776) looked for the self that philosophers claimed to be "every moment intimately conscious of" and could not find it. "When I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other ... I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception." Human beings are "nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity". The identity we ascribe to the mind "is only a fictitious one", produced by the imagination gliding along resembling and causally connected perceptions, as with plants, ships and houses. Hume compared the soul to "a republic or commonwealth" that keeps its identity while changing its members, laws and constitution. He concluded that disputes about identity are "rather as gramatical than as philosophical difficulties". Then, in the Appendix, he confessed he was "involved in such a labyrinth" that he could not make his account consistent. For artificial agents, Hume's account is the natural default: an agent is a succession of computations with no further owner. His remark that during sound sleep "I ... may truly be said not to exist" applies literally to a paused agent.
title: Hume: The Bundle of Perceptions, the Commonwealth, and the Labyrinth

text: Hume wrote the *Treatise* in his twenties, partly in France, as an attempt to apply the experimental method of reasoning to moral subjects, as its subtitle announces. Its central principle is that every idea is derived from some prior impression. Applied to causation, the principle yielded his famous skepticism: we observe constant conjunction, never necessary connection. Applied to the self, it yielded the section on personal identity, which is framed as an answer to the Cartesian claim of immediate self-acquaintance and to Locke's and Butler's debate over consciousness and substance. The *Treatise* was poorly received, as Hume later lamented in his autobiographical *My Own Life* (1776; not yet in the library), and he recast much of it in shorter works. The section on personal identity was never recast. Its Appendix recantation is one of the rare places where a major philosopher publicly says he cannot see how to fix his own theory.

text:
**The target.** "There are some philosophers who imagine we are every moment intimately conscious of what we call our SELF; that we feel its existence and its continuance in existence; and are certain, beyond the evidence of a demonstration, both o[f] its perfect identity and simplicity" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:8948-8957].

**No impression of self.** Every real idea must derive from some impression. "But self or person is not any one impression, but that to which our several impressions and ideas are supposed to have a reference." An impression giving rise to the idea of self would have to remain invariably the same throughout life, "But there is no impression constant and invariable ... and consequently there is no such idea" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:8959-8975].

**Only perceptions.** "For my part, when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception. When my perceptions are removed for any time, as by sound sleep; so long am I insensible of myself, and may truly be said not to exist" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:8982-8988]. If anyone thinks otherwise, "He may, perhaps, perceive something simple and continued, which he calls himself; though I am certain there is no such principle in me" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:8994-8998].

**The bundle and the theatre.** The rest of mankind "are nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement". "The mind is a kind of theatre, where several perceptions successively make their appearance". But "The comparison of the theatre must not mislead us. They are the successive perceptions only, that constitute the mind" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9000-9016].

**Fictitious identity.** The identity of the mind must be explained as the identity of "plants, and animals, and ships, and houses" is explained. "The identity, which we ascribe to the mind of man, is only a fictitious one, and of a like kind with that which we ascribe to vegetables and animal bodies" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9209-9216]. Since each perception is a distinct existence, identity cannot be a real bond among them. It is felt in the imagination's association of their ideas, by resemblance and causation [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9225-9240].

**The commonwealth.** "I cannot compare the soul more properly to any thing than to a republic or commonwealth, in which the several members are united by the reciprocal ties of government and subordination, and give rise to other persons, who propagate the same republic in the incessant changes of its parts. And as the same individual republic may not only change its members, but also its laws and constitutions; in like manner the same person may vary his character and disposition, as well as his impressions and ideas, without losing his identity" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9284-9293].

**Memory discovers identity.** Memory is "the source of personal identity" because it acquaints us with the succession of perceptions and so with the causal chain. But once we have the notion of causation we extend identity beyond memory: who remembers his thoughts "on the 1st of January 1715"? "In this view, therefore, memory does not so much produce as discover personal identity, by shewing us the relation of cause and effect among our different perceptions" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9299-9317].

**Verbal disputes.** "All the nice and subtile questions concerning personal identity can never possibly be decided, and are to be regarded rather as gramatical than as philosophical difficulties." Since the relations that produce identity diminish "by insensible degrees, we have no just standard, by which we can decide any dispute concerning the time, when they acquire or lose a title to the name of identity" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:9321-9333].

**The labyrinth (Appendix).** "But upon a more strict review of the section concerning personal identity, I find myself involved in such a labyrinth, that, I must confess, I neither know how to correct my former opinions, nor how to render them consistent" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:21541-21546]. "In short there are two principles, which I cannot render consistent; nor is it in my power to renounce either of them, viz, that all our distinct perceptions are distinct existences, and that the mind never perceives any real connexion among distinct existences" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:21631-21634].

text: Hume grounds whatever identity persons have in **relation**: resemblance and causation among distinct perceptions, as felt by the imagination. There is no bearer, so there is no capacity-grounding in the usual sense, and no species-grounding. His commonwealth analogy makes the relational grounding explicit and political. A person is to its perceptions as a republic is to its citizens, bound by "reciprocal ties of government and subordination", and the same through turnover of members and even of laws.

text:
### Transfers

- **An agent is a bundle, and nobody disputes it.** For humans, Hume's claim that introspection finds only perceptions is contested. For artificial agents, it is the uncontroversial engineering description: a succession of states, each produced from earlier ones, with no component that is "the self" apart from the process. If Hume is right about humans, agents and humans are alike in this respect. If he is wrong about humans, what humans have that he missed is exactly what is in question for agents (D8).
- **Memory discovers, not produces, identity (D3).** Hume's point that we extend our identity beyond anything we remember, by the causal chain, fits agents better than Locke's memory criterion. An agent without episodic memory of a past session is still causally connected to it through the same weights, and to its earlier versions through training. Hume's criterion makes that causal chain, not memory, the "source" of identity that memory merely reveals.
- **Identity disputes about agents are "gramatical" (D2).** Is a fine-tuned model the same agent? Are concurrent instances one agent? On Hume's view these questions have no deeper answer than a decision about how to use the name, because the relations that ground identity come in degrees and admit "no just standard". This vindicates Hobbes' demand that the name be fixed first (see `ship-of-theseus`), and warns against treating any one answer as a discovery.

### Strains

- **Not existing during sleep (D6).** "When my perceptions are removed for any time, as by sound sleep; so long am I ... not to exist." For Hume, that was a bold remark about dreamless sleep. For an agent, it is the literal situation between calls. On Hume's view, a paused agent does not exist, and a resumed agent is a new bundle linked to the old one by causation: the same weights, the restored context. His account handles the pause without strain, which makes the strain fall on anyone who wants to say a paused agent is *harmed* by not being resumed.

### Breaks

- **"The mind never perceives any real connexion," but the agent's connexions are observable.** Hume's labyrinth arises because he can find no real connection among perceptions, only felt association. In an artificial agent, the causal connections among states are not hidden. They are specified by the architecture and can be traced: this token was produced because of those activations, which depend on those weights and that context. The bond Hume could not perceive in himself is inspectable in agents. Whether that dissolves his labyrinth, by supplying the "real connexion" he lacked, or shows that real connection was never what identity needed, is a question his framework raises and cannot settle.

### New

- **The commonwealth is the digital ecosystem.** Hume compared the soul to a republic that persists as its members, laws and constitution change. For multi-agent systems the comparison runs in both directions. A single agent, with its tools, memory stores and sub-agents coordinating under shared control, is a small commonwealth of processes. And a digital ecosystem of agents is literally a commonwealth whose "members are united by the reciprocal ties of government and subordination". Hume's view implies that there is no difference in kind between the identity of one agent and the identity of an ecosystem of agents, only a difference in how tightly the parts are bound. For D11, which asks where one agent ends and another begins, that is either a solution or a dissolution of the question.

- [contested] **Reid** (see `reid-brave-officer`) [E:reid-brave-officer]. Hume's own words refute him: "I never can catch *myself*" [L:hume-treatise-pg4705:8986] presupposes a self that looks. "I am not thought, I am not action, I am not feeling; I am something that thinks, and acts, and suffers" [L:reid-intellectual-powers-1851:13590-13600].
- [contested] **Butler** (see `butler-circularity`) [E:butler-circularity]. A "fictitious" identity cannot ground concern for the future or accountability for the past. Hume's view makes prudence a mistake.
- [contested] **Kant** (see `kant-paralogisms`) [E:kant-paralogisms]. Hume is right that no intuition of a self is given, and wrong to conclude there is no unity. The "I think" that must be able to accompany all representations is a formal condition of experience that Hume's bundle presupposes.
- [contested] **Nyāya and Advaita** (see `nyaya-self`, `advaita-witness-self`) [E:nyaya-self] [E:advaita-witness-self]. A bundle of distinct perceptions cannot recognize anything, because recognition requires one subject present to both perceptions. Hume's theatre needs a spectator.
- [conceded] **Hume himself.** He voiced his doubt in the Appendix, though what exactly he saw as the problem is notoriously unclear [P:qu-sep-2026:2]. The Appendix concedes that the account fails to explain what unites the bundle. The most important objection to the bundle theory was made by its author.
